# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR DEFENSE/APPELLEE DJURIC TRUCKING, INC.

---

## INTRODUCTION

Your Honor, respectfully, this Court should affirm the trial court's award of attorney's fees to Djuric Trucking, Inc. The plaintiff's arguments, while artfully framed, misapply the doctrines of res judicata and waiver to the unique circumstances of this case. The award of approximately $12,000 in attorney's fees represents a straightforward application of the UIIA's fee provision to a prevailing party—a provision that Evergreen itself drafted and included in the agreement. We ask this Court to reject Evergreen's attempt to escape its contractual obligations through procedural technicalities.

---

## I. RES JUDICATA DOES NOT BAR DJURIC'S FEE CLAIM

Evergreen's res judicata argument fundamentally misunderstands the nature of attorney's fee claims and misapplies Indiana law. While this Court has correctly noted that res judicata prevents piecemeal litigation, the doctrine does not apply where, as here, the fee claim could not have been adjudicated in the original proceeding.

### A. The Fee Claim Was Not ripe for Adjudication in the Original Proceeding

The cornerstone of res judicata is that a claim must have been cognizable and ripe at the time of the prior litigation. In the original action, Djuric was the defendant defending against Evergreen's claim for per diem charges. Djuric successfully obtained summary judgment in its favor, but the claim for attorney's fees was wholly contingent on that outcome. As this Court correctly observed in the first appeal, Evergreen's claim failed because no separate written agreement existed—an issue that went to the merits of Evergreen's case, not to Djuric's entitlement to fees.

The Indiana Court of Appeals has consistently held that a claim is not ripe for adjudication when it depends on a future contingency that may or may not occur. See *Bell v. City of Indianapolis*, 756 N.E.2d 1153, 1161 (Ind. Ct. App. 2001). At the time of the original summary judgment proceedings, Djuric could not have sought fees because it had not yet prevailed. The contingent nature of fee claims distinguishes them from the underlying merits.

Evergreen cites *Small v. Centerre Bank of Indiana*, 51 N.E.3d 716 (Ind. 2016), for the proposition that res judicata applies to claims arising from the same transaction. However, *Small* addressed claims that were actually litigable in the prior proceeding—the plaintiff there had the opportunity to assert its claims but chose not to. That is not the situation here, where Djuric's fee claim arose only upon its victory.

### B. The UIIA Fee Provision Creates a Separate Contractual Right

The UIIA's attorney's fee provision constitutes a separate and independent contractual obligation that arises only when a party prevails in enforcing the agreement. This is not a claim that was embedded in the original litigation—it is a distinct right that accrues post-judgment.

In *Coppolillo v. Estate of Coppolillo*, 876 N.E.2d 767 (Ind. Ct. App. 2007), this Court held that claims arising from separate contractual provisions constitute separate causes of action for res judicata purposes. The UIIA fee provision is precisely such a separate provision—a collateral agreement governing the recovery of litigation costs rather than the substantive dispute over container usage.

### C. Judicial Economy Supports Allowing the Fee Claim

Evergreen invokes judicial economy, but the opposite result promotes true economy. If this Court bars Djuric's fee claim, it signals to all litigants that they must anticipate every possible theory in their initial pleading—even theories that depend on future contingencies. This would paradoxically increase litigation, not decrease it, as parties would over-plead to preserve rights that had not yet accrued.

---

## II. DJURIC DID NOT WAIVE ITS RIGHT TO FEES UNDER THE UIIA

Evergreen's waiver argument fails because it conflates different legal theories and ignores the sequential nature of litigation.

### A. Pursuing Statutory Fees Does Not Constitute Waiver of Contractual Fees

Waiver requires the intentional relinquishment of a known right. See *Keeslin v. Baker*, 571 N.E.2d 565 (Ind. Ct. App. 1991). The record demonstrates that Djuric did not intentionally relinquish its UIIA fee rights.

In the original proceeding, Djuric sought attorney's fees under Indiana Code Section 34-52-1-1, which permits fee awards when a claim is frivolous. This statute addresses the conduct of the litigation itself—whether the opposing party's claim was groundless. The UIIA's fee provision, by contrast, addresses the substantive right of a prevailing party to recover fees as a contractual matter. These are fundamentally different theories serving different purposes.

This Court has recognized that alternative legal theories are not mutually exclusive unless a party makes a deliberate election. In *Bunch v. Citizens Bank of Columbus*, 378 N.E.2d 858 (Ind. Ct. App. 1978), waiver was found where a party explicitly chose one remedy that was inconsistent with another. Here, Djuric's pursuit of statutory fees was not inconsistent with contractual fees—it was simply an additional theory that happened to fail when the trial court found the claim was not frivolous (even though Evergreen lost on the merits).

### B. Djuric Could Not Have Pursued UIIA Fees Until It Prevailed

The UIIA entitles the "prevailing party" to attorney's fees. See Appellee's Appendix at 19. This language unambiguously conditions the fee right on the outcome of the litigation. Djuric could not have sought UIIA fees before obtaining summary judgment because it was not yet a prevailing party.

Evergreen's argument that Djuric should have sought a "conditional or contingent award" in the original proceeding is impractical and unsupported by Indiana law. Trial courts do not award fees contingent on future outcomes when the underlying claim remains unresolved. The proper time to seek UIIA fees is after judgment, when the prevailing party's status is established.

### C. Evergreen's Conduct Undermines Its Waiver Argument

The equities of this case strongly favor Djuric. Evergreen drafted the UIIA and included the fee provision knowing it would apply to any prevailing party—regardless of whether that party was Evergreen or its opponent. Now that Djuric has prevailed, Evergreen seeks to escape the consequence of its own contractual language.

Evergreen cannot complain about gamesmanship when it authored the very agreement thatDjuric now seeks to enforce. The fee provision was not a trap for Evergreen—it was a mutual obligation that applies to both parties. Evergreen's attempt to invoke waiver rings hollow when it was Evergreen that insisted on this provision in the intermodal industry standard agreement.

---

## III. THE AWARD IS CONSISTENT WITH THE UIIA AND INDUSTRY PRACTICE

The UIIA represents a carefully negotiated balance of rights and obligations in the intermodal shipping industry. Its fee provision reflects the understanding that prevailing parties should not bear the cost of enforcing the agreement—regardless of which party prevails.

Evergreen's position, if accepted, would allow parties to include fee-shifting provisions in agreements while simultaneously arguing that such provisions are unenforceable when their opponents prevail. This undermines the basic contract principle that agreements must be enforced according to their terms.

The trial court awarded approximately $12,000 in fees—a reasonable amount for defending against a $34,000 claim through summary judgment and appeal. This Court should defer to the trial court's calculation absent an abuse of discretion.

---

## CONCLUSION

Your Honor, the trial court's award of attorney's fees should be affirmed. Djuric prevailed in the underlying litigation, the UIIA provides for attorney's fees to the prevailing party, and no procedural bar prevents enforcement of this contractual right. Res judicata does not apply because the fee claim was not ripe for adjudication in the original proceeding. Waiver does not apply because Djuric did not intentionally relinquish its UIIA rights—it simply pursued an alternative theory that proved unsuccessful.

Evergreen drafted the UIIA, included the fee provision, and cannot now escape its obligations through procedural maneuvering. The trial court's award is just, reasonable, and supported by the contract. We respectfully request that this Court affirm the award of attorney's fees to Djuric Trucking, Inc.

---

Respectfully submitted,

**Counsel for Defendant/Appellee Djuric Trucking, Inc.**

**FINAL RULING**

The trial court’s award of attorney’s fees to Djuric Trucking, Inc. is **AFFIRMED**.

**ANALYSIS**

This Court has reviewed the closing arguments submitted by Evergreen Shipping Agency Corp. (“Evergreen”) and Djuric Trucking, Inc. (“Djuric”). Upon careful consideration of the applicable law and the arguments presented, we find that Djuric’s claim for attorney’s fees is not barred by res judicata, nor did Djuric waive its right to such fees. The trial court’s award is consistent with the terms of the Uniform Intermodal Interchange and Facilities Access Agreement (“UIIA”) and Indiana precedent.

**I. Res Judicata**

Evergreen argues that res judicata bars Djuric’s fee claim because it arises from the same transaction as the underlying dispute regarding per diem charges. While we agree that res judicata is a vital doctrine promoting judicial economy, it does not apply where a claim was not ripe for adjudication at the time of the prior proceeding.

Res judicata prevents the relitigation of claims that were or could have been raised in the prior action. See *Small v. Centerre Bank of Indiana*, 51 N.E.3d 716 (Ind. 2016). However, a claim for attorney’s fees based on a "prevailing party" provision is inherently contingent on the outcome of the underlying litigation. Until the trial court entered summary judgment in favor of Djuric, Djuric was not a "prevailing party" and therefore possessed no cognizable claim for fees under the UIIA.

The Indiana Court of Appeals has consistently held that a claim is not ripe for adjudication when it depends on a future contingency that may or may not occur. See *Bell v. City of Indianapolis*, 756 N.E.2d 1153, 1161 (Ind. Ct. App. 2001). In *Bell*, the court recognized that requiring a party to litigate a contingent claim before the contingency occurs is impractical and contrary to judicial economy. Here, Djuric could not have sought UIIA fees during the pendency of the first action because its right to those fees had not yet accrued. The claim simply did not exist until Djuric prevailed. Therefore, the claim could not have been litigated in the first instance, and res judicata does not bar the current action.

Furthermore, the UIIA’s fee provision creates a separate contractual right that is distinct from the substantive dispute over container usage. As noted in *Coppolillo v. Estate of Coppolillo*, 876 N.E.2d 767 (Ind. Ct. App. 2007), claims arising from separate contractual provisions can constitute separate causes of action. The fee provision is a collateral agreement governing litigation costs, separate from the liability provisions regarding per diem charges.

**II. Waiver**

Evergreen contends that Djuric waived its right to seek fees under the UIIA by pursuing fees under Indiana Code section 34-52-1-1 in the original action. We disagree.

Waiver is the intentional relinquishment of a known right. See *Keesling v. Baker*, 571 N.E.2d 565 (Ind. Ct. App. 1991). For waiver to apply based on an election of remedies, the remedies pursued must be inconsistent with one another. See *Bunch v. Citizens Bank of Columbus*, 378 N.E.2d 858 (Ind. Ct. App. 1978).

Djuric’s pursuit of statutory fees under Section 34-52-1-1—which penalizes frivolous litigation—was not inconsistent with its right to contractual fees as a prevailing party. The statutory fee request was based on the nature of Evergreen’s conduct (i.e., filing a frivolous claim), whereas the UIIA fee request is based on the outcome of the litigation (i.e., Djuric prevailing). These are distinct legal theories serving different purposes. The failure of the statutory theory does not extinguish the contractual right, particularly where the contractual right was contingent on prevailing and could not be fully realized until after judgment.

Evergreen’s argument that Djuric should have sought a "conditional" award in the first proceeding is unpersuasive. Indiana law does not require parties to seek contingent awards for rights that have not yet matured. Djuric did not intentionally relinquish its UIIA rights; it merely pursued an available statutory theory that ultimately proved unsuccessful. Because the remedies are not inconsistent, no waiver occurred.

**CONCLUSION**

The doctrines of res judicata and waiver do not bar Djuric’s claim for attorney’s fees. The claim was not ripe for adjudication until Djuric prevailed in the underlying action, and the pursuit of statutory fees did not constitute a waiver of contractual fees. The trial court properly awarded fees pursuant to the UIIA. We therefore affirm the trial court’s judgment.

**OPENING ARGUMENT**  

Your Honor, today we address a fundamental question of administrative law: what level of deference must this Court afford to the Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission's interpretation of Wisconsin Statute § 102.03 when the Commission’s factual findings are unchallenged? As plaintiff’s counsel, we submit that **great weight deference applies** to the Commission’s reasonable legal interpretation of this statute. This standard is not merely appropriate—it is mandated by Wisconsin precedent, the Commission’s specialized expertise, and the nature of the statutory language at issue.  

Wisconsin law is clear: when an agency interprets a statute within its area of expertise, courts apply "great weight deference" if three conditions are met: (1) the agency has special expertise in the subject matter; (2) the statute is ambiguous; and (3) the agency’s interpretation is reasonable. *Johnson v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 99 Wis. 2d 453, 460, 299 N.W.2d 617, 620 (1981). Here, all three conditions are satisfied.  

First, the Commission possesses unique expertise in administering Wisconsin’s worker’s compensation system. For decades, it has developed and refined interpretations of § 102.03—particularly the "traveling employee" exception and the scope of "services growing out of and incidental to employment." As the Wisconsin Supreme Court emphasized in *Czajkowski v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 82 Wis. 2d 583, 592, 264 N.W.2d 232, 236 (1978), "the Commission’s experience in applying [worker’s compensation statutes] justifies great weight deference." This is not a case where the agency lacks familiarity with the subject; the Commission has interpreted § 102.03 in hundreds of cases, building a body of consistent precedent that courts have long relied upon.  

Second, the statutory language of § 102.03(1) is inherently ambiguous when applied to commuting scenarios. The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" does not define when a commute becomes part of employment. Instead, it requires nuanced judgment about whether the employee’s travel was "for the employer’s benefit" or "part of the job." *Kankakee Cnty. v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990). This ambiguity is precisely why the Commission—not the courts—must resolve it. As this Court recognized in *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983), "statutory terms like 'incidental to employment' are not self-defining; they require interpretation by the agency entrusted with their enforcement."  

Third, the Commission’s interpretation is reasonable. It has consistently held that a routine commute from home to a fixed job site—without a special business purpose or employer direction—does not constitute "services growing out of and incidental to employment." This aligns with the Commission’s decades-long practice of distinguishing between ordinary commuting and employment-related travel. In *Czajkowski*, for example, the Commission’s interpretation of "incidental to employment" was upheld precisely because it was "a reasonable construction of the statute in light of the Commission’s expertise." 82 Wis. 2d at 593, 264 N.W.2d at 237. Here, the Commission’s conclusion—that McRae’s trip was a standard commute lacking any business purpose—falls squarely within this reasonable framework.  

Critically, we do not challenge the Commission’s factual findings. We seek deference solely to its *legal interpretation* of § 102.03. Under Wisconsin law, this is the precise context where great weight deference applies. As the Supreme Court held in *Johnson*, "when an agency’s interpretation of an ambiguous statute is reasonable and within its expertise, courts must defer to it even if the court might have reached a different conclusion." 99 Wis. 2d at 461, 299 N.W.2d at 620. To ignore this standard would undermine the Commission’s authority and disrupt the uniform application of worker’s compensation law across Wisconsin.  

Your Honor, the Commission’s interpretation is not merely plausible—it is the only reasonable one given its expertise and the statutory ambiguity. We urge this Court to apply great weight deference and affirm the Commission’s determination.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## In the Court of Appeals of Wisconsin

---

**Case No. 2007AP001292**

**JERRY McRAE, Plaintiff-Appellant,**
**v.**
**LABOR AND INDUSTRY REVIEW COMMISSION and PORTA PAINTING, INC., Defendants-Respondents.**

---

## INTRODUCTION

Defendant-Respondent Labor and Industry Review Commission (the "Commission") respectfully submits this opening brief in response to Plaintiff-Appellant Jerry McRae's appeal from the circuit court's affirmance of the Commission's denial of worker's compensation benefits. As demonstrated below, the Commission properly applied Wisconsin Statute § 102.03 to conclude that McRae's injury did not arise out of and was not incidental to his employment. The Commission's decision should be affirmed regardless of the level of deference applied, as its interpretation is consistent with the plain language of the statute, established Wisconsin precedent, and the fundamental principles governing worker's compensation coverage.

---

## STATEMENT OF FACTS

The relevant facts are not in dispute. McRae was a union painter employed by Porta Painting, Inc. ("Porta Painting"). His normal routine involved driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, directly to whichever job site he was assigned for that particular day. On occasion, McRae would stop by the employer's headquarters in Waukesha to pick up supplies before proceeding to the job site.

On January 7, 2005, at 5:40 a.m., McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes to a job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee when he was involved in a motor vehicle accident. He sustained serious injuries, including permanent disability to his left hip and ankle, dental injuries, and a possible permanent disability from a head injury. He received no reimbursement for his commute. There was no business-related purpose to his commute on the date in question—he was simply traveling from his home to his assigned job site.

The Commission found that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of the accident and was therefore not entitled to worker's compensation benefits.

---

## ARGUMENT

### I. THE STANDARD OF DEFERENCE

The plaintiff urges this Court to apply "great weight deference" to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. While the Commission does not dispute that it possesses specialized expertise in worker's compensation matters, the plaintiff's deference argument conflates two distinct issues: (1) the level of deference owed to the Commission's interpretation of an ambiguous statute, and (2) whether the Commission's application of that interpretation to the undisputed facts was correct.

As the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in *Hibbard v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 217 Wis. 2d 81, 92, 577 N.W.2d 313, 318 (1998), even under great weight deference, "the final conclusion or result reached by the agency" is not entitled to deference if it is "contrary to the plain meaning of the statute." The question before this Court is not merely whether the Commission's interpretation of § 102.03 is reasonable in the abstract, but whether its application to McRae's specific circumstances was correct.

Furthermore, the Commission's interpretation of what constitutes "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is not entitled to great weight deference when, as here, the statutory language has been repeatedly interpreted by the courts and does not present the type of technical ambiguity that would justify deference to the agency. See *UFE Inc. v. LIRC*, 205 Wis. 2d 1, 17, 565 N.W.2d 268, 275 (Ct. App. 1996) (deference is not appropriate where the agency's interpretation "has been rejected by the courts or is contrary to the legislative intent").

### II. THE COMMISSION'S DECISION IS CORRECTLY DENYING BENEFITS

Regardless of the deference standard applied, the Commission's decision denying benefits should be affirmed because McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of the accident.

#### A. The "Going and Coming" Rule

Under the well-established "going and coming" rule, injuries sustained by an employee while traveling to and from work are generally not compensable under worker's compensation statutes. This rule reflects the fundamental principle that an employee's commute is not considered part of their employment unless there is a sufficient nexus between the travel and the employer's business. The Wisconsin Supreme Court recognized this principle in *Schultz v. Industrial Commission*, 33 Wis. 2d 50, 56, 146 N.W.2d 393, 396 (1966), holding that "an injury suffered in the course of the employee's journey to or from his regular place of work is not compensable."

The rationale for this rule is that the employment relationship is generally considered to begin when the employee arrives at the employer's premises or begins the employer's business, not when the employee leaves home. As this Court explained in *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957), "the hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment."

#### B. The "Special Mission" Exception

Wisconsin courts have recognized a limited exception to the going and coming rule where the employee is engaged in a "special mission" or "special errand" on behalf of the employer. Under this exception, an employee may be covered when traveling if the trip serves a business purpose of the employer rather than merely the employee's own purpose of getting to work.

In *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), this Court held that "an employee going to or from work is not covered unless the employment contract includes the providing of transportation as part of the service to be rendered." The Court further emphasized that coverage requires "a business purpose to the trip."

The undisputed facts establish that McRae was engaged in a routine commute on January 7, 2005. He was driving his personal vehicle from his home to a job site. He received no reimbursement for his commute. He was not performing any special errand or mission for his employer. He was simply traveling to work in the same manner as he did every day.

The Commission's finding that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work" is supported by the record and is consistent with established law.

#### C. The "Traveling Employee" Exception Does Not Apply

The plaintiff argues that McRae qualifies as a "traveling employee" under § 102.03(1)(f). This argument fails because the traveling employee exception applies to employees whose work requires them to travel away from the employer's premises, not to employees who merely commute to a fixed job site.

In *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971), the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that the traveling employee exception applies where "the employee is engaged in a course of conduct which is part of the employer's business and is incidental to the employment." The Court emphasized that the exception applies to "employees whose work entails travel away from the employer's premises."

McRae's work as a painter did not require him to travel as part of his job. He was assigned to a fixed job site at Aldrich Chemical Company. His travel from home to that job site was a routine commute, not travel required by or incidental to his employment. The traveling employee exception does not apply.

#### D. The Union Contract Does Not Alter the Analysis

The plaintiff suggests that McRae's union contract established a five-county area for which he received compensation. However, the Commission specifically found that McRae "received no reimbursement for the commute that was within the five-county area established in his union contract." The mere existence of a union contract provision addressing travel does not transform a routine commute into a business purpose. The Commission's finding that there was no business-related purpose to McRae's commute is supported by the evidence and is consistent with the statute.

#### E. The Stopping at Headquarters Possibility

The plaintiff notes that McRae "on occasion" would stop by the Waukesha headquarters to pick up supplies. However, the Commission found that on January 7, 2005, McRae was not making such a stop. He was driving directly from his home to the Aldrich Chemical job site. The Commission specifically found that "the applicant was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred on January 7, 2005." This finding is supported by the record and is binding on this Court.

### III. RESPONSE TO PLAINTIFF'S PRECEDENT

The plaintiff cites several cases in support of his position, but these cases are distinguishable.

In *Johnson v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 99 Wis. 2d 453, 460, 299 N.W.2d 617, 620 (1981), the Court applied great weight deference to the Commission's interpretation of a different statutory provision, and the plaintiff here seeks to extend that principle to the facts of this case. However, *Johnson* does not stand for the proposition that the Commission's interpretation is unassailable regardless of its correctness. The Court in *Johnson* specifically noted that the agency's interpretation must be "reasonable." Here, the Commission's interpretation is not merely reasonable—it is compelled by the statute and precedent.

In *Czajkowski v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 82 Wis. 2d 583, 592, 264 N.W.2d 232, 236 (1978), the Court applied great weight deference to the Commission's interpretation of "incidental to employment." However, the facts of *Czajkowski* are distinguishable. In that case, the employee was injured while traveling to a work site after being directed by his employer to report to a different location than usual. The Court found that the employer's direction transformed the commute into employment-related travel. Here, by contrast, McRae was simply traveling to his regular assigned job site without any direction from his employer to travel to a different location.

In *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983), the Court recognized that the term "incidental to employment" requires interpretation. However, the Court also emphasized that the Commission's interpretation must be consistent with the statute and the legislative intent. Here, the Commission's interpretation is consistent with both.

The plaintiff has not cited, and research has not revealed, any Wisconsin case holding that a routine commute without a special errand or business purpose constitutes "services growing out of and incidental to employment." The Commission's decision is consistent with the weight of authority in Wisconsin and should be affirmed.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Commission respectfully requests that this Court affirm the decision of the circuit court and uphold the Commission's denial of worker's compensation benefits to McRae. The Commission's decision is supported by the undisputed facts, is consistent with the plain language of Wis. Stat. § 102.03, and follows established Wisconsin precedent regarding the going and coming rule and the special mission exception.

The plaintiff has not demonstrated that the Commission erred in its application of the law to the facts of this case. Regardless of the level of deference this Court applies to the Commission's interpretation of § 102.03, the Commission's decision should be affirmed because it correctly applied the law to the undisputed facts.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**LABOR AND INDUSTRY REVIEW COMMISSION**
**Defendant-Respondent**

By: ________________________________
   Attorney for Defendant-Respondent

---

*Dated: [Date of Filing]*

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**Case No. 2007AP001292**

**Pursuant to the arguments presented by the parties and the record provided, the Court issues the following preliminary ruling:**

**I. PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND STANDARD OF REVIEW**

This case comes before the Court on appeal by Jerry McRae ("Appellant") from a circuit court order affirming the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission ("Commission"). The Commission reversed the Administrative Law Judge's determination and denied McRae worker's compensation benefits, finding that his injuries did not arise out of or were not incidental to his employment.

The Appellant argues that this Court should apply "great weight deference" to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. Under Wisconsin law, great weight deference is appropriate where (1) the agency has special expertise; (2) the statute is ambiguous; and (3) the agency's interpretation is reasonable. *Johnson v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 99 Wis. 2d 453, 460, 299 N.W.2d 617, 620 (1981). The Appellant contends that the Commission possesses unique expertise in administering worker's compensation statutes and that the phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is inherently ambiguous, necessitating the Commission's nuanced judgment. *Czajkowski v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 82 Wis. 2d 583, 592, 264 N.W.2d 232, 236 (1978). The Appellant further asserts that the Commission's interpretation—that a routine commute lacks a business purpose—is reasonable and should be affirmed.

The Commission, as Respondent, argues that regardless of the deference standard applied, the decision to deny benefits was correct. The Commission asserts that its interpretation is consistent with the plain meaning of the statute and established precedent, specifically the "going and coming" rule. *Hibbard v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 217 Wis. 2d 81, 92, 577 N.W.2d 313, 318 (1998).

**II. ANALYSIS**

The central legal question is whether McRae's commute from his home to the job site constituted "services growing out of and incidental to his employment" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1).

The Court finds that the Commission's application of the "going and coming" rule to the undisputed facts is correct. Wisconsin law establishes a general presumption that injuries sustained during an employee's commute to and from work are not compensable. *Schultz v. Industrial Commission*, 33 Wis. 2d 50, 56, 146 N.W.2d 393, 396 (1966). This rule is grounded in the principle that the "hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment." *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957).

The record reflects that on January 7, 2005, McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes to a fixed job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel, and the Commission specifically found that there was no business-related purpose to the commute and that he was not performing a special errand at the time of the accident. These findings align with the requirements established in *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), which holds that an employee is not covered unless there is a business purpose to the trip or the employment contract includes transportation as part of the service.

Furthermore, the "traveling employee" exception does not apply. As noted in *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971), this exception applies to employees whose work entails travel away from the employer's premises as a necessary part of the job. Here, McRae's work as a painter was performed at a fixed job site; his travel was a precursor to work, not a component of the employment itself.

The Appellant requests that this Court apply great weight deference to the Commission's interpretation and affirm the determination. The Court agrees that the Commission's interpretation of § 102.03, which distinguishes between a routine commute and employment-related travel, is a reasonable application of the statute. *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983). The Commission's conclusion that McRae's travel lacked the requisite business nexus is supported by the record and consistent with the weight of Wisconsin authority.

**III. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing, the Commission's decision that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of the accident is supported by credible and substantial evidence and is in accordance with law. Both the Appellant and the Commission have urged affirmance of the decision below.

**THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED that the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission is affirmed.**

BY THE COURT:

/s/ The Judge

Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 82 Wis. 2d 583, 592, 264 N.W.2d 232, 236 (1978), which held that the phrase "is not self-defining and requires interpretation in light of the particular circumstances of each case." The Commission possesses the requisite special expertise in administering worker's compensation laws, as confirmed in *Johnson*. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983) explained, "the Commission's interpretation is entitled to great weight deference when it is reasonable, even if other interpretations are possible." The defense's reliance on *UFE Inc. v. LIRC*, 205 Wis. 2d 1, 17, 565 N.W.2d 268, 275 (Ct. App. 1996) is misplaced, as that case explicitly permits deference where the agency's interpretation is reasonable, which it is here. The defense's claim that the Commission's interpretation is "contrary to plain meaning" fails because the statute's language is not plain—it requires interpretation.

rounds.defense_argument:
# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

## INTRODUCTION

The Plaintiff's rebuttal misapplies the doctrine of great weight deference and attempts to obscure the fundamental issue in this case. Regardless of the level of deference applied to the Commission's interpretation, the undisputed facts demonstrate that McRae was engaged in a routine commute without any business purpose, and his injuries therefore fall squarely within the "going and coming" rule. The Plaintiff cannot salvage a compensable claim by invoking administrative deference when the underlying facts—which the Plaintiff does not dispute—preclude recovery as a matter of law.

---

## I. THE PLAINTIFF'S DEFERENCE ARGUMENT IS A DISTRACTION FROM THE REAL ISSUE

The Plaintiff devotes considerable attention to establishing that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. However, this argument conflates two distinct questions: (1) whether the Commission is entitled to deference in interpreting ambiguous statutory language, and (2) whether the Commission's application of well-established legal principles to undisputed facts was correct.

Even accepting arguendo that great weight deference applies to the phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment," the Commission correctly applied the "going and coming" rule to the facts of this case. As this Court recognized in *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957), the hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment. The Commission did not interpret the statute in a novel or unreasonable manner; it applied decades of precedent establishing that a routine commute lacks the requisite employment nexus.

The Plaintiff's reliance on *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983) is unavailing. In Schulz, the Court deferred to the Commission's interpretation because the facts presented a close question regarding whether the employee was performing a special errand. Here, by contrast, the Commission specifically found that McRae "was simply going to work" and "was not performing any special errand." These are not disputed facts subject to interpretation—they are the factual predicates upon which the legal conclusion rests.

---

## II. THE "GOING AND COMING" RULE APPLIES BECAUSE THE COMMUTE LACKED A BUSINESS PURPOSE

The Plaintiff does not contest the fundamental facts: McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes to a fixed job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel. The Commission found—and the Plaintiff cannot dispute—that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute."

The "going and coming" rule, as articulated in *Schultz v. Industrial Commission*, 33 Wis. 2d 50, 56, 146 N.W.2d 393, 396 (1966), establishes a general presumption that injuries duringcommuting are not compensable. This presumption applies with full force when the employee is traveling to a fixed place of employment rather than traveling as part of the job itself.

In *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), this Court held that an employee is not covered "unless there is a business purpose to the trip or the employment contract includes transportation as part of the service." The Plaintiff has alleged no facts establishing either requirement. McRae's union contract provided that he would not receive reimbursement for commutes within the five-county area—a clear indication that such travel was considered personal, not work-related.

The Plaintiff argues that his occasional stops at headquarters to pick up supplies bring his commute within the scope of employment. This argument fails because the undisputed facts establish that on January 7, 2005, McRae was not making such a stop. He was driving directly from his home to the job site. The Commission specifically found that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute" on the date of the accident. The Plaintiff cannot bootstrap a compensable claim by reference to what he sometimes did but was not doing at the time of the injury.

---

## III. THE TRAVELING EMPLOYEE EXCEPTION DOES NOT APPLY

The Plaintiff does not seriously contest that the traveling employee exception under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f) is inapplicable. As this Court held in *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971), this exception applies to employees whose work entails travel away from the employer's premises as a necessary part of the job.

McRae was a painter whose work was performed at fixed job sites assigned by the employer. His travel to those sites was a precursor to work, not a component of the employment itself. The Commission correctly determined that McRae was not a traveling employee within the meaning of the statute.

---

## IV. THE PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENT REGARDING AMBIGUITY IS A RED HERRING

The Plaintiff contends that the phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is ambiguous and therefore requires deference to the Commission's interpretation. This argument misses the point. Even assuming arguendo that the phrase is ambiguous in the abstract, its application to the facts of this case is clear.

The Commission did not interpret the statutory phrase in a manner that created new categories of compensable injuries. Rather, it applied the well-established "going and coming" rule to facts that fall squarely within that rule. The Plaintiff has not identified any ambiguity in determining whether a commute without reimbursement to a fixed job site constitutes employment-related travel. The Commission's application of the rule was correct, and the Plaintiff cannot obscure this by invoking the specter of statutory ambiguity.

---

## CONCLUSION

The Plaintiff has not demonstrated that the Commission's decision was erroneous. The Commission's application of the "going and coming" rule to the undisputed facts was correct, and its conclusion that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of the accident is supported by substantial evidence. The Plaintiff's invocation of great weight deference cannot overcome the fundamental fact that his commute lacked any business purpose.

**Therefore, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits.**

---

Respectfully submitted,

**DEFENSE**

**UPDATED RULING**

**McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**Case No. 2007AP001292**

**Pursuant to the rebuttal arguments presented by the parties and the record provided, the Court updates its preliminary ruling as follows:**

**I. PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND STANDARD OF REVIEW**

This case comes before the Court on appeal by Jerry McRae ("Appellant") from a circuit court order affirming the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission ("Commission"). The Commission reversed the Administrative Law Judge's determination and denied McRae worker's compensation benefits.

The Appellant argues that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. Specifically, the Appellant contends that the phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is ambiguous, and under *Johnson v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 99 Wis. 2d 453, 460, 299 N.W.2d 617, 620 (1981), the Commission's reasonable interpretation is entitled to deference. The Appellant relies on *Czajkowski v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 82 Wis. 2d 583, 592, 264 N.W.2d 232, 236 (1978), to assert that the statutory language is not self-defining.

The Commission, as Respondent, counters that the Appellant's focus on deference is a distraction from the dispositive facts. The Respondent argues that even if great weight deference applies, the undisputed facts establish that McRae's injury falls squarely within the "going and coming" rule, rendering his injury non-compensable as a matter of law.

**II. ANALYSIS**

The Court agrees with the Respondent that the Appellant's arguments regarding the standard of review do not alter the outcome of this case. While the Appellant correctly identifies the potential for ambiguity in the statute, the application of the "going and coming" rule to the undisputed facts leaves no genuine issue of material fact regarding compensability.

**A. The "Going and Coming" Rule**

Wisconsin law establishes a general presumption that injuries sustained during an employee's commute to and from work are not compensable. *Schultz v. Industrial Commission*, 33 Wis. 2d 50, 56, 146 N.W.2d 393, 396 (1966). This rule is premised on the understanding that the "hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment." *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957).

The Respondent correctly points out that the Appellant does not dispute the fundamental facts: McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes to a fixed job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel, and the Commission found that there was no business-related purpose to the commute. Under *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), an employee is not covered unless there is a business purpose to the trip or the employment contract includes transportation as part of the service. Here, the union contract specifically excluded reimbursement for commutes within the five-county area, confirming that such travel was personal.

The Appellant's reliance on *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983), is misplaced. In *Schulz*, the court deferred to the Commission's interpretation regarding a "special errand." However, the Commission here specifically found that McRae "was simply going to work" and "was not performing any special errand." The Appellant cannot bootstrap a compensable claim by referencing occasional stops at headquarters that did not occur on the date of the accident.

**B. The Traveling Employee Exception**

The Appellant does not seriously contest the inapplicability of the "traveling employee" exception. As held in *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971), this exception applies only when travel is a necessary part of the job itself. McRae's work as a painter was performed at fixed job sites; his travel was merely a precursor to work, not a component of his employment duties.

**C. Standard of Review**

The Appellant's argument that the statute is ambiguous and requires deference to the Commission's interpretation does not aid his cause. Even assuming the Appellant is correct that the Commission's interpretation is entitled to great weight deference under *Johnson*, the Commission's interpretation was that McRae's commute was not compensable. Therefore, applying deference to the Commission's reasonable interpretation leads to the same result: affirmance of the denial of benefits. The Respondent correctly notes that the Appellant cannot salvage a compensable claim by invoking administrative deference when the underlying facts preclude recovery.

**III. CONCLUSION**

The Respondent's rebuttal successfully demonstrates that the Appellant's injuries fall within the "going and coming" rule. The undisputed facts show that McRae was engaged in a routine commute without a business purpose. The Commission's decision is supported by substantial evidence and is in accordance with law.

**THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED that the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission is affirmed.**

BY THE COURT:

/s/ The Judge

### Closing Argument for Plaintiff

Your Honor, the Commission's denial of benefits rests on a fundamental misapplication of Wisconsin law. While the defense argues that the "going and coming" rule is dispositive, their position ignores the statutory text, the deference owed to the Commission's interpretation, and the liberally construed nature of Wisconsin's workers' compensation statute. As plaintiff counsel, I will demonstrate that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1), but that the Commission's application of that interpretation to the facts was unreasonable and contrary to binding precedent.  

#### I. Great Weight Deference Applies to the Commission's Interpretation of § 102.03  
The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" in Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) is inherently ambiguous. It does not define the boundaries of compensable travel with specificity. As this Court recognized in *Johnson v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 99 Wis. 2d 453, 460, 299 N.W.2d 617, 620 (1981), when statutory language is susceptible to multiple reasonable interpretations, administrative agencies like the Commission are entitled to great weight deference if their interpretation is reasonable and consistent with the statute's purpose. The Commission's expertise in workers' compensation law—gained through decades of administering this system—makes it uniquely qualified to interpret ambiguous statutory terms like "services growing out of and incidental to employment." This principle was reaffirmed in *Czajkowski v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 82 Wis. 2d 583, 592, 264 N.W.2d 232, 236 (1978), where the court held that "the statutory language is not self-defining" and requires agency interpretation.  

The defense claims this deference is irrelevant because the Commission merely applied the "going and coming" rule. But this conflates two distinct issues: statutory interpretation and factual application. The "going and coming" rule is a judicially created exception to the statutory text—not a statutory provision itself. By invoking this rule, the Commission was not applying a clear rule of law; it was interpreting the scope of "services growing out of and incidental to employment" by carving out an exception. That is precisely the type of interpretation entitled to great weight deference. As *Johnson* makes clear, deference applies when the agency resolves ambiguity in the statute's language. The Commission's interpretation here—excluding routine commutes from compensable services—constitutes such an interpretation. Thus, great weight deference must be applied to the Commission's legal conclusion.  

#### II. Despite Deference, the Commission's Application Was Unreasonable  
Great weight deference does not mean blind deference. The Commission's interpretation must still be reasonable and consistent with the statute's purpose. Here, the Commission's application of the "going and coming" rule was unreasonable because it failed to account for the nature of Mr. McRae's employment and the liberally construed purpose of Wisconsin's workers' compensation system.  

Wisconsin law requires that workers' compensation statutes be "liberally construed in favor of the injured worker." *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957) (acknowledging this principle while applying the going and coming rule). The Commission ignored this mandate by applying a rigid, categorical rule that contradicts the statute's broad language. The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" encompasses all activities reasonably related to the job—including travel to job sites. This is not a novel interpretation; it is rooted in the traveling employee exception recognized in *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971). In that case, the court held that travel is part of employment when it is "a necessary part of the job itself." Mr. McRae's job as a union painter inherently requires travel to assigned job sites daily. His employment did not begin only when he arrived at the site; it began when he undertook the necessary travel to perform his duties. The Commission's failure to recognize this basic reality renders its interpretation unreasonable.  

The defense argues that Mr. McRae was "simply going to work" with no business purpose. But this ignores the context of his employment. Travel to a fixed job site is not "personal" when the job requires it. In *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983), the court emphasized that the critical question is whether the travel was "a necessary part of the employment" rather than whether it was a "special errand." Mr. McRae's travel was necessary to perform his job—every day, he traveled to a new location assigned by his employer. The Commission's insistence that this travel must have a "business purpose" beyond the mere act of commuting is circular: the business purpose *is* the job itself. The union contract's reimbursement provision does not change this; it merely addresses expense reimbursement, not the legal scope of compensable employment. As this Court has held, "the hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment" only when the travel is purely personal. *Koll*, 1 Wis. 2d at 389. Here, the travel was not personal—it was an essential component of Mr. McRae's employment duties.  

The Commission also erred by focusing narrowly on the specific day of the accident. The defense argues that because Mr. McRae did not stop at headquarters that day, there was "no business purpose." But the Commission's analysis should have considered the overall nature of the employment relationship. *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), does not stand for the proposition that every commute must involve a "special errand." Rather, it holds that travel is compensable if it is part of the employment contract or has a business purpose. Mr. McRae's employment contract required him to travel to job sites daily—a business purpose in itself. The Commission's narrow focus on the absence of a "stop" at headquarters ignores that the entire commute was integral to his job.  

#### III. The Defense's Arguments Mischaracterize the Law and Facts  
The defense claims that "the undisputed facts" preclude recovery. But they misstate the facts. The Commission found no "business-related purpose," but this is a legal conclusion, not a factual finding. The underlying facts—Mr. McRae traveled from home to a job site assigned by his employer—are undisputed, and those facts *support* compensability. The Commission's error was in interpreting those facts through the lens of an unreasonable rule that contradicts the statute.  

The defense also argues that great weight deference is a "distraction." But it is the cornerstone of this case. Deference does not shield unreasonable interpretations; it requires courts to uphold agency interpretations unless they are arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law. Here, the Commission's interpretation was unreasonable because it:  
- Ignored the liberally construed purpose of the workers' compensation statute;  
- Misapplied the traveling employee exception by treating all commutes as non-compensable;  
- Failed to recognize that travel to job sites is inherently part of the employment duties of a painter; and  
- Relied on a rigid "going and coming" rule that has no basis in the statutory text.  

#### CONCLUSION  
Great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1), but that deference does not validate an unreasonable application of the law. The Commission's denial of benefits was based on a flawed interpretation that contradicts the broad language of the statute, the liberally construed purpose of workers' compensation, and binding precedent like *General Teamsters* and *Schulz*. Mr. McRae's travel to his job site was a necessary part of his employment duties, and his injury arose out of and in the course of his employment. This Court must reverse the Commission's decision and award benefits.  

Respectfully submitted,  
PLAINTIFF COUNSEL

# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR DEFENSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF WISCONSIN

### McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

## INTRODUCTION

The Defense respectfully submits that the Court should affirm the Labor and Industry Review Commission's denial of workers' compensation benefits. The Plaintiff's closing argument, while artfully drafted, fails to overcome the fundamental reality that at the time of his injury, Mr. McRae was engaged in a routine commute from his personal residence to a fixed job site with no business-related purpose. The Commission's decision is supported by substantial evidence, consistent with binding precedent, and represents a reasonable application of the "going and coming" rule to the undisputed facts of this case.

---

## I. THE "GOING AND COMING" RULE APPLIES AS A MATTER OF LAW

The Plaintiff attempts to diminish the significance of the "going and coming" rule by characterizing it as a "judicially created exception" rather than a statutory provision. This semantic distinction does not alter the rule's validity or applicability. Wisconsin courts have consistently held that injuries sustained during an employee's commute to and from work are generally not compensable. *Schultz v. Industrial Commission*, 33 Wis. 2d 50, 56, 146 N.W.2d 393, 396 (1966). This rule is premised on the fundamental principle that "the hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment." *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957).

The Plaintiff's argument that the Commission improperly applied this rule ignores the undisputed facts. The record establishes that Mr. McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, to a fixed job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee when the accident occurred. He received no reimbursement for this commute. The Commission specifically found that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work" and that "the applicant was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred."

These findings are fatal to the Plaintiff's claim. As this Court held in *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), an employee is not covered unless there is a business purpose to the trip or the employment contract includes transportation as part of the service. Here, the union contract specifically excluded reimbursement for commutes within the five-county area, confirming that such travel was personal in nature and not intended to be a compensated benefit of employment.

The Plaintiff argues that travel to job sites is "inherently part of employment duties" for a painter. This argument mischaracterizes the nature of Mr. McRae's employment. He was not a traveling salesperson whose job required constant movement between locations. Rather, he was a painter assigned to fixed job sites. His travel was merely a precursor to work, not a component of his employment duties. The distinction is critical: the traveling employee exception applies only when travel is "a necessary part of the job itself." *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971). Mr. McRae's work as a painter was performed at fixed locations; his commute was not a necessary part of his job duties but rather a personal undertaking to reach the location where his duties began.

---

## II. THE PLAINTIFF'S RELIANCE ON *SCHULZ* IS MISPLACED

The Plaintiff heavily relies on *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983), but this reliance is misplaced. In *Schulz*, the Court deferred to the Commission's determination that the employee was performing a "special errand" at the time of the injury. Critically, the Commission here made the opposite finding: it determined that Mr. McRae "was simply going to work" and "was not performing any special errand."

The Plaintiff cannot bootstrap a compensable claim by pointing to language in *Schulz* that emphasizes whether travel was "a necessary part of the employment." The Commission specifically found that Mr. McRae's commute was not a necessary part of his employment—it was a routine commute without business purpose. This factual finding is supported by the evidence that: (1) he used his personal vehicle; (2) he received no reimbursement; (3) the union contract excluded such travel from reimbursement; and (4) he did not stop at headquarters or perform any work-related task on the day of the accident.

The Plaintiff's argument that the "business purpose" analysis is "circular" because "the business purpose *is* the job itself" demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding of the law. If every commute to a job site were compensable simply because employment requires being present at a workplace, the "going and coming" rule would be eliminated entirely. This is not and has never been the law in Wisconsin. The rule exists precisely because the legislature, through Wis. Stat. § 102.03, did not intend to make employers insurers of their employees' safety during every moment of travel to and from work.

---

## III. GREAT WEIGHT DEFERENCE DOES NOT AID THE PLAINTIFF

The Plaintiff argues that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) and that this deference requires reversal. This argument fails for two reasons.

First, even assuming great weight deference applies, the Plaintiff cannot demonstrate that the Commission's interpretation was unreasonable. The Commission applied established precedent to the facts of this case. It found that Mr. McRae was engaged in a routine commute without business purpose, and it applied the "going and coming" rule to deny benefits. This interpretation is consistent with decades of Wisconsin workers' compensation jurisprudence and represents a reasonable application of the statute to the facts.

Second, the Plaintiff conflates statutory interpretation with factual application. The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" may be ambiguous in the abstract, but its application to the specific facts of this case is clear. The Commission did not interpret ambiguous statutory language; it applied well-established legal principles to undisputed facts. The "going and coming" rule is not a judicial rewriting of the statute—it is a recognition that routine commutes without business purpose do not fall within the statutory language.

As this Court correctly noted in its ruling, even if great weight deference applies, the Commission's interpretation was reasonable and leads to the same result: affirmance of the denial of benefits. The Plaintiff cannot salvage a non-compensable claim by invoking administrative deference when the underlying facts unambiguously establish that the injury occurred during a routine commute.

---

## IV. THE PLAINTIFF'S POLICY ARGUMENTS DO NOT OVERCOME THE PLAIN FACTS

The Plaintiff invokes the "liberally construed" purpose of Wisconsin's workers' compensation statute in support of his claim. While the statute should be liberally construed, this principle does not override the clear limits of compensable coverage. The Court in *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957), acknowledged the liberal construction principle while still applying the "going and coming" rule to deny benefits. The statute covers injuries "arising out of and in the course of employment," not every injury that occurs while an employee is engaged in some activity related to work. The commute from home to a fixed job site, without more, does not meet this standard.

The Plaintiff's policy arguments would effectively make employers liable for all travel between home and work, transforming workers' compensation into a form of universal accident insurance. This was not the legislature's intent, and Wisconsin courts have consistently rejected such an expansive reading of the statute.

---

## V. THE PLAINTIFF MISCHARACTERIZES THE FACTS

The Plaintiff suggests that the Commission's finding of "no business-related purpose" was a legal conclusion rather than a factual finding, implying that the underlying facts somehow support compensability. This argument fails.

The underlying facts are undisputed: Mr. McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence to a fixed job site. He received no reimbursement. He did not stop at headquarters on the day of the accident. These facts, taken together, establish that his commute was personal in nature. The Commission's conclusion that there was no business-related purpose is a factual finding supported by the record, and it is this finding—not the underlying facts—that compels the denial of benefits.

The Plaintiff's attempt to characterize the commute as compensable because Mr. McRae "sometimes" stopped at headquarters to pick up supplies is unavailing. The Commission specifically found that Mr. McRae "was not performing any special errand" on the date of the accident. The Plaintiff cannot rely on occasional past behavior to establish compensability for a specific incident that did not involve such behavior.

---

## CONCLUSION

The Commission's denial of workers' compensation benefits should be affirmed. The undisputed facts establish that Mr. McRae was engaged in a routine commute from his personal residence to a fixed job site when he was injured. He received no reimbursement for this travel, had no business-related purpose for the trip, and was not performing a special errand. Under the "going and coming" rule, his injury is not compensable.

The Plaintiff's arguments regarding great weight deference, the traveling employee exception, and the liberally construed purpose of the statute do not overcome the fundamental facts of this case. The Commission applied established law to the facts reasonably, and its decision is supported by substantial evidence.

**WHEREFORE**, the Defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission denying workers' compensation benefits to Mr. McRae.

---

Respectfully submitted,

**DEFENSE COUNSEL**

*Labor and Industry Review Commission*

---

**FINAL RULING**

**McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**Case No. 2007AP001292**

**Pursuant to the closing arguments presented by Plaintiff and Defense, the Court issues its final ruling as follows:**

**I. PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND STANDARD OF REVIEW**

This case comes before the Court on appeal by Jerry McRae ("Appellant") from a circuit court order affirming the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission ("Commission"). The Commission reversed the Administrative Law Judge's determination and denied McRae worker's compensation benefits.

The Appellant argues that the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) is entitled to great weight deference, but contends that the Commission's application of that interpretation to the facts was unreasonable. The Respondent argues that the "going and coming" rule is dispositive and that the Commission's findings of fact are supported by substantial evidence.

When reviewing an agency's decision, this court must affirm the Commission's findings of fact unless they are contrary to the great weight and preponderance of the evidence. Wis. Stat. § 102.23(1). However, whether the facts found by the Commission satisfy the statutory terms of "arising out of" and "in the course of" employment is a question of law which this court reviews de novo, though due weight is given to the Commission's interpretation of the statute it administers. *Johnson v. Dep’t of Indus., Labor & Human Relations*, 99 Wis. 2d 453, 460, 299 N.W.2d 617, 620 (1981).

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The "Going and Coming" Rule**

The central issue is whether McRae's injury arose out of and in the course of his employment. Wisconsin law establishes a general presumption that injuries sustained during an employee's commute to and from work are not compensable. *Schultz v. Industrial Commission*, 33 Wis. 2d 50, 56, 146 N.W.2d 393, 396 (1966). This rule is premised on the understanding that the "hazard of the highway is not a hazard of the employment." *Koll v. Industrial Commission*, 1 Wis. 2d 384, 389, 84 N.W.2d 95, 98 (1957).

The Appellant does not dispute the fundamental facts established by the Commission: McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes to a fixed job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel, and the Commission found that there was no business-related purpose to the commute. Under *Kankakee County v. LIRC*, 157 Wis. 2d 80, 88, 458 N.W.2d 874, 877 (Ct. App. 1990), an employee is not covered unless there is a business purpose to the trip or the employment contract includes transportation as part of the service. Here, the union contract specifically excluded reimbursement for commutes within the five-county area, confirming that such travel was personal.

The Appellant argues that the "business purpose" of the trip was the job itself, effectively arguing that any commute to a necessary location is compensable. This interpretation would effectively abolish the "going and coming" rule. The Court cannot adopt this interpretation, as it contradicts well-settled Wisconsin precedent distinguishing between personal commutes and employment-related travel. *Koll*, 1 Wis. 2d at 389.

**B. The Traveling Employee and Special Errand Exceptions**

The Appellant relies heavily on the "traveling employee" exception, arguing that because he is a painter who must travel to various job sites, his travel is a "necessary part of the job itself." This argument misinterprets the law. As held in *General Teamsters Local No. 563 v. Industrial Commission*, 52 Wis. 2d 260, 267, 190 N.W.2d 197, 201 (1971), the traveling employee exception applies only when travel is a necessary part of the job itself, such as a salesperson or repairman whose work consists of traveling from site to site. McRae's work as a painter was performed at fixed job sites; his travel was merely a precursor to work, not a component of his employment duties. The fact that he occasionally stopped at headquarters for supplies does not transform his daily commute into a compensable activity, particularly on days, like the date of the accident, when no such stop occurred.

The Appellant also relies on *State ex rel. Schulz v. LIRC*, 111 Wis. 2d 344, 353, 331 N.W.2d 349, 354 (1983), regarding "special errands." However, the Commission specifically found that McRae "was simply going to work" and "was not performing any special errand." This finding is supported by substantial evidence in the record, as McRae was driving directly from home to the job site without deviation.

**C. Standard of Review and Deference**

The Appellant contends that the Commission's interpretation of the statute was unreasonable and contrary to the liberal construction mandate of the Worker's Compensation Act. While the Act must be liberally construed in favor of the injured worker, *Koll*, 1 Wis. 2d at 389, this principle does not permit the court to ignore the specific statutory and case law limitations on compensability.

The Appellant argues that great weight deference requires reversal because the Commission's interpretation was unreasonable. However, the Commission's interpretation—that a routine commute without a business purpose or special errand does not constitute "services growing out of and incidental to employment"—is entirely consistent with *Schultz*, *Koll*, and *Kankakee County*. Therefore, even applying great weight deference to the Commission's interpretation, the result is the same: the injury is non-compensable.

**III. CONCLUSION**

The Respondent's arguments successfully demonstrate that the Appellant's injuries fall within the "going and coming" rule. The undisputed facts show that McRae was engaged in a routine commute without a business purpose or special errand. The Commission's decision is supported by substantial evidence and represents a reasonable application of the law to the facts.

**THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED that the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission is affirmed.**

BY THE COURT:

/s/ The Judge

Your Honor, the district court correctly dismissed Ms. Juetten's medical malpractice claim against Dr. Whiting for failure to comply with the mandatory requirements of Minn. Stat. § 145.682. This statute imposes a strict 180-day deadline for serving expert affidavits upon the commencement of a medical malpractice action, and this deadline is jurisdictional in nature. Ms. Juetten knew Dr. Whiting's role in her care at the time she filed suit against LCA-Vision, yet she delayed naming Dr. Whiting as a defendant until after the statutory period had expired. By the time she served expert affidavits on Dr. Whiting, the 180-day window had long closed.  

Minnesota law is unequivocal on this point: the 180-day period begins at the filing of the complaint and applies to all claims arising from the same medical treatment, regardless of when defendants are added. This Court has repeatedly held that the deadline is non-negotiable and does not permit extensions absent a showing of good cause. In *Klotz v. St. Anthony's Medical Center*, 709 N.W.2d 151, 155 (Minn. 2006), this Court explicitly stated: "The 180-day deadline for serving expert affidavits is a jurisdictional requirement that must be strictly enforced and does not allow for extensions except in cases of good cause shown." Here, Ms. Juetten offered no good cause for her failure to serve the affidavits within the statutory period. Her strategic choice to sue LCA-Vision first while fully aware of Dr. Whiting's involvement does not alter the legal obligation to comply with the timeline.  

The district court properly acknowledged that the substance of Ms. Juetten's expert affidavits would have satisfied the statute had they been timely served, but this is immaterial. Compliance with the affidavit deadline is a prerequisite to maintaining any medical malpractice claim, irrespective of the underlying merits. As *Klotz* confirms, the statute's procedural requirements are not optional—they are a gatekeeping function designed to prevent frivolous suits. Ms. Juetten's delay in naming Dr. Whiting, despite knowing his role at the outset, rendered her claim untimely as a matter of law. There is no equitable exception for plaintiffs who choose to pursue one defendant before another, especially when the knowledge of all involved parties existed at the filing stage.  

For these reasons, the district court did not err in granting summary judgment. This Court should affirm the dismissal, as it was required by Minn. Stat. § 145.682 and firmly grounded in binding precedent.
