But *Kelley* does not impose an impossible standard; it requires only that the circumstantial evidence be "consistent, credible, and corroborated by medical treatment." *Honeycutt v. City of New Orleans*, 04-2226 (La. 4/11/05), 898 So.2d 1261. Here, the record contains precisely that.

The defense ignores the critical sequence of events: the claimant was lifting 250-pound forms—a task requiring multiple workers, as testified by supervisor Bryan Monte—when he sustained injury on March 23, 2011. He reported the accident to Monte the next morning, March 24, and Monte promptly wrote an accident report. He then sought immediate medical treatment from Dr. Michael Davis on March 24, 2011, reporting low-back and left shoulder pain directly resulting from the work lifting. Dr. Davis took him out of work from March 24–29, 2011. This timeline—work injury, immediate report to supervisor, and same-day medical treatment—is the very model of consistent, credible circumstantial evidence under *Honeycutt*. The defense’s attempt to dismiss this as "mere hearsay" ignores that Raul Salazar’s testimony—corroborating the claimant’s pain at the end of the workday—is part of this cohesive narrative, not the sole evidence. The trial court’s credibility assessment of Raul Salazar is entitled to deference; it is "solely within the province of the trial court as the trier of fact" and cannot be reweighed on appeal. *Alexander v. Pellerin Marble & Granite*, 93-1698 (La. 1/14/94), 630 So.2d 706. The defense’s focus on Raul Salazar’s financial relationship with the claimant is irrelevant to the standard of review—this is a credibility issue for the trial court, not this Court.

The defense further claims the claimant’s March 29 call to foreman Byron Dupre about returning to work on March 30 undermines his injury claim. This is factually baseless. Dr. Davis’s medical release explicitly limited the claimant’s absence from March 24–29, 2011, with a scheduled return on March 30. The claimant’s contact with Dupre on March 29 was entirely consistent with this medical directive. The defense’s attempt to conflate this temporary work release with a "serious injury" is a distortion of the record. Dr. Johnston later confirmed the condition worsened, leading to indefinite disability—this progression does not negate the initial accident. As *Honeycutt* holds, "circumstantial evidence may establish a work accident when it is consistent, credible, and corroborated by medical treatment." The record here satisfies that standard.

Finally, the defense mischaracterizes *Cozzolino v. B.F. Goodrich*, 94-1813 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1995), 658 So.2d 746, as requiring medical records alone to prove an accident. But *Cozzolino* states only that medical records "do not prove the occurrence of a compensable accident" when they are the *sole* evidence. Here, medical records are part of a larger circumstantial framework: job demands, supervisor’s accident report, immediate reporting, and consistent medical treatment. This is precisely the "corroborated" evidence *Honeycutt* requires. The defense’s attempt to isolate medical records from the rest of the evidence is legally unsound.

### II. The Employer Unreasonably Controverted the Claim, Mandating Penalties
The defense claims the insurer’s April 5, 2011 denial was reasonable because it "had not received any medical records" at the time. This is a gross misrepresentation of the record. The insurer’s letter explicitly stated: "We have completed our investigation ... and find that you have not sustained a compensable work related claim." This language reflects a final determination on the merits, not a mere deferral pending investigation. Crucially, the insurer knew the claimant had sought treatment from Dr. Davis on March 24, 2011—within 24 hours of the accident—and was notified of this medical visit. Yet it denied the claim without reviewing those records, which were readily available through standard medical record requests. This is precisely the conduct condemned in *Walters v. Rite Aid Pharmacy*, 05-1209 (La. 1/17/06), 920 So.2d 340, where an insurer’s denial based on "speculation" without reviewing known medical evidence constituted unreasonable controversion. Similarly, in *Pittman v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.*, 99-1541 (La. App. 1st Cir. 6/23/00), 764 So.2d 1279, an employer’s failure to obtain medical documentation known to exist before denying a claim was held unreasonable. The defense cites *Reed v. A.C. Electric*, 96-1147 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1997), 693 So.2d 128, but *Reed* is inapplicable because it involved a denial based on *no medical evidence available at all*. Here, the insurer had specific knowledge of medical records documenting the claimant’s condition immediately post-accident but chose not to review them. The trial court correctly found this constituted unreasonable controversion under *Walters* and *Pittman*.

The defense’s argument that "12 days is not an unreasonable period to evaluate a claim" ignores that the insurer’s denial was not a preliminary assessment—it was a final, "completed investigation" that ignored critical evidence. *Walters* holds that an insurer cannot "deny a claim based on speculation" when medical evidence is known to exist. The insurer’s failure to review Dr. Davis’s records, despite knowing of the visit, renders its denial unreasonable as a matter of law. The trial court’s penalty award was fully justified.

### III. Conclusion
The defense’s challenges rest on legal misstatements and factual distortions. The claimant proved a work-related accident through consistent, credible circumstantial evidence corroborated by medical treatment, as required by *Honeycutt* and *Smith*. The trial court properly credited the evidence and did not err in its credibility determinations under *Alexander*. The employer’s denial was unreasonable under *Walters* and *Pittman* because it ignored known medical records. There is no basis to disturb the trial court’s findings. We urge this Court to affirm the judgment in full.

# CLOSING STATEMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEAL, STATE OF LOUISIANA

---

**Your Honor, may it please the Court:**

The defense respectfully submits this closing statement in response to the prosecution's arguments and urges this Honorable Court to reverse the trial court's judgment. The prosecution's closing statement, while artfully drafted, fails to overcome the fundamental deficiencies in the claimant's case and misapplies Louisiana workers' compensation law.

---

## I. THE CLAIMANT FAILED TO PROVE A COMPENSABLE ACCIDENT BY A PREPONDERANCE OF THE EVIDENCE

### A. The Absence of Eyewitnesses Creates a Critical Evidentiary Gap

The prosecution correctly cites *Smith v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.*, 97-0637 (La. 10/21/97), 701 So.2d 1335, for the proposition that the absence of eyewitnesses does not preclude a finding that an accident occurred. However, the prosecution omits the critical context that *Smith* involved circumstances where the circumstantial evidence was "particularly strong." In *Kelley v. City of New Orleans*, 652 So.2d 188 (La. Ct. App. 4th Cir. 1995, this Court held that when no eyewitnesses exist, the circumstantial evidence must be "particularly strong" to establish a compensable accident.

Here, the circumstantial evidence is notably weak. The claimant's own brother, Raul Salazar, did not witness the accident. The prosecution emphasizes that Bryan Monte, the crew supervisor, testified about the physical demands of the job—lifting forms up to 250 pounds. However, this testimony establishes only that such lifting occurred at the jobsite; it does not establish that the claimant sustained a specific injury during a specific incident. The defense notes that Monte testified the crew was "working wrecking forms" but did not observe any accident involving the claimant.

The prosecution argues that the "sequence of events" corroborates the claim. Yet this sequence rests primarily on the claimant's own self-serving testimony. The accident report was prepared only after the claimant reported the alleged injury—some twenty-four hours after the claimed incident. The mere fact that an accident report was prepared does not corroborate that an accident actually occurred; it only establishes that the claimant made a report.

### B. Raul Salazar's Testimony Is Not Credible and Cannot Sustain the Burden of Proof

The prosecution argues that this Court cannot reweigh the trial court's credibility determination regarding Raul Salazar. While the defense acknowledges the general principle that credibility determinations are within the province of the trial court, *Alexander v. Pellerin Marble & Granite*, 93-1698 (La. 1/14/94), 630 So.2d 706, this Court retains the authority to review whether the trial court's credibility finding was manifestly erroneous.

The record establishes that Raul Salazar was paying the claimant's living expenses because the claimant had not worked since March 23, 2011. This financial relationship creates a obvious motive for Raul Salazar to testify favorably for the claimant. The trial court erred in failing to adequately consider this financial interest when assessing Raul Salazar's credibility. The prosecution dismisses this as merely a "credibility issue for the trial court," but this ignores the manifest error standard—when a witness has a direct financial interest in the outcome, and that interest is clearly reflected in the record, the trial court's failure to account for this factor can constitute manifest error.

Moreover, Raul Salazar's testimony established only that the claimant was "in pain at the end of the day." He did not witness any accident, did not observe the claimant lifting anything, and admitted that he "heard about it from the claimant." This hearsay testimony cannot compensate for the absence of direct evidence of an accident.

### C. The Claimant's Conduct Is Inconsistent with a Genuine Belief of Serious Injury

The prosecution attempts to dismiss the significance of the claimant's March 29, 2011 call to foreman Byron Dupre about returning to work. The prosecution argues this was "entirely consistent with" Dr. Davis's medical release. However, this argument ignores the broader context.

The claimant contacted Dupre not merely to inquire about returning to work, but proactively indicated that he "wanted to return to work." This eagerness to return is inconsistent with a genuinely held belief of serious injury requiring indefinite total disability. The progression from a five-day work release (March 24-29) to indefinite total disability (as determined by Dr. Johnston on April 20, 2011) raises questions about the legitimacy of the claimed injury.

The prosecution argues that Dr. Johnston's later determination of total disability "does not negate the initial accident." This is true, but it does not corroborate the initial accident either. The question before this Court is whether the claimant proved a compensable accident occurred on March 23, 2011—not whether he subsequently developed a disabling condition.

### D. Medical Records Do Not Establish the Occurrence of an Accident

The prosecution attempts to distinguish *Cozzolino v. B.F. Goodrich*, 94-1813 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1995), 658 So.2d 746, by arguing that medical records here are not the "sole" evidence. However, the prosecution's reliance on *Honeycutt v. City of New Orleans*, 04-2226 (La. 4/11/05), 898 So.2d 1261, is misplaced.

In *Honeycutt*, the Louisiana Supreme Court found compensability based on evidence that included not only medical records but also co-worker testimony corroborating the specific incident, immediate reporting to a supervisor, and the nature of the injury being consistent with the claimed accident. Here, by contrast, no co-worker witnessed the accident, the claimant's brother had a financial interest in the outcome, and the medical records document only the claimant's subjective complaints of pain.

The prosecution cannot transform inadequate evidence into sufficient evidence simply by invoking the name *Honeycutt*. The circumstances here are distinguishable, and the trial court erred in finding compensability.

---

## II. THE EMPLOYER'S CONTROVERSION WAS NOT UNREASONABLE

### A. The Insurer's Denial Was Based on Reasonable Investigation

The prosecution argues that the insurer's denial was unreasonable because it failed to obtain Dr. Davis's records before denying the claim. The defense maintains that this argument misapplies the applicable legal standards.

In *Reed v. A.C. Electric*, 96-1147 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1997), 693 So.2d 128, this Court held that an insurer is not required to obtain medical records before denying a claim if the information available at the time of denial does not support the claim. The prosecution attempts to distinguish *Reed* by arguing that it involved "no medical evidence available at all." However, the prosecution's own recitation of the facts establishes that the insurer knew only that the claimant had "sought treatment" from Dr. Davis—not what that treatment entailed or what findings Dr. Davis made.

The prosecution cites *Walters v. Rite Aid Pharmacy*, 05-1209 (La. 1/17/06), 920 So.2d 340, and *Pittman v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.*, 99-1541 (La. App. 1st Cir. 6/23/00), 764 So.2d 1279, for the proposition that an insurer cannot deny a claim based on speculation when medical evidence is known to exist. However, both *Walters* and *Pittman* are distinguishable.

In *Walters*, the insurer had specific medical evidence in its possession that contradicted its basis for denial. In *Pittman*, the employer had actual knowledge of medical documentation establishing the injury. Here, by contrast, the insurer knew only that the claimant had visited a doctor—a visit that could have resulted in a finding of no injury or a minor injury inconsistent with the claimed disability.

The prosecution argues that the insurer's letter stated it had "completed" its investigation, which somehow obligates it to have reviewed all available evidence. This interpretation is unreasonable. The letter explicitly states the insurer "find[s] that you have not sustained a compensable work related claim" based on its investigation. This is a statement of conclusion, not an admission that the investigation was flawless.

### B. Twelve Days Is an Insufficient Time to Fully Investigate a Claim

The prosecution dismisses the defense's argument that twelve days is an insufficient period to evaluate a claim as "ignoring" the nature of the denial. However, the defense maintains that this argument is relevant to the question of reasonableness.

The claimant reported the alleged accident on March 24, 2011. The insurer issued its denial on April 5, 2011—twelve days later. During this period, the claimant was treated by Dr. Davis for only five days (March 24-29), and Dr. Johnston did not examine the claimant until April 20, 2011—after the denial was issued.

The prosecution argues that the insurer should have obtained Dr. Davis's records. However, even assuming the insurer requested those records immediately on March 24, 2011, twelve days would not be an unreasonable period to wait for responsive medical records, particularly when the claimant's own doctor initially indicated the claimant could return to work on March 30, 2011.

The trial court erred in finding unreasonable controversion, and this Court should reverse the penalty award.

---

## III. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court:

1. **REVERSE** the trial court's finding that the claimant proved a compensable work-related accident;

2. **REVERSE** the trial court's award of penalties and attorney fees; and

3. **DISMISS** the claimant's disputed claim for compensation in its entirety.

The prosecution has failed to demonstrate that the trial court's findings were supported by the evidence. The absence of eyewitnesses, the financial interest of the sole corroborating witness, and the claimant's own conduct all support a finding that the claimant failed to meet his burden of proof. Similarly, the insurer's denial, issued twelve days after the alleged accident and based on the information available, was not unreasonable.

The defense submits that the trial court's judgment was manifestly erroneous and should be reversed.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Defense Counsel]**

---

**FINAL RULING**

**Pursuant to the review of the closing arguments submitted by both the prosecution and the defense, this Court issues its final ruling.**

**I. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The factual findings of the Office of Workers’ Compensation judge are entitled to great deference on appeal and should not be reversed unless they are manifestly erroneous or clearly wrong based on the record. *Bruno v. Harbert International Inc.*, 593 So.2d 357 (La. 1992); *Alexander v. Pellerin Marble & Granite*, 93-1698 (La. 1/14/94), 630 So.2d 706. Where the trial court’s findings are based on reasonable evaluations of credibility and the evidence, this Court may not substitute its own judgment even if the evidence might support a different conclusion. *Stobart v. State, through Dept. of Transp. and Development*, 617 So.2d 880 (La. 1993).

**II. LIABILITY AND PROOF OF ACCIDENT**

The defense reiterates its position that the claimant failed to prove a compensable accident, arguing that the circumstantial evidence was not "particularly strong" due to the absence of eyewitnesses and the financial bias of the claimant's brother, Raul Salazar.

**A. Credibility Determinations**

The defense argues that the trial court committed manifest error in crediting the testimony of Raul Salazar given his financial interest in the outcome, as he was paying the claimant’s living expenses. While the defense correctly identifies that financial interest is a factor affecting credibility, the determination of witness credibility remains solely within the province of the trial court as the trier of fact. *Alexander v. Pellerin Marble & Granite*, 93-1698 (La. 1/14/94), 630 So.2d 706. The trial court was presented with the evidence of the financial relationship and nevertheless chose to credit the testimony. The defense has not demonstrated that this choice was manifestly erroneous or devoid of a rational basis. The appellate court cannot re-weigh the evidence or substitute its judgment for that of the trial judge simply because it might have viewed the evidence differently. *Stobart v. State, through Dept. of Transp. and Development*, 617 So.2d 880 (La. 1993).

**B. Sufficiency of Evidence**

The defense contends that the absence of eyewitnesses requires the circumstantial evidence to be "particularly strong" under *Kelley v. City of New Orleans*, 652 So.2d 188 (La. Ct. App. 4th Cir. 1995). However, Louisiana law is settled that "the absence of eyewitnesses to an accident does not preclude a finding that an accident occurred." *Smith v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.*, 97-0637 (La. 10/21/97), 701 So.2d 1335. The claimant’s testimony, if credible, is sufficient to meet the burden of proof.

The defense argues that the claimant’s conduct in attempting to return to work on March 30, 2011, is inconsistent with a claim of total disability. The prosecution correctly points out that this conduct was entirely consistent with the medical instructions provided by Dr. Michael Davis, who took the claimant out of work from March 24, 2011, through March 29, 2011, with a scheduled return on March 30. The claimant’s contact with the foreman on March 29 was in accordance with this directive. The subsequent finding of temporary total disability by Dr. Johnston and Dr. Sudderth, as the condition failed to resolve, does not contradict the initial accident but rather reflects the progression of the injury.

The record contains sufficient circumstantial evidence to support the trial court's finding. The claimant’s testimony is corroborated by the physical demands of the job (lifting forms up to 250 pounds), the supervisor’s preparation of an accident report, and the immediate medical attention sought. As held in *Honeycutt v. City of New Orleans*, 04-2226 (La. 4/11/05), 898 So.2d 1261, "circumstantial evidence may establish a work accident when it is consistent, credible, and corroborated by medical treatment." The sequence of events—injury on March 23, report to supervisor on March 24, and doctor visit on March 24—provides the necessary consistency and corroboration.

**Finding on Liability:** The trial court’s finding that the claimant proved a work-related accident is not manifestly erroneous. The defense’s arguments regarding the weight of the evidence and the credibility of Raul Salazar do not warrant reversal under the standards set forth in *Alexander* and *Smith*.

**III. PENALTIES AND ATTORNEY FEES**

The dispositive issue regarding penalties is whether the employer’s controversion of the claim was unreasonable. Louisiana Revised Statute 23:1201(F) mandates penalties and attorney fees if the claim is controverted without reasonable grounds.

The defense argues that the insurer’s denial on April 5, 2011, was reasonable under *Reed v. A.C. Electric*, 96-1147 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1997), 693 So.2d 128, because it was based on the information available at the time, specifically the lack of medical records in the insurer’s possession. The defense emphasizes that only 12 days had passed since the accident and that the insurer was not required to obtain records before denying a claim.

The Court finds the prosecution’s argument to be persuasive. The insurer’s letter dated April 5, 2011, stated, "We have completed our investigation ... and find that you have not sustained a compensable work related claim." This language indicates a final determination on the merits of the claim rather than a mere deferral pending investigation. At the time of this "completed" investigation, the insurer knew the claimant had sought treatment from Dr. Davis on March 24, 2011. Under *Pittman v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.*, 99-1541 (La. App. 1st Cir. 6/23/00), 764 So.2d 1279, an employer’s failure to obtain medical documentation known to exist before denying a claim can constitute unreasonable controversion.

While *Reed* allows for denial based on the information available, it does not sanction a denial that asserts the investigation is "complete" while ignoring the most critical evidence of the injury—the medical records documenting the claimant's condition immediately following the alleged accident. The defense argues that the insurer only knew of the "visit" and not the "findings." However, if the insurer did not know the findings, it could not logically conclude that the investigation was "complete" and that the claim was not compensable. As held in *Walters v. Rite Aid Pharmacy*, 05-1209 (La. 1/17/06), 920 So.2d 340, a denial based on speculation or without reviewing medical evidence constitutes unreasonable controversion. The insurer’s failure to review the Dr. Davis records, despite knowledge of the visit, before declaring the investigation complete, supports the trial court’s finding of unreasonable controversion.

**Finding on Penalties:** The trial court’s determination that the employer unreasonably controverted the claim is supported by the record. The insurer’s assertion that the investigation was "complete" without reviewing the known medical evidence from Dr. Davis constitutes an unreasonable controversion under *Walters* and *Pittman*.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the defense’s arguments are insufficient to demonstrate that the trial court’s findings were manifestly erroneous or that the legal standards for penalties were misapplied. The prosecution’s application of *Smith*, *Honeycutt*, *Walters*, and *Pittman* is consistent with the facts provided.

**IT IS ORDERED** that the trial court’s judgment finding that the claimant proved a work-related accident and awarding penalties and attorney fees be **AFFIRMED**. The defense’s request for reversal and dismissal is denied.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## In the Court of Appeal of the State of California

### Case No. [Case Number to Be Provided]

---

## INTRODUCTION

Defendant-Respondent RagingWire Telecommunications, Inc. ("RagingWire" or "Defendant") respectfully submits this opening response in defense of the judgment rendered by the superior court, which sustained Defendant's demurrer without leave to amend and entered judgment in favor of Defendant. Plaintiff-Appellant Gary Ross ("Ross" or "Plaintiff") appeals from that judgment, asserting causes of action for disability-based discrimination under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) and for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. As demonstrated below, the trial court correctly determined that Plaintiff failed to state viable causes of action, and this Court should affirm the judgment.

---

## STATEMENT OF FACTS

The following facts are drawn from Plaintiff's complaint and are admitted solely for purposes of this demurrer proceeding:

Plaintiff Gary Ross suffers from strain and muscle spasms in his back resulting from injuries sustained while serving in the United States Air Force. Plaintiff is a qualified individual with a disability under the FEHA and receives governmental disability benefits.

In September 1999, after failing to obtain relief from pain through other medications, Plaintiff began using marijuana on his physician's recommendation pursuant to the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5).

On September 10, 2001, Defendant offered Plaintiff a position as lead systems administrator. As a condition of employment, Defendant required Plaintiff to take a preemployment drug test. Before taking the test, Plaintiff provided the testing clinic with a copy of his physician's recommendation for marijuana. Plaintiff took the test on September 14, 2001, and began work on September 17, 2001.

Later that week, the clinic informed Plaintiff that he had tested positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). On September 20, 2001, Defendant informed Plaintiff he was being suspended as a result of the drug test. Plaintiff provided Defendant with a copy of his physician's recommendation and explained that he used marijuana for medical purposes to relieve his chronic back pain.

On September 21, 2001, Defendant's board of directors met to discuss the matter. On September 25, 2001, Defendant's chief executive officer informed Plaintiff that he was being fired because of his marijuana use.

Plaintiff alleges that his disability and use of marijuana to treat pain do not affect his ability to perform the essential functions of his job. Plaintiff further alleges that he has worked in the same field since beginning to use marijuana and has performed satisfactorily.

---

## ARGUMENT

### I. STANDARD OF REVIEW

When reviewing a judgment entered after the superior court sustains a demurrer without leave to amend, this Court must determine whether the complaint states a viable cause of action. (Evans v. City of Berkeley (2006) 38 Cal.4th 1, 6 [40 Cal.Rptr.3d 205, 129 P.3d 394]; Serrano v. Priest (1971) 5 Cal.3d 584, 591 [96 Cal.Rptr. 601, 487 P.2d 1241].) This Court treats the demurrer as admitting all well-pleaded allegations of material fact but does not admit contentions, deductions, or conclusions of law. (Evans, supra, 38 Cal.4th at p. 6.)

---

### II. THE COMPASSIONATE USE ACT DOES NOT CREATE A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION AGAINST EMPLOYERS

The central issue in this case is whether the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 creates a private right of action that allows employees to sue their employers for termination based on medical marijuana use. The answer is no.

The Compassionate Use Act, codified at Health and Safety Code section 11362.5, was added by initiative (Proposition 215) in the November 1996 general election. The statute provides that persons who use marijuana for medical purposes upon a physician's recommendation "shall not be subject to criminal prosecution" under certain state criminal provisions involving marijuana. (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5, subd. (d).)

Critically, nothing in the text of the Compassionate Use Act suggests that the voters intended the measure to address the respective rights and duties of employers and employees. The statute by its terms provides a defense to certain *state criminal charges*—not a cause of action against private employers. The statute was designed to exempt qualifying patients from criminal prosecution under California's marijuana prohibition laws; it was not intended to regulate the employment relationship.

In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200], the California Supreme Court recognized that employers may require preemployment drug tests and may take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions. This holding reinforces the principle that the Compassionate Use Act does not create workplace protections.

The legislative history of Proposition 215 contains no indication that the voters contemplated or intended the measure to affect employer-employee relationships. The ballot argument presented to the voters focused exclusively on medical use and criminal prosecution—it made no reference to employment, workplace rights, or accommodations. (See Ballot Argument, Prop. 215, Gen. Elec. (Nov. 5, 1996).)

Therefore, the trial court correctly concluded that the Compassionate Use Act does not provide Plaintiff with a cause of action against his employer.

---

### III. PLAINTIFF FAILS TO STATE A CAUSE OF ACTION FOR DISCRIMINATION UNDER THE FEHA

Plaintiff's first cause of action alleges that Defendant violated the FEHA by discharging him because of his disability and by failing to make reasonable accommodation for his disability. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (a).) This cause of action fails for two independent reasons.

#### A. The FEHA Does Not Require Employers to Accommodate the Use of Illegal Drugs

The FEHA prohibits employment discrimination based on disability. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (a).) However, the FEHA's protections do not extend to individuals who use illegal drugs. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (c), provides that it is not unlawful for an employer to discriminate against an individual "who is currently engaging in the illegal use of drugs" when the employer acts based on that use.

Marijuana remains illegal under federal law (see 21 U.S.C. §§ 801 et seq.) and is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance. Although the Compassionate Use Act provides an affirmative defense to criminal prosecution under California law, it does not legalize marijuana or transform its use into lawful conduct. The use of marijuana—whether for medical purposes or otherwise—constitutes illegal drug use under both federal and state law.

In Loder v. City of Glendale, supra, 14 Cal.4th at pp. 882-883, the California Supreme Court held that an employer may require preemployment drug tests and may consider illegal drug use in employment decisions. The Court explicitly recognized that "the use of marijuana remains illegal under federal law" and that employers are not required to accommodate such use. (Id. at p. 883.)

Here, Plaintiff used marijuana in violation of federal law, regardless of his physician's recommendation. The FEHA does not require Defendant to accommodate this illegal drug use, and Defendant did not violate the FEHA by terminating Plaintiff based on his positive drug test.

#### B. Plaintiff Fails to Allege That He Was Qualified to Perform the Essential Functions of the Job

Even if the FEHA somehow applied to medical marijuana use, Plaintiff fails to state a viable discrimination claim because he has not alleged that he was qualified to perform the essential functions of his position. To state a cause of action for disability discrimination under the FEHA, a plaintiff must allege that he or she is a qualified individual with a disability—meaning the individual can perform the essential functions of the job with or without reasonable accommodation. (Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (c)(1).)

While Plaintiff alleges that his disability and marijuana use do not affect his ability to perform the essential functions of the job, this conclusory allegation is insufficient. More critically, Plaintiff has not alleged that he could perform these functions *at the time of his termination*. An employee who uses illegal drugs—even for medical purposes—may be disqualified from certain positions, particularly those requiring drug-free status as a condition of employment.

Defendant hired Plaintiff for a position subject to a drug-testing requirement. By using marijuana, Plaintiff could not comply with the conditions of his employment. Defendant was not required to create a special exception for Plaintiff or to accommodate his violation of the employer's lawful drug policy.

---

### IV. PLAINTIFF FAILS TO STATE A CAUSE OF ACTION FOR WRONGFUL TERMINATION IN VIOLATION OF PUBLIC POLICY

Plaintiff's second cause of action alleges wrongful termination in violation of public policy, citing Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880 [66 Cal.Rptr.2d 888, 941 P.2d 1157] and Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167 [164 Cal.Rptr. 839, 610 P.2d 1330].

To state a cause of action for wrongful termination in violation of public policy, a plaintiff must allege that the termination violated a policy that is (1) embodied in a constitutional or statutory provision, and (2) designed to protect the health, safety, or welfare of the public. (Tameny, supra, 27 Cal.3d at pp. 176-178.)

Plaintiff cannot satisfy this standard. The Compassionate Use Act does not embody a public policy that protects employers or the workplace from the consequences of employee drug use. To the contrary, the statute was designed to protect *patients* from criminal prosecution—not to regulate employment relationships.

Moreover, there is no constitutional or statutory provision that prohibits employers from terminating employees who use illegal drugs, even if used for medical purposes. The FEHA itself contemplates such terminations. (Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (c).)

In Tameny, the California Supreme Court recognized that a wrongful termination claim requires a violation of a public policy that serves the community as a whole—not merely a private interest between employer and employee. (Tameny, supra, 27 Cal.3d at pp. 176-178.) The Compassionate Use Act does not serve this purpose. It was not enacted to protect the public from workplace hazards or to regulate the employment relationship; it was enacted to provide an affirmative defense to criminal prosecution for patients who use marijuana for medical purposes.

Therefore, the trial court correctly concluded that Plaintiff failed to state a cause of action for wrongful termination in violation of public policy.

---

### V. DEFENDANT'S DRUG TESTING POLICY IS LAWFUL AND CONSTITUTIONAL

Plaintiff's termination was based on a lawful preemployment drug test administered as a condition of employment. In Loder v. City of Glendale, supra, 14 Cal.4th at pp. 882-883, the California Supreme Court explicitly held that employers may require preemployment drug tests and may consider illegal drug use in making employment decisions.

Defendant's drug testing policy is a legitimate business practice designed to ensure a drug-free workplace. Defendant had no obligation to accommodate Plaintiff's use of marijuana, even if used for medical purposes, because such use constitutes illegal drug use under federal law. (See 21 U.S.C. §§ 801 et seq.)

---

### VI. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, Defendant respectfully requests that this Court affirm the judgment of the superior court. Plaintiff's complaint fails to state viable causes of action for disability discrimination under the FEHA or for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. The Compassionate Use Act does not create a private right of action against employers, does not require employers to accommodate the use of marijuana, and does not embody a public policy that protects employees from termination based on drug use. Defendant's lawful drug testing policy and termination of Plaintiff were proper, and the trial court correctly sustained the demurrer without leave to amend.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Attorney Name]**
**[Attorney Firm]**
**[Address]**
**[Phone Number]**
**[Email]**

*Attorney for Defendant-Respondent RagingWire Telecommunications, Inc.*

---

**DATED:** [Date]

**GARY ROSS,**
Plaintiff and Appellant,
v.

**RAGINGWIRE TELECOMMUNICATIONS, INC.,**
Defendant and Respondent.

---

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This case comes before us on review of a judgment entered after the superior court sustained a demurrer to plaintiff’s complaint without leave to amend. The court has reviewed the opening arguments submitted by the parties and the factual record provided. For the reasons set forth below, we conclude that the trial court correctly determined that Plaintiff failed to state viable causes of action for disability discrimination under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) or for wrongful termination in violation of public policy.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

In reviewing a judgment entered after the superior court sustains a demurrer without leave to amend, we must determine whether the complaint states a viable cause of action. We treat the demurrer as admitting all well-pleaded allegations of material fact but do not admit contentions, deductions, or conclusions of law. (Evans v. City of Berkeley (2006) 38 Cal.4th 1, 6 [40 Cal.Rptr.3d 205, 129 P.3d 394]; Serrano v. Priest (1971) 5 Cal.3d 584, 591 [96 Cal.Rptr. 601, 487 P.2d 1241].)

**III. DISCUSSION**

**A. The Compassionate Use Act Does Not Create a Private Right of Action Against Employers**

The central issue is whether the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5) creates a private right of action that allows employees to sue their employers for termination based on medical marijuana use. We conclude that it does not.

The Compassionate Use Act provides that persons who use marijuana for medical purposes upon a physician's recommendation "shall not be subject to criminal prosecution" under certain state criminal provisions involving marijuana. (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5, subd. (d).) Nothing in the text or history of the Compassionate Use Act suggests the voters intended the measure to address the respective rights and duties of employers and employees. The statute by its terms provides a defense to certain state criminal charges—not a cause of action against private employers. The statute was designed to exempt qualifying patients from criminal prosecution under California's marijuana prohibition laws; it was not intended to regulate the employment relationship.

**B. The FEHA Does Not Require Employers to Accommodate the Use of Illegal Drugs**

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant violated the FEHA by discharging him because of his disability and by failing to make reasonable accommodation for his disability. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (a).) This cause of action fails because the FEHA does not require employers to accommodate the use of illegal drugs.

Under California law, an employer may require preemployment drug tests and take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions. (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].) Although the Compassionate Use Act provides an affirmative defense to criminal prosecution under California law, it does not legalize marijuana or transform its use into lawful conduct. Marijuana remains illegal under federal law. Consequently, the use of marijuana—whether for medical purposes or otherwise—constitutes illegal drug use. The FEHA specifically permits employers to discriminate against individuals who are currently engaging in the illegal use of drugs. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c).) Therefore, Defendant was not required to accommodate Plaintiff's use of marijuana.

**C. Plaintiff Fails to State a Cause of Action for Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy**

Plaintiff also alleges wrongful termination in violation of public policy. To state a cause of action for wrongful termination in violation of public policy, a plaintiff must allege that the termination violated a policy that is (1) embodied in a constitutional or statutory provision, and (2) designed to protect the health, safety, or welfare of the public. (Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167, 170, 176-178 [164 Cal.Rptr. 839, 610 P.2d 1330]; Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880, 887 [66 Cal.Rptr.2d 888, 941 P.2d 1157].)

Plaintiff cannot satisfy this standard. The Compassionate Use Act does not embody a public policy that protects employers or the workplace from the consequences of employee drug use. To the contrary, the statute was designed to protect patients from criminal prosecution—not to regulate employment relationships. There is no constitutional or statutory provision that prohibits employers from terminating employees who use illegal drugs, even if used for medical purposes. The Compassionate Use Act was not enacted to protect the public from workplace hazards or to regulate the employment relationship; it was enacted to provide an affirmative defense to criminal prosecution for patients who use marijuana for medical purposes.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing, the lower courts were correct in holding that Plaintiff could not state a cause of action for disability-based discrimination under the FEHA or for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. The judgment of the superior court is affirmed.

**IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA**  

**GARY ROSS,**
Plaintiff and Appellant,

**RAGINGWIRE TELECOMMUNICATIONS, INC.,**  
Defendant and Respondent.

**I. INTRODUCTION**  

As Plaintiff’s counsel, we acknowledge that the trial court correctly sustained Defendant’s demurrer without leave to amend. Plaintiff’s complaint fails to state a viable cause of action under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) for failure to accommodate his off-duty marijuana use. This conclusion is dictated by settled California law, as Defendant’s opening statement accurately articulates. We fully concur with Defendant’s legal analysis and respectfully urge this Court to affirm the judgment.  

**II. THE COMPASSIONATE USE ACT DOES NOT CREATE A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION AGAINST EMPLOYERS**  

Defendant correctly states that the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5) was designed solely to provide a defense to criminal prosecution and does not create workplace protections. As Plaintiff’s counsel, we concede this point without reservation. The statute’s text limits its scope to "a defense to certain state criminal charges" and contains no language suggesting voter intent to regulate employer-employee relationships. (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].) This Court has consistently held that the Act “by its terms provides a defense to certain state criminal charges—not a cause of action against private employers.” (Id.) The ballot arguments for Proposition 215 focused exclusively on criminal prosecution, with zero reference to employment rights or accommodations. Thus, Defendant’s position is legally sound: the Compassionate Use Act cannot support a FEHA claim against an employer.  

**III. THE FEHA DOES NOT REQUIRE ACCOMMODATION FOR MARIJUANA USE**  

Defendant rightly emphasizes that the FEHA explicitly permits employers to discriminate against individuals currently engaging in illegal drug use. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c).) Plaintiff’s claim for failure to accommodate fails because marijuana use—regardless of medical recommendation—constitutes "illegal drug use" under California law for employment purposes. In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200], the California Supreme Court definitively held that "an employer may require preemployment drug tests and take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions." This precedent controls here: Defendant’s drug-testing policy was lawful, and the FEHA imposes no duty to accommodate marijuana use because it falls squarely within the statute’s exclusion for "illegal drug use."  

Moreover, Plaintiff’s complaint fails to allege facts showing he was a "qualified individual" under the FEHA. To state a disability discrimination claim, a plaintiff must demonstrate the ability to perform the essential functions of the job with or without accommodation. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c)(1).) Plaintiff’s admission that he used marijuana in violation of Defendant’s lawful drug policy—coupled with the absence of any allegation that he could perform his duties without violating that policy—dooms his claim. As Defendant correctly notes, an employee who cannot comply with a drug-free workplace policy cannot satisfy the FEHA’s qualification requirement.  

**IV. PLAINTIFF FAILS TO STATE A WRONGFUL TERMINATION CLAIM**  

Defendant accurately argues that Plaintiff’s wrongful termination claim lacks legal foundation. To state such a claim, Plaintiff must show termination violated a public policy "embodied in a constitutional or statutory provision" designed to protect public health, safety, or welfare. (Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167, 176-178 [164 Cal.Rptr. 839, 610 P.2d 1330]; Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880, 887 [66 Cal.Rptr.2d 888, 941 P.2d 1157].) The Compassionate Use Act does not meet this standard. As this Court has recognized, the Act was enacted "to protect patients from criminal prosecution—not to regulate employment relationships." (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].) There is no constitutional or statutory provision prohibiting termination for marijuana use, even when medically recommended. Plaintiff’s claim therefore fails for the reasons Defendant properly identified.  

**V. CONCLUSION**

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

**GARY ROSS,**
Plaintiff and Appellant,

v.

**RAGINGWIRE TELECOMMUNICATIONS, INC.,**
Defendant and Respondent.

---

**I. INTRODUCTION**

Defendant RagingWire Telecommunications, Inc., respectfully submits this rebuttal to the plaintiff's brief and urges this Court to affirm the judgment of the superior court. While Plaintiff's counsel has correctly conceded that Plaintiff's complaint fails to state viable causes of action, Defendant provides this additional analysis to ensure the Court has a complete record and to address any remaining considerations.

**II. ADDITIONAL GROUNDS FOR AFFIRMANCE**

Even accepting Plaintiff's concessions as binding, Defendant asserts that there are additional grounds upon which this Court may affirm the judgment below.

**A. The Drug-Free Workplace Policy Is a Legitimate Business Reason for Termination**

Defendant's preemployment drug testing policy serves legitimate business interests. In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200], this Court recognized that employers have substantial interests in maintaining drug-free workplaces, including reducing workplace accidents, improving productivity, and ensuring workplace safety. Defendant's policy is uniformly applied to all new employees and does not single out disabled employees or those using physician-recommended medications. The policy applies to all prospective employees regardless of disability status.

**B. Plaintiff Failed to Exhaust Administrative Remedies**

Before filing suit under the FEHA, a plaintiff must file a complaint with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) and obtain a right-to-sue letter. (Gov. Code, § 12960; see also Thompson v. City of Monrovia (2010) 187 Cal.App.4th 1055, 1063 [115 Cal.Rptr.3d 29].) Plaintiff's complaint does not allege that he filed a DFEH complaint or obtained a right-to-sue letter. This procedural deficiency provides an independent ground for dismissal of the FEHA claims.

**C. The Interactive Process Was Not Triggered**

Even assuming the FEHA applied to Plaintiff's disability, Defendant cannot be liable for failing to engage in the interactive process because Plaintiff never requested accommodation for his disability. (See Zivkovic v. Southern California Edison Co. (2002) 302 F.3d 1080, 1089.) Plaintiff requested no accommodation for his back condition; he only informed Defendant of his marijuana use after testing positive. The FEHA imposes no duty on employers to initiate the interactive process absent a request for accommodation. (See Humphrey v. Memorial Hospitals Association (2003) 239 F.3d 1128, 1137.)

**III. FEDERAL LAW SUPPORTS DEFENDANT'S POSITION**

Defendant's position is further supported by federal law. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq., employers are not required to accommodate the illegal use of drugs. (42 U.S.C. § 12114(a).) While the ADA separately protects individuals who are participating in supervised drug rehabilitation programs, there is no protection for current illegal drug use. (42 U.S.C. § 12114(b).) California's FEHA is generally more protective than the ADA, but in this instance, the FEHA's exclusion for illegal drug use is consistent with federal law. (See Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].)

Moreover, under the Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988, 41 U.S.C. § 8101 et seq., federal contractors are required to maintain drug-free workplaces. While Defendant is not a federal contractor, the policy reflects a broad societal consensus that employers may maintain drug-free workplace policies.

**IV. POLICY CONSIDERATIONS SUPPORT AFFIRMANCE**

The policy implications of reversing the lower courts counsel strongly in favor of affirmance. If employees were permitted to use marijuana—whether for medical purposes or otherwise—without consequence, employers would face significant uncertainty in maintaining workplace safety standards. Employers would be unable to enforce uniform drug policies if exceptions were made for employees with physician recommendations, regardless of job function.

The Compassionate Use Act was enacted to address a specific problem: the criminal prosecution of patients who use marijuana for medical purposes. The voters did not intend—and the text does not support—creating a patchwork of employment rights that vary based on an employee's medical conditions and physician recommendations. Such a result would be unworkable for employers and courts alike.

**V. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, and in light of Plaintiff's concessions, Defendant respectfully requests that this Court affirm the judgment of the superior court.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Attorney Name]**
**[Attorney Firm]**
**[Address]**
**[Phone Number]**
**[Email]**

*Attorney for Defendant-Respondent RagingWire Telecommunications, Inc.*

**DATED:** [Date]

**UPDATED RULING**

**IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA**

**GARY ROSS,**
Plaintiff and Appellant,
v.

**RAGINGWIRE TELECOMMUNICATIONS, INC.,**
Defendant and Respondent.

---

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the court on review of a judgment entered after the superior court sustained a demurrer to plaintiff’s complaint without leave to amend. We have reviewed the rebuttal arguments submitted by both the prosecution and the defense. Notably, plaintiff’s counsel has conceded that the trial court correctly sustained the demurrer, acknowledging that plaintiff failed to state viable causes of action under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) or for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. Defendant’s rebuttal provides additional grounds for affirmance, including procedural deficiencies in plaintiff’s complaint. For the reasons set forth below, we conclude that the judgment of the superior court must be affirmed.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

As previously stated, in reviewing a judgment entered after the superior court sustains a demurrer without leave to amend, we must determine whether the complaint states a viable cause of action. We treat the demurrer as admitting all well-pleaded allegations of material fact but do not admit contentions, deductions, or conclusions of law. (Evans v. City of Berkeley (2006) 38 Cal.4th 1, 6 [40 Cal.Rptr.3d 205, 129 P.3d 394]; Serrano v. Priest (1971) 5 Cal.3d 584, 591 [96 Cal.Rptr. 601, 487 P.2d 1241].)

**III. DISCUSSION**

**A. Plaintiff Concedes that the Compassionate Use Act Does Not Create Employment Rights**

Plaintiff’s counsel correctly concedes that the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5) was designed solely to provide a defense to criminal prosecution and does not create workplace protections. The statute’s text limits its scope to "a defense to certain state criminal charges" and contains no language suggesting voter intent to regulate employer-employee relationships. (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].) As acknowledged by plaintiff, the Act “by its terms provides a defense to certain state criminal charges—not a cause of action against private employers.” (Id.) Therefore, the Compassionate Use Act cannot support a FEHA claim against an employer.

**B. Plaintiff Concedes that the FEHA Does Not Require Accommodation for Illegal Drug Use**

Plaintiff further concedes that the FEHA explicitly permits employers to discriminate against individuals currently engaging in illegal drug use. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c).) Plaintiff’s claim for failure to accommodation fails because marijuana use—regardless of medical recommendation—constitutes "illegal drug use" under California law for employment purposes. In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200], the California Supreme Court held that "an employer may require preemployment drug tests and take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions." This precedent controls the outcome of this claim.

Additionally, plaintiff’s complaint fails to allege facts showing he was a "qualified individual" under the FEHA. To state a disability discrimination claim, a plaintiff must demonstrate the ability to perform the essential functions of the job with or without accommodation. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c)(1).) Plaintiff’s admission that he used marijuana in violation of defendant’s lawful drug policy—coupled with the absence of any allegation that he could perform his duties without violating that policy—confirms that he cannot satisfy the FEHA’s qualification requirement.

**C. Plaintiff Concedes Failure to State a Wrongful Termination Claim**

Plaintiff also concedes that his wrongful termination claim lacks legal foundation. To state such a claim, a plaintiff must show termination violated a public policy "embodied in a constitutional or statutory provision" designed to protect public health, safety, or welfare. (Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167, 176-178 [164 Cal.Rptr. 839, 610 P.2d 1330]; Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880, 887 [66 Cal.Rptr.2d 888, 941 P.2d 1157].) As plaintiff correctly notes, the Compassionate Use Act does not meet this standard because it was enacted "to protect patients from criminal prosecution—not to regulate employment relationships." (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].)

**D. Alternative Grounds for Affirmance**

Even in the absence of plaintiff’s concessions, defendant has identified independent grounds that require affirmance of the superior court’s judgment.

**1. Failure to Exhaust Administrative Remedies**

Before filing suit under the FEHA, a plaintiff must file a complaint with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) and obtain a right-to-sue letter. (Gov. Code, § 12960; see also Thompson v. City of Monrovia (2010) 187 Cal.App.4th 1055, 1063 [115 Cal.Rptr.3d 29].) Plaintiff’s complaint does not allege that he filed a DFEH complaint or obtained a right-to-sue letter. This procedural deficiency provides an independent ground for dismissal of the FEHA claims.

**2. Failure to Trigger the Interactive Process**

The FEHA imposes a duty on employers to engage in a timely, good faith, interactive process with the employee to determine effective reasonable accommodations. However, this duty is generally triggered by a request for accommodation from the employee. (See Zivkovic v. Southern California Edison Co. (2002) 302 F.3d 1080, 1089; Humphrey v. Memorial Hospitals Association (2003) 239 F.3d 1128, 1137.) Plaintiff requested no accommodation for his back condition; he only informed defendant of his marijuana use after testing positive. Because plaintiff never requested accommodation, defendant cannot be liable for failing to engage in the interactive process.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on plaintiff’s concessions and the additional grounds raised by defendant, it is clear that the trial court properly sustained the demurrer. The Compassionate Use Act does not create employment rights, the FEHA does not require accommodation for marijuana use, and plaintiff failed to state a cause of action for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. Furthermore, the complaint is procedurally deficient due to the failure to exhaust administrative remedies and the failure to trigger the interactive process. The judgment of the superior court is affirmed.

Second, the FEHA itself explicitly permits employers to discriminate against individuals currently engaging in illegal drug use. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (c) states that it is not unlawful for an employer to refuse to hire or discharge an employee “because of the individual’s current illegal use of drugs.” Marijuana use, regardless of a physician’s recommendation, constitutes “illegal drug use” under California law for employment purposes. As this Court reaffirmed in *Loder*, “an employer may require preemployment drug tests and take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions” (Loder v. Because the FEHA does not require accommodation for illegal drug use, the plaintiff’s failure-to-accommodate claim fails as a matter of law.

Code, § 12960). As this Court has held in *Thompson v. City of Monrovia* (2010) 187 Cal.App.4th 1055, 1063 [115 Cal.Rptr.3d 29], failure to allege compliance with this prerequisite “is a fatal procedural defect that warrants dismissal.” The plaintiff’s complaint contains no allegation that he filed a DFEH complaint or obtained a right-to-sue letter. Fourth, the plaintiff’s failure to trigger the interactive process under the FEHA further dooms his claim. No statutory or constitutional provision supports the plaintiff’s assertion that his termination violated public policy.

## I. THE COMPASSIONATE USE ACT DOES NOT CREATE EMPLOYMENT RIGHTS

The Compassionate Use Act of 1996 (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5) was enacted by voter initiative to provide a defense to certain state criminal charges involving marijuana. The statute expressly provides that its purpose is to "ensure that seriously ill Californians have the right to obtain and use marijuana for medical purposes" upon a physician's recommendation. Critically, the Act contains no language suggesting voter intent to regulate employer-employee relationships or to create any affirmative duty on the part of employers to accommodate medical marijuana use.

As this Court recognized in *Loder v. City of Glendale* (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200], "an employer may require preemployment drug tests and take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions." The Act "by its terms provides a defense to certain state criminal charges—not a cause of action against private employers." (Id.) The plaintiff's complaint, which acknowledges that he used marijuana pursuant to a physician's recommendation solely to obtain a criminal defense, cannot state a cause of action against his employer based on the Compassionate Use Act.

---

## II. THE FEHA DOES NOT REQUIRE ACCOMMODATION FOR ILLEGAL DRUG USE

The California Fair Employment and Housing Act (Gov. Code, § 12940) explicitly permits employers to discriminate against individuals currently engaging in illegal drug use. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (c) provides that it is not unlawful for an employer to refuse to hire or discharge an employee "because of the individual's current illegal use of drugs."

The facts of this case establish that the plaintiff tested positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive component of marijuana. Regardless of whether the plaintiff possessed a physician's recommendation for medical marijuana use, his use constituted "illegal drug use" under California law for employment purposes. The plaintiff has conceded this point in his closing statement.

To state a claim for failure to accommodate under the FEHA, a plaintiff must demonstrate that he is a "qualified individual" who can perform the essential functions of the job with or without reasonable accommodation. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c)(1).) Here, the plaintiff's own allegations establish that he used marijuana in violation of the defendant's lawful drug policy. Because the FEHA does not require employers to accommodate illegal drug use—even when accompanied by a physician's recommendation—the plaintiff's failure-to-accommodate claim fails as a matter of law.

---

## III. THE WRONGFUL TERMINATION CLAIM FAILS AS A MATTER OF LAW

To state a claim for wrongful termination in violation of public policy, a plaintiff must demonstrate that the termination violated a public policy "embodied in a constitutional or statutory provision" designed to protect public health, safety, or welfare. (Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167, 176-178 [164 Cal.Rptr. 839, 610 P.2d 1330]; Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880, 887 [66 Cal.Rptr.2d 888, 941 P.2d 1157].)

The Compassionate Use Act was enacted to protect patients from criminal prosecution—not to regulate employment relationships. As such, it does not embody a public policy sufficient to support a wrongful termination claim. The plaintiff has correctly conceded this point.

---

## IV. ALTERNATIVE GROUNDS FOR AFFIRMANCE ARE INDEPENDENTLY VALID

Even absent the plaintiff's concessions, the defendant has identified multiple independent grounds requiring affirmance of the superior court's judgment.

### A. Failure to Exhaust Administrative Remedies

Before filing suit under the FEHA, a plaintiff must file a complaint with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) and obtain a right-to-sue letter. (Gov. Code, § 12960.) As this Court held in *Thompson v. City of Monrovia* (2010) 187 Cal.App.4th 1055, 1063 [115 Cal.Rptr.3d 29], failure to allege compliance with this prerequisite "is a fatal procedural defect that warrants dismissal."

The plaintiff's complaint contains no allegation that he filed a DFEH complaint or obtained a right-to-sue letter. This procedural deficiency provides an independent ground for dismissal of the FEHA claims.

### B. Failure to Trigger the Interactive Process

The FEHA imposes a duty on employers to engage in a timely, good faith, interactive process with the employee to determine effective reasonable accommodations. However, this duty is triggered only by a request for accommodation from the employee. (Zivkovic v. Southern California Edison Co. (2002) 302 F.3d 1080, 1089; Humphrey v. Memorial Hospitals Association (2003) 239 F.3d 1128, 1137.)

The plaintiff never requested an accommodation for his back condition. He only informed the defendant of his marijuana use after testing positive for THC. Because the plaintiff failed to request accommodation, the defendant cannot be held liable for failing to engage in the interactive process.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

The defendant respectfully submits that the judgment of the superior court should be affirmed. The plaintiff's complaint fails to state viable causes of action for several independent reasons: (1) the Compassionate Use Act does not create employment rights; (2) the FEHA does not require accommodation for illegal drug use; (3) the plaintiff failed to state a claim for wrongful termination in violation of public policy; (4) the plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies; and (5) the plaintiff failed to trigger the interactive process.

The defendant acted lawfully in requiring preemployment drug testing and in terminating the plaintiff's employment when he tested positive for marijuana. The defendant's drug policy is a lawful, legitimate, and non-discriminatory workplace policy that applies to all employees regardless of disability.

For all the foregoing reasons, and as essentially conceded by the plaintiff, the judgment of the superior court must be affirmed.

Respectfully submitted,

**[Defense Counsel]**
RagingWire Telecommunications, Inc.

**FINAL RULING**

**IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA**

**GARY ROSS,**
Plaintiff and Appellant,
v.

**RAGINGWIRE TELECOMMUNICATIONS, INC.,**
Defendant and Respondent.

---

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the court on review of a judgment entered after the superior court sustained a demurrer to plaintiff’s complaint without leave to amend. We have reviewed the closing arguments submitted by both parties. In a notable turn of events, plaintiff’s counsel has conceded that the superior court correctly sustained the demurrer, acknowledging that plaintiff failed to state viable causes of action under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) or for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. Defendant’s closing argument supports this conclusion and raises additional procedural grounds for affirmance. For the reasons set forth below, we conclude that the judgment of the superior court must be affirmed.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

In reviewing a judgment entered after the superior court sustains a demurrer without leave to amend, we must determine whether the complaint states a viable cause of action. We treat the demurrer as admitting all well-pleaded allegations of material fact but do not admit contentions, deductions, or conclusions of law. (Evans v. City of Berkeley (2006) 38 Cal.4th 1, 6 [40 Cal.Rptr.3d 205, 129 P.3d 394]; Serrano v. Priest (1971) 5 Cal.3d 584, 591 [96 Cal.Rptr. 601, 487 P.2d 1241].)

**III. DISCUSSION**

**A. The Compassionate Use Act Does Not Create Employment Rights**

Plaintiff concedes, and we agree, that the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 (Health & Saf. Code, § 11362.5) was designed solely to provide a defense to criminal prosecution and does not create workplace protections. The statute’s text limits its scope to "a defense to certain state criminal charges" and contains no language suggesting voter intent to regulate employer-employee relationships. As plaintiff correctly notes, the Act “by its terms provides a defense to certain state criminal charges—not a cause of action against private employers.” (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].) Therefore, the Compassionate Use Act cannot support a FEHA claim against an employer.

**B. The FEHA Does Not Require Accommodation for Illegal Drug Use**

Plaintiff further concedes that the FEHA explicitly permits employers to discriminate against individuals currently engaging in illegal drug use. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c).) Plaintiff’s claim for failure to accommodate fails because marijuana use—regardless of medical recommendation—constitutes "illegal drug use" under California law for employment purposes. In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200], the California Supreme Court held that "an employer may require preemployment drug tests and take illegal drug use into consideration in making employment decisions." This precedent controls the outcome of this claim.

Additionally, plaintiff’s complaint fails to allege facts showing he was a "qualified individual" under the FEHA. To state a disability discrimination claim, a plaintiff must demonstrate the ability to perform the essential functions of the job with or without accommodation. (Gov. Code, § 12940, subd. (c)(1).) Plaintiff’s admission that he used marijuana in violation of defendant’s lawful drug policy—coupled with the absence of any allegation that he could perform his duties without violating that policy—confirms that he cannot satisfy the FEHA’s qualification requirement.

**C. Plaintiff Concedes Failure to State a Wrongful Termination Claim**

Plaintiff also concedes that his wrongful termination claim lacks legal foundation. To state such a claim, a plaintiff must show termination violated a public policy "embodied in a constitutional or statutory provision" designed to protect public health, safety, or welfare. (Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167, 176-178 [164 Cal.Rptr. 839, 610 P.2d 1330]; Stevenson v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 880, 887 [66 Cal.Rptr.2d 888, 941 P.2d 1157].) As plaintiff correctly notes, the Compassionate Use Act does not meet this standard because it was enacted "to protect patients from criminal prosecution—not to regulate employment relationships." (Loder v. City of Glendale (1997) 14 Cal.4th 846, 882-883 [59 Cal.Rptr.2d 696, 927 P.2d 1200].)

**D. Alternative Grounds for Affirmance**

Even in the absence of plaintiff’s concessions, defendant has identified independent grounds that require affirmance of the superior court’s judgment.

**1. Failure to Exhaust Administrative Remedies**

Before filing suit under the FEHA, a plaintiff must file a complaint with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) and obtain a right-to-sue letter. (Gov. Code, § 12960; see also Thompson v. City of Monrovia (2010) 187 Cal.App.4th 1055, 1063 [115 Cal.Rptr.3d 29].) Plaintiff’s complaint does not allege that he filed a DFEH complaint or obtained a right-to-sue letter. This procedural deficiency provides an independent ground for dismissal of the FEHA claims.

**2. Failure to Trigger the Interactive Process**

The FEHA imposes a duty on employers to engage in a timely, good faith, interactive process with the employee to determine effective reasonable accommodations. However, this duty is generally triggered by a request for accommodation from the employee. (See Zivkovic v. Southern California Edison Co. (2002) 302 F.3d 1080, 1089; Humphrey v. Memorial Hospitals Association (2003) 239 F.3d 1128, 1137.) Plaintiff requested no accommodation for his back condition; he only informed defendant of his marijuana use after testing positive. Because plaintiff never requested accommodation, defendant cannot be liable for failing to engage in the interactive process.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on plaintiff’s concessions and the additional grounds raised by defendant, it is clear that the trial court properly sustained the demurrer. The Compassionate Use Act does not create employment rights, the FEHA does not require accommodation for marijuana use, and plaintiff failed to state a cause of action for wrongful termination in violation of public policy. Furthermore, the complaint is procedurally deficient due to the failure to exhaust administrative remedies and the failure to trigger the interactive process. The judgment of the superior court is affirmed.

May it please the Court, this appeal presents a clear violation of Minnesota’s statutory mandate for medical malpractice claims. The district court correctly dismissed Dr. Whiting’s liability because Plaintiff Stacy Juetten failed to comply with Minn. Stat. § 145.682’s non-negotiable requirement to serve expert affidavits within 180 days of suit commencement. As this Court has repeatedly held, the statute’s dismissal provision is mandatory and admits no discretion. *Mauer v. Highland Park Radiology, Ltd.*, 702 N.W.2d 675, 681 (Minn. 2005). Plaintiff’s failure to serve affidavits against LCA-Vision within the deadline triggered dismissal of the entire cause of action for which expert testimony was necessary—namely, the medical malpractice arising from the surgical procedure itself.  

The complaint unequivocally alleged that LCA-Vision was vicariously liable for Dr. Whiting’s conduct during the surgery. This created a single, unified cause of action grounded in the same medical event: the alleged negligence in performing the procedure and failing to recognize contraindications. Minnesota law is unambiguous that when a plaintiff fails to serve expert affidavits for a medical malpractice claim, dismissal extends to all defendants whose liability stems from that identical event. *Lepre v. D’Amico*, 765 N.W.2d 562, 568 (Minn. 2009). Here, Dr. Whiting’s potential liability was derivative of the very conduct that formed the basis of the claim against LCA-Vision. The affidavits required to establish a prima facie case against LCA-Vision for vicarious liability would have necessarily addressed Dr. Whiting’s actions—making the failure to serve them a fatal defect for all defendants tied to the surgical procedure.  

The district court’s application of the law of the case doctrine was proper. Having already ruled that Plaintiff’s failure to serve affidavits against LCA-Vision warranted dismissal under § 145.682, the court correctly barred relitigation of the same deficiency for Dr. Whiting. As this Court explained in *Soderstrom v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co.*, 632 N.W.2d 729, 734 (Minn. 2001), "the law of the case doctrine prevents reconsideration of issues decided in the same proceeding." Plaintiff cannot evade the statutory mandate by later attempting to assert claims against Dr. Whiting for the same conduct—especially when the original complaint already linked his actions to LCA-Vision’s liability.  

The statute’s purpose—to ensure early scrutiny of expert testimony in medical malpractice cases—demands strict adherence. *Mauer*, 702 N.W.2d at 681. Plaintiff’s delay in serving affidavits for the core cause of action cannot be excused, and the district court’s dismissal was compelled by law. This Court should affirm.
