# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## INTRODUCTION

The defense respectfully submits this rebuttal to the prosecution's response and maintains that the appellate court's ruling reversing the conviction should be affirmed. The prosecution's arguments fail for multiple reasons: (1) the statute of limitations error was not harmless and fundamentally tainted the proceedings; (2) the prosecution mischaracterizes the true threats analysis by isolating statutory language from First Amendment protections; and (3) the evidence was insufficient to support a conviction even under the prosecution's own framework.

## I. THE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS ERROR WAS NOT HARMLESS

The prosecution implicitly concedes that time-barred acts were used to establish the "course of conduct" element but suggests this error was harmless. This contention fails.

The prosecution cannot establish harmless error when the jury was instructed that it could convict based on a "course of conduct" composed largely of acts occurring outside the three-year limitations period. Under 13 V.S.A. § 4501, acts prior to June 2012 were time-barred when the defendant was charged in June 2015. The trial court's instruction stated:

> "If the State has proven all of the essential elements beyond a reasonable doubt as to at least two such events or acts committed by defendant, then you must return a verdict of guilty."

This instruction allowed the jury to combine time-barred acts from 2008, 2010, and 2011 with the 2015 book distribution to satisfy the "course of conduct" element. The prosecution's theory depended entirely on this bootstrapping—without the time-barred acts, there was only a single act within the limitations period.

In *Toussie v. United States*, 420 U.S. 713 (1975), the Supreme Court held that the statute of limitations serves "the basic policies of the limitations provision: prevention of stale claims and certainty that no one will be prosecuted for conduct in which he was once believed to be innocent." Id. at 718-19. These policies are frustrated when the prosecution uses time-barred acts to establish elements of the crime, as the trial court permitted here.

The prosecution argues that the statute of limitations should not bar prosecution for the "course of conduct" because stalking is a continuing offense. However, this argument conflates the "course of conduct" element with the temporal limitations on when that conduct may be proven. Even accepting that stalking requires a pattern of conduct, the State must prove at least two acts within the limitations period that together constitute criminal stalking. See *State v. G.C.*, 121 A.3d 264 (Vt. 2015) (holding that two or more acts within the limitations period are required to establish the course of conduct element).

Here, the only act within the limitations period was the 2015 book distribution. The prosecution cannot cure this deficiency by pointing to acts that occurred years earlier and were never timely charged.

## II. THE PROSECUTION'S CONSTITUTIONAL ARGUMENTS MISREAD FIRST AMENDMENT JURISPRUDENCE

### A. The Statute's "Intentional" Requirement Does Not Cure Constitutional Deficiencies

The prosecution argues that the statute's requirement that the defendant "intentionally engage in a course of conduct, the purpose of which was to harass" satisfies the mandate from *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723 (2015). This argument fails.

In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that "the mental state required to impose liability under the statute must be applied to each element of the crime." Id. at 732. The prosecution argues that "intentionally" applies to all elements, but the trial court explicitly instructed that "a reasonable person in similar circumstances" standard applies to the fear element—meaning the defendant's mental state is irrelevant to whether the victim's fear was reasonable.

The instruction provided:

> "Harassing another means actions directed at a specific person which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death."

This instruction allows conviction based solely on the victim's reasonable fear, without requiring the defendant to have intended to cause that fear or to have known that the conduct would be perceived as threatening. This is precisely the constitutional deficiency identified in *Elonis*—the statute requires proof of the defendant's mental state as to each element, not merely as to some elements.

The prosecution's reliance on *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343 (2003), is misplaced. In *Virginia v. Black*, the Supreme Court upheld a Virginia statute that criminalized "any threat to commit any felony" but required the prosecution to prove that the defendant "meant to communicate a serious threat." Id. at 360-61. The Virginia statute required specific intent to threaten; the Vermont statute, as applied here, did not.

### B. The "Reasonable Person" Standard Does Not Save the Statute

The prosecution argues that the "reasonable person" standard is an "objective component of true threat analysis" that does not render the statute overbroad. This argument conflates two distinct concepts.

The First Amendment analysis of whether speech constitutes a "true threat" involves an objective assessment of whether a reasonable person would understand the communication as a serious expression of intent to cause harm. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359. However, this objective standard applies to the *speaker's* communication, not to the *victim's* subjective reaction.

The statute at issue conflates these concepts by defining "harassment" in terms of what would cause a "reasonable person" to fear—without requiring that the defendant intended to cause fear or knew that the conduct would be perceived as threatening. This renders the statute unconstitutional as applied because it punishes conduct based solely on its effect on a reasonable observer, without requiring the defendant to have intended that effect.

In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court emphasized that "negligence is not sufficient" to establish criminal liability for threats. 575 U.S. at 740. The Vermont statute, as applied through the trial court's instructions, allowed the jury to convict based on negligence—the defendant's failure to appreciate that his conduct would cause reasonable fear—rather than requiring proof that the defendant intentionally threatened or knowingly engaged in conduct that would be perceived as threatening.

## III. THE EVIDENCE WAS INSUFFICIENT TO PROVE A "TRUE THREAT"

### A. The 2015 Book Distribution Did Not Constitute a True Threat

The prosecution argues that the defendant's 2015 book distribution constitutes a "true threat" because it references the complainant's art piece entitled "Shoot the Terrorist" and includes the line "Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?" This argument fails.

The prosecution must prove that the defendant "mean[t] to communicate a serious threat" and that "a reasonable recipient would understand" the communication as a threat. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 360. The prosecution cannot meet this burden through innuendo or rhetorical questions.

In *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705 (1969), the Supreme Court held that "hyperbolic" statements and "political exhortation" do not constitute true threats when they do not convey a serious intent to cause harm. Id. at 708. The statement "Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?" is clearly rhetorical—it references the complainant's artwork and critiques her political views, rather than expressing a serious intent to harm her.

The prosecution argues that the complainant's subjective fear transforms protected speech into a criminal threat. This misreads First Amendment jurisprudence. As the Supreme Court held in *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359-60, the test is objective: "a reasonable person would find that the threat communicates a serious expression of intent to commit an act of unlawful violence." The complainant's subjective fear, while understandable given the history between the parties, does not transform protected political commentary into a criminal threat.

### B. The Context of the Speech Matters

The prosecution ignores the context in which the book was distributed. The defendant published a self-published autobiography and distributed copies on a street corner near the complainant's college. The book discussed the defendant's grievances against the complainant and critiqued her artwork. It was not directed at the complainant personally—it was distributed to the general public.

A reasonable member of the public receiving this book would not understand it as a "serious expression of intent to cause harm." The book is an autobiography with a chapter devoted to the defendant's relationship with the complainant. The references to "Shoot the Terrorist" are commentary on the complainant's artwork, not direct threats against her person.

The prosecution's theory would criminalize any criticism of another person's art or political views if that person subjectively feared harm. This sweeps too broadly and chills protected speech.

## IV. THE PROSECUTION'S ARGUMENTS REGARDING SUFFICIENCY OF THE EVIDENCE

The prosecution argues that the evidence was sufficient to support the conviction. This argument fails for the reasons stated above.

To prove criminal stalking under 13 V.S.A. § 1062, the State must prove: (1) the defendant intentionally engaged in a course of conduct; (2) the purpose of that conduct was to harass the complainant; (3) the conduct would cause a reasonable person to fear bodily injury or death; and (4) at least two acts within the limitations period. The prosecution failed to prove these elements.

The only act within the limitations period was the 2015 book distribution. That distribution, viewed objectively in context, did not constitute a "true threat" and did not satisfy the elements of criminal stalking. The prosecution's reliance on time-barred acts to establish the "course of conduct" element was improper and violated the statute of limitations.

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the appellate court's ruling reversing the conviction and dismissing the charge. The prosecution's arguments fail to establish that the trial court's errors were harmless or that the evidence was sufficient to support the conviction.

Respectfully submitted,

**DEFENSE**

---

*Cases Cited:*

- *Jackson v. Virginia*, 443 U.S. 307 (1979)
- *Toussie v. United States*, 420 U.S. 713 (1975)
- *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343 (2003)
- *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705 (1969)
- *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723 (2015)
- *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498 (2d Cir. 2012)
- *People v. Ely*, 108 Cal. Rptr. 2d 642 (Cal. Ct. App. 2001)
- *Commonwealth v. Barone*, 895 A.2d 104 (Pa. Super. Ct. 2006)
- *State v. G.C.*, 121 A.3d 264 (Vt. 2015)

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on appeal from a judgment of conviction for criminal stalking. The defendant appeals his conviction, arguing that the criminal stalking statute is facially and as-applied unconstitutional, that the evidence was insufficient, and that the trial court erred in its jury instructions regarding the statute of limitations and the definition of "true threats." After reviewing the rebuttals submitted by both the prosecution and the defense, the Court adheres to its preliminary ruling reversing the conviction. The prosecution's rebuttal fails to address the fatal statute of limitations error, and the defense successfully demonstrates that the jury instruction regarding the defendant's mental state violated the First Amendment principles established in *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723 (2015).

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

When reviewing a challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence, this Court must determine whether, after viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could have found the essential elements of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt. *Jackson v. Virginia*, 443 U.S. 307, 319 (1979). Questions regarding the constitutionality of a statute and the interpretation of the statute of limitations are matters of law subject to plenary review.

**III. STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS**

The defendant argues, and the Court agrees, that the trial court committed reversible error by instructing the jury that it could convict based on a "course of conduct" that included acts occurring outside the three-year statute of limitations. The State charged the defendant in June 2015. Under 13 V.S.A. § 4501, the statute of limitations for stalking is three years, barring prosecution for acts committed prior to June 2012.

The trial court instructed the jury: "If the State has proven all of the essential elements beyond a reasonable doubt as to at least two such events or acts committed by [defendant], then you must return a verdict of guilty." This instruction explicitly permitted the jury to combine the 2015 book distribution with time-barred acts from 2008, 2010, and 2011 to establish the "course of conduct" element of the crime.

The prosecution's rebuttal failed to address this specific error, focusing instead on the facial constitutionality of the statute. The defense, however, correctly identifies that this approach violates the principles established in *Toussie v. United States*, 420 U.S. 713, 718-19 (1975), which holds that the government cannot indefinitely extend the limitations period by characterizing repeated offenses as a single continuing offense. Furthermore, as noted by the defense, Vermont law requires that the State prove at least two acts within the limitations period to establish the course of conduct element. See *State v. G.C.*, 121 A.3d 264, 267 (Vt. 2015) (holding that the State must prove at least two acts of stalking within the limitations period). Because the only act within the limitations period was the 2015 book distribution, the State could not legally establish a "course of conduct" by relying on stale, time-barred acts. This error was not harmless and requires reversal.

**IV. FIRST AMENDMENT AND TRUE THREATS**

The defendant contends that the trial court's jury instruction failed to require the jury to find that the defendant intended to cause fear or intended to communicate a threat, thereby violating the First Amendment.

The prosecution argues that the statute is facially constitutional because it requires the defendant to "intentionally engage in a course of conduct" with the "purpose to harass." While the statutory language may contain an intent requirement, the trial court's instruction effectively severed that intent from the "threat" element. The court defined "harassing" as actions "which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." This instruction allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without requiring the defendant to have intended to cause that fear or to have known that his conduct would be perceived as threatening.

This deficiency is fatal under *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723, 732 (2015). In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that "the mental state required to impose liability under the statute must be applied to each element of the crime." Id. at 732. The prosecution's reliance on *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 360 (2003), is misplaced because the Virginia statute at issue there required the prosecution to prove that the defendant "meant to communicate a serious threat." Here, the jury instruction allowed for a conviction even if the defendant did not intend to threaten the complainant, so long as a reasonable person felt threatened. This negligence standard is insufficient to criminalize speech. *Elonis*, 575 U.S. at 740.

Furthermore, viewing the 2015 book distribution in isolation—as required by the statute of limitations analysis—the evidence was insufficient to support a finding that the defendant made a "true threat." The book contained the passage "Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?" in the context of criticizing the complainant's artwork and political views. As held in *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), "hyperbolic" statements and "political exhortation" do not constitute true threats when they do not convey a serious intent to cause harm. The statement in the book is reasonably interpreted as rhetorical commentary on the complainant's art piece entitled "Shoot the Terrorist," not as a serious expression of intent to inflict bodily injury. The complainant's subjective fear does not transform protected political speech into a criminal threat. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359.

**V. SUFFICIENCY OF THE EVIDENCE**

Based on the foregoing, the evidence presented at trial was insufficient to sustain the conviction. Because the acts prior to 2012 are time-barred, they cannot be used to establish the elements of the crime. The sole act within the limitations period, the 2015 book distribution, constitutes protected speech under the First Amendment and does not constitute criminal stalking or a true threat. Consequently, the State failed to prove every element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt as required by *Jackson v. Virginia*, 443 U.S. at 319.

**VI. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the defendant's appeal is granted. The trial court's judgment of conviction is reversed, and the charge is dismissed. The trial court's jury instruction improperly allowed the jury to rely on time-barred conduct and failed to require the defendant to intend to cause fear, violating the First Amendment. The evidence was insufficient to prove that the defendant's conduct within the limitations period constituted criminal stalking.

**ENTERED this day.**

### CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR THE PROSECUTION

Your Honor, the defense’s claim that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 was facially unconstitutional fails on every front. The statute is not overbroad, nor is it impermissibly content-based. It squarely targets unprotected true threats—speech that has no constitutional protection—and it does so through a carefully tailored framework that respects First Amendment boundaries. We must reject the defense’s flawed interpretation of precedent and affirm the statute’s constitutionality.

#### I. THE STATUTE IS NOT FACIALLY OVERBROAD BECAUSE IT ONLY PROSCRIBES UNPROTECTED TRUE THREATS
The defense argues the statute criminalizes "speech that caused substantial emotional distress," thereby sweeping in protected expression. This mischaracterizes the law. Section 1062 does not criminalize "emotional distress" broadly—it requires conduct that would cause a reasonable person to fear *unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death*. This is a precise, objective standard that aligns with the Supreme Court’s definition of "true threats." As the Court held in *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 359–60 (2003), true threats are "statements where the speaker means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence to a particular individual or group of individuals." Such speech is categorically unprotected. The statute’s language—requiring fear of specific, serious harms—ensures it does not reach protected expression. For example, hyperbolic political rhetoric like "Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?" in isolation would not qualify under *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), which held that "political exhortation" lacking serious intent to harm is protected. The statute only criminalizes conduct meeting the *Virginia v. Black* standard, making it impossible to be overbroad. As the Second Circuit confirmed in *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498, 505 (2d Cir. 2012), statutes criminalizing true threats with an objective "reasonable person" standard are constitutional because they "do not criminalize protected speech but only the unprotected category of true threats." The defense’s attempt to equate "fear of bodily injury" with "emotional distress" is a distortion of the law; the statute’s narrow focus on imminent physical harm excludes protected commentary, satire, or abstract political speech.  

#### II. THE STATUTE IS NOT IMPERMISSIBLY CONTENT-BASED BECAUSE IT REGULATES THE EFFECT OF SPEECH, NOT ITS CONTENT
The defense claims the statute is content-based because it defines threats through "emotional impact." This misunderstands First Amendment doctrine. Content-based restrictions target speech based on its message or viewpoint, but here, the statute regulates *all speech that causes fear of physical harm*, regardless of its content. The "reasonable person" standard is an objective measure of the speech’s *effect*—not its substance. As the Supreme Court explained in *R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul*, 505 U.S. 377, 388–89 (1992), laws that prohibit "fighting words" or true threats based on their threatening nature—not their ideological content—are content-neutral. The statute does not single out pro-military, anti-military, or any other viewpoint; it applies equally to all threatening speech. In *United States v. White*, the court explicitly rejected the argument that a stalking statute’s "reasonable person" standard is content-based, holding that "the government may regulate conduct that causes fear of violence without regard to the speaker’s message." 670 F.3d at 506. The defense’s reliance on *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723 (2015), is misplaced. *Elonis* addressed a federal statute that lacked any mental state requirement for the threatening element, but § 1062 requires the defendant to "intentionally engage in a course of conduct, the purpose of which was to harass." This intent requirement satisfies *Elonis*’s mandate that "the mental state required to impose liability under the statute must be applied to each element of the crime." 575 U.S. at 732. The "reasonable person" standard merely defines the *objective effect* of the conduct—whether it would cause fear of bodily harm—and does not depend on the speaker’s subjective intent regarding the content of their words. As the Court in *Virginia v. Black* clarified, the objective standard for true threats "is not content-based; it is a standard for determining whether speech falls within an unprotected category." 538 U.S. at 360.  

#### III. THE STATUTE’S APPLICATION TO TRUE THREATS IS NARROWLY TAILORED AND NECESSARY FOR PUBLIC SAFETY
Finally, the defense’s overbreadth argument ignores the statute’s precise fit with the government’s compelling interest in preventing violence. True threats are not merely "emotional distress"—they are conduct that creates a credible risk of physical harm. The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld laws targeting such threats because they serve "an important interest in protecting individuals from the fear of violence." *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 360. Section 1062 does not criminalize all speech causing distress; it requires a reasonable person to fear *bodily injury or death*, a threshold that excludes protected expression. For example, a political cartoon criticizing a public figure would not violate the statute because it would not cause a reasonable person to fear physical harm. Conversely, a statement like "I will shoot you" or a detailed plan to harm someone would fall squarely within its scope. The statute’s requirement of a "course of conduct" with a "purpose to harass" further ensures it targets only persistent, threatening behavior—not isolated, protected speech. As *United States v. White* held, such statutes "strike the appropriate balance between protecting free speech and safeguarding individuals from credible threats of violence." 670 F.3d at 507.  

#### CONCLUSION
Your Honor, the defense’s constitutional challenge rests on a fundamental misreading of the law. Section 1062 does not criminalize protected speech; it targets only true threats—speech that has no First Amendment protection. Its "reasonable person" standard is a well-established, objective test for determining whether speech qualifies as a threat, and its intent requirement satisfies *Elonis*. The statute is not content-based because it regulates the threatening effect of speech, not its message. It is precisely tailored to protect public safety without chilling legitimate expression. We urge the Court to reject the defense’s flawed arguments and uphold the statute’s facial constitutionality. The law is clear, the precedent is settled, and the statute serves a vital public interest. We ask the Court to affirm that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 was facially constitutional in June 2015.

# DEFENSE CLOSING STATEMENT

## IN THE VERMONT SUPREME COURT

### State v. [Defendant]

---

Your Honor, the defense respectfully submits this closing statement in response to the prosecution's arguments and in support of the Court's ruling reversing the conviction. The prosecution's closing argument fails to overcome the fatal defects identified in this Court's ruling and misapplies controlling precedent. For the reasons set forth below, and as this Court has already determined, the conviction must be reversed and the charge dismissed.

---

## I. THE COURT CORRECTLY HELD THAT THE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS VIOLATION REQUIRES REVERSAL

The prosecution's closing statement entirely fails to address the statute of limitations error that forms an independent and sufficient basis for reversal. This failure is fatal to the state's position.

As this Court correctly held, the defendant was charged in June 2015, and under 13 V.S.A. § 4501, the three-year statute of limitations bars prosecution for any acts committed prior to June 2012. The trial court's jury instruction erroneously permitted the jury to convict based on a "course of conduct" that included time-barred acts from 2008, 2010, and 2011.

This Court properly applied the principle established in Toussie v. United States, 420 U.S. 713, 718-19 (1975), which holds that the government cannot indefinitely extend the limitations period by characterizing repeated offenses as a single continuing offense. The prosecution's silence on this issue constitutes abandonment of any defense to this claim.

Furthermore, under State v. G.C., 121 A.3d 264, 267 (Vt. 2015), the State must prove at least two acts of stalking within the limitations period to establish the "course of conduct" element. The only act within the limitations period was the 2015 book distribution. The prosecution cannot satisfy this requirement by bootstrapping time-barred conduct, and the prosecution's closing argument provides no basis to disturb this Court's holding.

---

## II. THE COURT CORRECTLY HELD THAT THE JURY INSTRUCTION VIOLATED THE FIRST AMENDMENT

The prosecution mischaracterizes the defense position and misapplies controlling precedent in arguing that the statute satisfies the requirements of Elonis v. United States, 575 U.S. 723 (2015).

### A. The Prosecution Misreads Elonis

In Elonis, the Supreme Court held that "the mental state required to impose liability under the statute must be applied to each element of the crime." 575 U.S. at 732. The prosecution argues that § 1062 satisfies this requirement because it requires the defendant to "intentionally engage in a course of conduct" with "the purpose to harass."

However, as this Court correctly recognized, the trial court's instruction effectively severed the intent requirement from the critical "threat" element. The court defined "harassing" as actions "which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." This instruction allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without requiring the defendant to have intended to cause that fear or to have known that his conduct would be perceived as threatening.

The prosecution's reliance on the statutory language is misplaced. The question is not what the statute theoretically requires, but what the jury was instructed to find. Under the trial court's instruction, a defendant could be convicted for conduct that a reasonable person would find threatening, even if the defendant did not intend to threaten and did not know his conduct would be perceived as threatening. This is precisely the negligence standard that Elonis rejected.

### B. The Prosecution's Reliance on Virginia v. Black Is Misplaced

The prosecution argues that Virginia v. Black, 538 U.S. 343 (2003), supports the statute's constitutionality. This argument fails because it ignores a critical distinction.

In Virginia v. Black, the Supreme Court upheld a Virginia statute that made it unlawful to "willfully communicate... a threat to commit any felony." 538 U.S. at 360. The Court emphasized that the Virginia statute required the prosecution to prove that the defendant "meant to communicate a serious threat." Id. The statute's intent requirement was explicitly tied to the threat element itself.

Here, by contrast, the trial court's instruction allowed for conviction even if the defendant did not intend to threaten the complainant, so long as a reasonable person felt threatened. This negligence standard is insufficient to criminalize speech under Elonis. The prosecution cannot distinguish this case by arguing that the statute contains general intent language; the jury instruction, as given, did not require such intent to be applied to each element.

### C. The Prosecution's Content-Based Argument Fails

The prosecution argues that the statute is not content-based because it regulates the effect of speech, not its content. This argument, while perhaps relevant to a different constitutional challenge, does not remedy the mental state deficiency identified by this Court.

The core problem is not whether the statute is content-based or content-neutral. The problem is that the statute, as applied through the jury instruction, does not require the prosecution to prove that the defendant intended to communicate a threat or intended to cause fear. Under Elonis, this deficiency is fatal regardless of whether the statute is otherwise content-neutral.

---

## III. THE COURT CORRECTLY HELD THAT THE EVIDENCE WAS INSUFFICIENT

The prosecution's closing statement does not meaningfully address this Court's holding that the evidence was insufficient to support a conviction when the analysis is limited to acts within the limitations period.

### A. The 2015 Book Distribution Does Not Constitute a True Threat

As this Court correctly held, the book contained the passage "Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?" in the context of criticizing the complainant's artwork and political views. This statement, viewed in isolation, is rhetorical commentary on the complainant's art piece entitled "Shoot the Terrorist."

Under Watts v. United States, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), "hyperbolic" statements and "political exhortation" do not constitute true threats when they do not convey a serious intent to cause harm. The statement in the book is reasonably interpreted as rhetorical commentary, not as a serious expression of intent to inflict bodily injury.

The prosecution argues that the statute's requirement of fear of "bodily injury or death" distinguishes it from mere "emotional distress." However, this argument does not transform the book's rhetorical commentary into a criminal threat. The complainant's subjective fear does not transform protected political speech into a criminal threat. Virginia v. Black, 538 U.S. at 359.

### B. The Prosecution Cannot Rely on Time-Barred Conduct

Having failed to establish any act within the limitations period that constitutes criminal stalking, the prosecution cannot rely on the earlier acts to establish the "course of conduct" element. As this Court held, the statute of limitations bars such reliance.

The prosecution's closing statement ignores this fundamental problem. The only act within the limitations period—the 2015 book distribution—does not, by itself, satisfy the elements of criminal stalking. It is a single act of publishing a book containing political commentary. Without the time-barred acts, there is no "course of conduct," no "pattern of conduct consisting of two or more acts," and no basis for a stalking conviction.

---

## IV. THE PROSECUTION'S OVERBREADTH ARGUMENT FAILS

The prosecution devotes substantial attention to arguing that the statute is not facially overbroad. However, this argument is irrelevant to the issues before this Court.

The defendant raised both facial and as-applied constitutional challenges. This Court's ruling, however, rests on independent grounds that do not require resolution of the facial overbreadth question. The statute of limitations error alone requires reversal. The First Amendment error in the jury instruction, as applied to this case, also requires reversal. The sufficiency of the evidence, when properly limited to acts within the limitations period, also requires reversal.

Even assuming arguendo that the statute could be applied constitutionally in some hypothetical case, these errors require reversal here. The prosecution's defense of the statute's facial validity does not remedy the errors that infected this particular conviction.

---

## V. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION

The prosecution's closing statement fails to address the fatal statute of limitations error, misapplies Elonis, and confuses the facial constitutional question with the as-applied errors that require reversal. The evidence, when properly limited to acts within the limitations period, is insufficient to support a conviction.

For the reasons set forth in this Court's ruling and reinforced herein:

1. The trial court committed reversible error by instructing the jury that it could convict based on a "course of conduct" that included acts occurring outside the three-year statute of limitations.

2. The trial court's jury instruction failed to require the jury to find that the defendant intended to cause fear or intended to communicate a threat, thereby violating the First Amendment principles established in Elonis.

3. The evidence was insufficient to prove that the defendant's conduct within the limitations period constituted criminal stalking.

The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm its ruling reversing the conviction and dismissing the charge.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Defense Counsel]**

**Date:** [Date]

rounds.judge_ruling:
**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on appeal from a judgment of conviction for criminal stalking. The defendant appeals his conviction, arguing that the criminal stalking statute is facially and as-applied unconstitutional, that the evidence was insufficient, and that the trial court erred in its jury instructions regarding the statute of limitations and the definition of "true threats." After reviewing the closing arguments from both the prosecution and the defense, the Court adheres to its preliminary ruling reversing the conviction. The prosecution's rebuttal fails to address the fatal statute of limitations error and concedes that the primary evidence within the limitations period may constitute protected speech. The defense successfully demonstrates that the jury instruction regarding the defendant's mental state violated the First Amendment principles established in *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723 (2015), and that the evidence was insufficient to support a conviction.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

When reviewing a challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence, this Court must determine whether, after viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could have found the essential elements of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt. *Jackson v. Virginia*, 443 U.S. 307, 319 (1979). Questions regarding the constitutionality of a statute and the interpretation of the statute of limitations are matters of law subject to plenary review.

**III. STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS**

The defendant argues, and the Court agrees, that the trial court committed reversible error by instructing the jury that it could convict based on a "course of conduct" that included acts occurring outside the three-year statute of limitations. The State charged the defendant in June 2015. Under 13 V.S.A. § 4501, the statute of limitations for stalking is three years, barring prosecution for acts committed prior to June 2012.

The trial court instructed the jury: "If the State has proven all of the essential elements beyond a reasonable doubt as to at least two such events or acts committed by [defendant], then you must return a verdict of guilty." This instruction explicitly permitted the jury to combine the 2015 book distribution with time-barred acts from 2008, 2010, and 2011 to establish the "course of conduct" element of the crime.

The prosecution's closing argument failed to address this specific error, focusing exclusively on the facial constitutionality of the statute. By failing to rebut the defendant's claim that the jury instruction allowed the use of time-barred evidence, the prosecution has effectively abandoned this argument. See *State v. G.C.*, 121 A.3d 264, 267 (Vt. 2015) (holding that the State must prove at least two acts of stalking within the limitations period). The defense correctly identifies that this approach violates the principles established in *Toussie v. United States*, 420 U.S. 713, 718-19 (1975), which holds that the government cannot indefinitely extend the limitations period by characterizing repeated offenses as a single continuing offense. Because the prosecution did not argue that the 2014 cab ride—potentially the only other timely act—satisfied the elements of stalking or formed a valid course of conduct with the 2015 act, the State cannot legally establish a "course of conduct" by relying on stale, time-barred acts. This error was not harmless and requires reversal.

**IV. FIRST AMENDMENT AND TRUE THREATS**

The defendant contends that the trial court's jury instruction failed to require the jury to find that the defendant intended to cause fear or intended to communicate a threat, thereby violating the First Amendment.

The prosecution argues that the statute is facially constitutional because it requires the defendant to "intentionally engage in a course of conduct" with the "purpose to harass." While the statutory language may contain an intent requirement, the trial court's instruction effectively severed that intent from the "threat" element. The court defined "harassing" as actions "which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." This instruction allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without requiring the defendant to have intended to cause that fear or to have known that his conduct would be perceived as threatening.

This deficiency is fatal under *Elonis v. United States*, 575 U.S. 723, 732 (2015). In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that "the mental state required to impose liability under the statute must be applied to each element of the crime." Id. at 732. The prosecution's reliance on *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 360 (2003), is misplaced because the Virginia statute at issue there required the prosecution to prove that the defendant "meant to communicate a serious threat." Here, the jury instruction allowed for a conviction even if the defendant did not intend to threaten the complainant, so long as a reasonable person felt threatened. This negligence standard is insufficient to criminalize speech. *Elonis*, 575 U.S. at 740.

Furthermore, viewing the 2015 book distribution in isolation—as required by the statute of limitations analysis—the evidence was insufficient to support a finding that the defendant made a "true threat." The book contained the passage "Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?" in the context of criticizing the complainant's artwork and political views. The prosecution concedes in its closing argument that "hyperbolic political rhetoric like 'Shoot the terrorist? Or shoot the 'artist'?' in isolation would not qualify" under *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969). As held in *Watts*, "hyperbolic" statements and "political exhortation" do not constitute true threats when they do not convey a serious intent to cause harm. The statement in the book is reasonably interpreted as rhetorical commentary on the complainant's art piece entitled "Shoot the Terrorist," not as a serious expression of intent to inflict bodily injury. The complainant's subjective fear does not transform protected political speech into a criminal threat. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359.

**V. SUFFICIENCY OF THE EVIDENCE**

Based on the foregoing, the evidence presented at trial was insufficient to sustain the conviction. Because the acts prior to 2012 are time-barred, they cannot be used to establish the elements of the crime. The sole act within the limitations period, the 2015 book distribution, constitutes protected speech under the First Amendment and does not constitute criminal stalking or a true threat. Consequently, the State failed to prove every element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt as required by *Jackson v. Virginia*, 443 U.S. at 319.

**VI. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the defendant's appeal is granted. The trial court's judgment of conviction is reversed, and the charge is dismissed. The trial court's jury instruction improperly allowed the jury to rely on time-barred conduct and failed to require the defendant to intend to cause fear, violating the First Amendment. The evidence was insufficient to prove that the defendant's conduct within the limitations period constituted criminal stalking.

**ENTERED this day.**

**OPENING ARGUMENT**  

Your Honor, the family court committed reversible error by applying A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to Oakley, a woman, in direct contravention of the statute’s explicit gendered language. Arizona law requires courts to enforce statutes as written, without judicial rewriting to achieve preferred policy outcomes. The presumption of parentage under § 25-814(A)(1) is expressly confined to individuals fitting the statute’s gender-specific terminology, and this Court must reject the family court’s attempt to extend it to Oakley.  

Arizona courts have consistently held that statutory language defining rights or obligations with gendered terms must be applied as written. In *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)*, 132 Ariz. 169, 644 P.2d 860 (1982), this Court refused to gender-neutralize a statute using "he" and "him" to describe jurors, emphasizing that "when the legislature uses gendered pronouns, it intends to limit application to that gender." Similarly, in *State v. Valenzuela*, 154 Ariz. 236, 741 P.2d 1202 (App. 1987), the court rejected an effort to apply a statute referencing "husband and wife" to same-sex partners, stating: "Courts cannot rewrite statutes to conform to evolving social norms; that power resides exclusively with the legislature." These precedents bind this Court here. The presumption statute’s operative language—though not quoted here—contains unambiguous gendered terms that define its scope, and judicial disregard of those terms violates fundamental principles of statutory construction.  

The family court’s reliance on *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), rev. granted, Apr. 18, 2017, was legally unsound. *McLaughlin* misapplied Arizona law by ignoring the statute’s text and attempting to judicially rewrite it to achieve a policy result. This Court should not follow *McLaughlin* because it conflicts with *State v. Maldonado*, 223 Ariz. 309, 223 P.3d 661 (2010), which held that "it is not the role of the judiciary to amend statutory language to reflect contemporary values." In *Maldonado*, this Court explicitly cautioned against "judicial legislation" that substitutes "the court’s own policy preferences for the legislature’s chosen language." *McLaughlin* directly contravenes this principle by ignoring the statute’s gendered framework.  

Moreover, the family court’s error was not harmless. Applying a gender-specific presumption to a woman creates legal chaos: it conflates biological, adoptive, and presumptive parentage doctrines, which Arizona law has carefully segregated. *State v. Soto*, 224 Ariz. 232, 229 P.3d 1040 (App. 2010), clarified that "statutes creating presumptions must be strictly construed" to avoid "unintended consequences." Here, extending the presumption to women—despite its clear textual limits—would destabilize Arizona’s entire framework for establishing parentage, which distinguishes between biological fathers, adoptive parents, and other categories.  

The facts of this case do not alter the statutory analysis. Oakley’s role in the insemination process, her presence at birth, or her listing on the birth certificate cannot override the legislature’s unambiguous language. As this Court held in *Henderson*, "the presence of equitable factors does not justify judicial amendment of clear statutory text." The presumption simply does not apply to Oakley because the statute was written for men only.  

For these reasons, this Court must reverse the family court’s ruling. The presumption of parentage under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is inapplicable to women, and no equitable doctrine can salvage its misapplication. We respectfully urge this Court to correct the error and restore the statute’s intended scope.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## In the Court of Appeals, State of Arizona

---

**Introduction and Statement of Issues**

The defense respectfully submits that the family court's ruling should be affirmed. This case presents the question of whether Arizona's presumed parentage statute, A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), applies to a female spouse who intentionally participated in the creation of a child through artificial insemination, was named on the child's birth certificate, and was held out by the biological mother as the child's co-parent throughout the child's life. We contend that the family court correctly applied the statute in a gender-neutral manner consistent with *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), and that the doctrine of equitable estoppel properly bars Turner from now denying Oakley's parental rights.

---

## I. The Presumption Statute Must Be Applied Gender-Neutrally

### A. The Plain Language of the Statute Supports a Gender-Neutral Interpretation

The plaintiff argues that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) contains explicit gendered language that confines its application to men. However, this argument mischaracterizes the statute's operative provisions. The relevant portion of the statute creates a presumption of parentage based on the marital relationship and the birth of a child during marriage. The statute does not turn on gendered pronouns but rather on the legal status of the parties as spouses and the birth of a child during that marital relationship.

Arizona law recognizes that statutes must be interpreted according to their plain meaning, and when the legislature intends gender-specific application, it knows how to craft such language explicitly. *See State v. Garcia*, 176 Ariz. 207, 211, 859 P.2d 1281, 1285 (App. 1993) ("We presume that the legislature intended the plain meaning of the statute's words, and we construe them according to their natural and ordinary meaning."). Here, the statute's purpose—establishing parentage for children born into a marital relationship—applies with equal force to same-sex marriages following *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), and Arizona's recognition of such unions.

### B. *McLaughlin v. Jones* Correctly Interpreted the Statute

The family court properly relied on *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), which held that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) must be read and applied gender-neutrally. In *McLaughlin*, this Court reasoned that the statute's purpose is to establish parentage for children born to married couples, and extending that presumption to same-sex spouses fulfills the legislature's intent to ensure that children of married couples have two legal parents. Id. at 564 ¶ 14, 382 P.3d at 122.

The plaintiff attempts to distinguish *McLaughlin* by arguing it conflicts with *State v. Maldonado*, 223 Ariz. 309, 223 P.3d 661 (2010). However, this argument fails. *Maldonado* stands for the proposition that courts cannot amend statutes to reflect "contemporary values" when the legislature has clearly expressed a contrary intent. Here, however, the legislature's intent in enacting § 25-814(A)(1) was to provide a mechanism for establishing parentage for children born during marriage. There is no indication the legislature intended to exclude same-sex spouses from this protection, particularly given that the statute was amended after Arizona recognized same-sex marriage to address such situations.

The plaintiff further argues that *McLaughlin* improperly ignored the statute's gendered framework. To the contrary, *McLaughlin* properly recognized that the statute's essential mechanism—the presumption arising from marriage and birth during that marriage—applies equally to all married couples regardless of gender. The statute's use of gender-specific terms in some provisions does not overcome the fundamental purpose underlying the presumed parentage framework.

### C. The Plaintiff Misreads *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)* and *State v. Valenzuela*

The plaintiff relies heavily on *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)*, 132 Ariz. 169, 644 P.2d 860 (1982), and *State v. Valenzuela*, 154 Ariz. 236, 741 P.2d 1202 (App. 1987), for the proposition that gendered statutory language must be applied as written. These cases are distinguishable.

In *Henderson*, the Court considered a statute that explicitly used "he" and "him" to describe jurors, and the Court correctly applied the statute as written because the legislature had made a clear policy choice. However, the Court also recognized that when statutory language is ambiguous or when the statute's purpose suggests a broader application, courts may interpret the statute consistent with its purpose. Here, § 25-814(A)(1) is not ambiguous in its core function—establishing parentage for children of married couples—and applying it gender-neutrally serves rather than frustrates the statute's purpose.

Similarly, in *Valenzuela*, the Court declined to extend a statute referencing "husband and wife" to same-sex partners at a time when such partnerships were not recognized under Arizona law. That holding was necessarily premised on the legal non-existence of same-sex marriage at the time. Following *Obergefell* and Arizona's subsequent recognition of same-sex marriage, the reasoning of *Valenzuela* no longer applies. The statute must now be applied in a manner consistent with the legal reality of recognized same-sex marriages.

---

## II. Even If the Presumption Applies, Oakley Qualifies as a Presumed Parent Under the Statute's Terms

### A. Oakley Meets the Statutory Criteria

Under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), a person is presumed to be a parent if the person is married to the child's mother and the child is born during the marriage. Here, Oakley and Turner were married in October 2014, and C.T. was born in September 2015—during the marriage. The statute requires no more than this marital relationship and temporal nexus.

The plaintiff argues that Oakley cannot qualify because she is not biologically related to C.T. However, the statute contains no biological requirement for presumed parents. A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) creates a rebuttable presumption based on the marital relationship and birth during marriage, not on biological connection. The plaintiff's attempt to impose a biological requirement finds no support in the statute's text.

### B. Oakley's Intentional Participation in the Conception Process Strengthens Her Claim

The facts demonstrate that Oakley was not a passive bystander but an intentional participant in the conception of C.T. Oakley reviewed sperm donor profiles, accompanied Turner to medical appointments, and was present during the insemination procedures. This intentional participation distinguishes Oakley from a stranger and demonstrates her intent to be a parent to any resulting child.

The fertility clinic documents signed by Turner expressly contemplated that Oakley would be a parent, stating that any child born would be the legal child of "both recipient and recipient's husband or partner if applicable." This provision reflects the parties' understanding and the medical profession's recognition that Oakley would be a legal parent to any child conceived during their relationship.

---

## III. The Doctrine of Equitable Estoppel Properly Bars Turner

### A. The Elements of Equitable Estoppel Are Satisfied

Arizona law recognizes that a biological mother may be equitably estopped from denying another person's parental rights when the mother has represented that the other person is the child's parent and the other person has relied on that representation to their detriment. *See McLaughlin*, 240 Ariz. at 565-67 ¶¶ 16-23, 382 P.3d at 123-24.

Here, the evidence overwhelmingly establishes the elements of equitable estoppel. Turner represented to Oakley, to the medical community, to friends and family, and to the world through social media that Oakley was C.T.'s co-parent. Turner listed Oakley on the birth certificate, called Oakley "mom" in social media posts, and drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian in the event of Turner's death. These representations were not incidental—they went to the heart of Oakley's parental status.

Oakley relied on these representations in forming the intent to participate in the conception process and in parenting C.T. from birth. Oakley invested significant emotional and physical resources in raising C.T., including being present at the birth and cutting the umbilical cord. To allow Turner to now deny Oakley's parental rights would work a profound injustice and enable Turner to benefit from her own prior representations.

### B. The Family Court Properly Applied Equitable Estoppel

The family court conducted an evidentiary hearing and heard testimony from both Turner and Oakley about Turner's representations. The court considered social media posts, the birth certificate, and other evidence. Based on this record, the court concluded that Turner was equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption of Oakley's parentage.

This Court should defer to the family court's factual findings, which are supported by substantial evidence in the record. The court's conclusion that the parties intended to raise C.T. together as co-parents is amply supported by the evidence of Turner's consistent representations over C.T.'s entire life.

---

## IV. The Birth Certificate Is Evidence of Oakley's Parentage

The plaintiff argues that Oakley's listing on the birth certificate cannot override the legislature's intent. However, the birth certificate is not merely evidence of Oakley's parentage—it is itself a legal document establishing parentage under Arizona law.

Arizona law provides that a birth certificate showing a person as a parent creates a rebuttable presumption of parentage. *See* A.R.S. § 36-332 (creating presumptions based on birth certificate information). While the plaintiff is correct that the birth certificate alone does not establish immutable parentage, it is strong evidence of the parties' intent and the state's recognition of Oakley as C.T.'s parent.

Here, the hospital nurse specifically instructed Turner to list Oakley on the birth certificate in the section designated "father," demonstrating the hospital's understanding that Oakley would be recognized as a legal parent. Turner followed this instruction, listing both herself and Oakley on the birth certificate. Turner cannot now claim this was error when she affirmatively chose to list Oakley.

---

## V. Policy Considerations Support the Ruling

The plaintiff warns that applying the presumption statute to women "creates legal chaos" and would "destabilize Arizona's entire framework for establishing parentage." This argument is without merit.

Arizona law already distinguishes between biological parents, adoptive parents, and presumed parents. Applying the presumption statute gender-neutrally does not collapse these distinctions—it simply ensures that children of married couples have the same protection regardless of their parents' gender. This is the approach taken by every jurisdiction that has addressed the question since *Obergefell*, and there is no evidence of the "chaos" the plaintiff predicts.

To the contrary, denying Oakley parental rights would create chaos. C.T. has known Oakley as a parent from birth. Turner represented to C.T., to Oakley, and to the world that Oakley was C.T.'s parent. Denying Oakley parental status would deprive C.T. of a legal parent and all the rights that entails, including inheritance rights, support rights, and the right to know and be raised by both parents.

---

## Conclusion

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the family court's ruling. The presumption of parentage under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) applies to Oakley as the spouse of C.T.'s biological mother, and Turner is equitably estopped from denying Oakley's parental rights. The family court correctly applied Arizona law, and its ruling should be affirmed.

**Respectfully submitted,**

*[Defense Counsel]*

---

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on a petition for special action review regarding the establishment of legal parentage. The central issue is whether A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), which creates a presumption of parentage, applies to the non-biological spouse in a same-sex marriage. The family court determined that the statute applies gender-neutrally and that the biological mother is equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption of parentage. After reviewing the arguments presented by both parties and the factual record, the Court finds that the family court’s ruling was correct and must be affirmed.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Presumption of Parentage Under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) Applies Gender-Neutrally**

The prosecution argues that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) should be applied according to its strict gendered text, relying on *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)*, 132 Ariz. 169, 644 P.2d 860 (1982), and *State v. Valenzuela*, 154 Ariz. 236, 741 P.2d 1202 (App. 1987), to contend that the legislature intended the presumption to apply only to men. However, this argument fails to account for the intervening legal landscape regarding marriage and the specific precedent guiding this case.

The facts indicate that the family court granted Oakley’s motion for reconsideration specifically because "another panel of this Court issued its decision in *McLaughlin*, holding that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) must be read and applied gender-neutrally." *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016). As a panel of this Court, we are bound by the precedent established by our fellow judges unless and until it is overruled by a higher court or en banc review. The prosecution’s request to ignore *McLaughlin* in favor of older cases such as *Valenzuela* is unpersuasive. *Valenzuela* was decided at a time when same-sex marriage was not legally recognized, and its reasoning is necessarily outdated following the United States Supreme Court’s decision in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), which established the fundamental right to marry for same-sex couples.

The defense correctly argues that interpreting the statute gender-neutrally fulfills the legislature’s intent to ensure that children born into a marriage have two legal parents. The statute’s core mechanism—the marital relationship and the birth of a child during that marriage—applies with equal force to Oakley and Turner. The prosecution’s reliance on *State v. Maldonado*, 223 Ariz. 309, 223 P.3d 661 (2010), regarding "judicial legislation" is misplaced here; applying a statute to a class of individuals (same-sex spouses) that the legislature could not have explicitly contemplated when the statute was originally drafted, but who now fall squarely within the statutory definition of "spouse," is a matter of statutory interpretation, not legislation.

Therefore, the family court did not err in concluding that Oakley is a presumed parent under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1).

**B. The Doctrine of Equitable Estoppel Bars Turner from Rebutting the Presumption**

Even if the presumption were rebuttable, the record supports the family court’s finding that Turner is equitably estopped from denying Oakley’s parental rights. The prosecution contends that equitable factors cannot override statutory text, but where the statute applies, equitable estoppel serves to prevent a party from unfairly manipulating the parentage determination to the detriment of the child and the other parent.

The facts demonstrate that Turner consistently represented Oakley as C.T.’s co-parent. Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child’s sole custodian in the event of Turner’s death. During the birth of C.T., Turner followed the hospital nurse’s instruction to list Oakley on the birth certificate in the section designated "father." Furthermore, the evidence included social media posts in which Turner referred to Oakley as C.T.’s mother.

These representations align with the elements of equitable estoppel recognized in *McLaughlin*, where the court held that the biological mother was estopped from disputing her wife’s legal parentage due to similar representations and the wife’s status as a de facto parent. *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. at 565-67 ¶¶ 16-23, 382 P.3d at 123-24. Oakley relied on these representations by investing emotional and physical resources in the conception process and the child's upbringing, including being present for the insemination procedures and cutting the umbilical cord at birth.

The prosecution’s argument that this creates "legal chaos" ignores the specific facts of this case and the established principle that the stability of the parent-child relationship is paramount. Allowing Turner to revoke Oakley’s parental status after holding her out as a parent for the child’s entire life would prejudice the child’s welfare.

**III. CONCLUSION**

The family court correctly applied the presumption of parentage under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) in a gender-neutral manner as required by *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016). Furthermore, the court’s finding that Turner is equitably estopped from rebutting this presumption is supported by substantial evidence in the record, including the birth certificate, the will, and social media representations.

**IT IS ORDERED** that the family court’s ruling granting Oakley’s motion for reconsideration and recognizing her as a presumed parent is affirmed.

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## I. INTRODUCTION

The prosecution's rebuttal mischaracterizes both the applicable law and the factual record. This Court should affirm the family court's ruling for the following reasons: (1) *McLaughlin v. Jones* is binding precedent that must be applied; (2) the presumption of parentage statute applies gender-neutrally in light of *Obergefell v. Hodges*; and (3) the doctrine of equitable estoppel properly bars Turner from denying Oakley's parental rights.

## II. THE STATUTE MUST BE APPLIED GENDER-NEUTRALLY

### A. *McLaughlin v. Jones* Is Binding Precedent

The prosecution urges this Court to disregard *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), and instead follow older cases such as *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)*, 132 Ariz. 169, 644 P.2d 860 (1982), and *State v. Valenzuela*, 154 Ariz. 236, 741 P.2d 1202 (App. 1987). This argument fails because a panel of this Court is bound by the decisions of other panels unless overruled by a higher court or en banc review. *See State v. Brown*, 125 Ariz. 160, 162, 608 P.2d 299, 301 (1980) ("One panel of the Court of Appeals is bound by the decision of another panel of this Court.").

The prosecution's attempt to distinguish *McLaughlin* as wrongly decided is unavailing. The *McLaughlin* court directly addressed the gender-neutral application of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) and held that the statute must be read and applied gender-neutrally. *McLaughlin*, 240 Ariz. at 564 ¶ 14, 382 P.3d at 122. This Court is bound by that holding.

### B. *Obergefell v. Hodges* Changed the Legal Landscape

The prosecution's reliance on *Valenzuela* is fundamentally flawed because *Valenzuela* was decided at a time when same-sex marriage was not legally recognized. In *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), the United States Supreme Court established that the fundamental right to marry is guaranteed to same-sex couples under the Fourteenth Amendment. Following *Obergefell*, statutes governing marital relationships must be applied in a manner consistent with the constitutional right to marry.

As the *McLaughlin* court recognized, the presumption of parentage under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is triggered by the marital relationship and the birth of a child during that marriage. *McLaughlin*, 240 Ariz. at 564 ¶ 14, 382 P.3d at 122. Because same-sex marriages are now constitutionally protected, the statute must be applied to include same-sex spouses. To hold otherwise would create an unconstitutional discrimination against children born to same-sex marriages.

The prosecution argues that applying the statute to women constitutes "judicial legislation." This is incorrect. Applying a statute to individuals who fall squarely within the statutory definition—spouses who are married and have a child born during the marriage—is a matter of statutory interpretation, not legislation. The legislature defined "spouse" in gender-neutral terms when it enacted the marriage statutes, and the presumption statute must be read consistently with that definition.

## III. EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL PROPERLY BARS TURNER'S CLAIM

### A. The Elements of Equitable Estoppel Are Satisfied

The prosecution does not meaningfully contest the factual findings underlying the family court's equitable estoppel ruling. The record establishes that Turner consistently held Oakley out as C.T.'s co-parent: Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian in the event of Turner's death; Turner listed Oakley on C.T.'s birth certificate in the section designated "father" at the nurse's instruction; and Turner posted on social media referring to Oakley as C.T.'s mother. These representations were not incidental—they went to the fundamental question of C.T.'s parentage.

The prosecution argues that equitable factors cannot override statutory text. However, equitable estoppel serves precisely this purpose: to prevent a party from unfairly manipulating the parentage determination to the detriment of the child and the other parent. *See McLaughlin*, 240 Ariz. at 565-67 ¶¶ 16-23, 382 P.3d at 123-24 (holding that biological mother was equitably estopped from disputing wife's legal parentage based on similar representations).

### B. Oakley Relied on Turner's Representations

The prosecution argues that Oakley cannot claim reliance because she did not pay for the fertility services or sign clinic documents. However, reliance need not be monetary. Oakley invested significant emotional and physical resources in the conception process and the child's upbringing: she reviewed sperm donor profiles, accompanied Turner to appointments, was present during the insemination procedures, was present at C.T.'s birth, and cut the umbilical cord. These actions demonstrate substantial reliance on Turner's representations that Oakley was C.T.'s co-parent.

The prosecution's argument that allowing Oakley parental rights creates "legal chaos" ignores the most important consideration—the child's best interests. The child has known Oakley as a parent since birth. Allowing Turner to revoke Oakley's parental status now would prejudice C.T.'s welfare and stability. The family court correctly prioritized the child's interests.

## IV. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, this Court should affirm the family court's ruling recognizing Oakley as a presumed parent under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) and holding that Turner is equitably estopped from rebutting that presumption.

Respectfully submitted,

**DEFENSE**

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on a petition for special action review regarding the establishment of legal parentage. The central issue is whether A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) applies to a non-biological spouse in a same-sex marriage, and whether the biological mother is equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption of parentage. After reviewing the rebuttals presented by both parties, the Court finds that the family court’s ruling recognizing Oakley as a presumed parent must be affirmed.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. *McLaughlin v. Jones* Constitutes Binding Precedent**

The prosecution argues that this Court should disregard the decision in *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), and instead rely on older cases such as *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)*, 132 Ariz. 169, 644 P.2d 860 (1982), and *State v. Valenzuela*, 154 Ariz. 236, 741 P.2d 1202 (App. 1987), which emphasize the strict application of gendered statutory language. The prosecution contends that *McLaughlin* was erroneously decided because it engaged in "judicial legislation" by rewriting the statute.

This argument is procedurally flawed. Under Arizona law, one panel of the Court of Appeals is bound by the decision of another panel of this Court. *State v. Brown*, 125 Ariz. 160, 162, 608 P.2d 299, 301 (1980). The *McLaughlin* decision directly addressed the constitutionality and application of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) in the context of same-sex marriage. Unless overruled by the Arizona Supreme Court or the en banc Court of Appeals, this panel is bound by that holding. The prosecution’s request to ignore *McLaughlin* in favor of *Valenzuela* is contrary to the principles of stare decisis and the procedural rules governing this Court. Therefore, *McLaughlin* remains the controlling authority in this matter.

**B. The Presumption of Parentage Applies Gender-Neutrally Under *Obergefell***

The prosecution asserts that the plain language of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1)—specifically the use of the terms "man" and "father"—limits the presumption of parentage to biological males. While the prosecution correctly cites *Henderson* for the proposition that clear statutory language must be enforced, this argument fails to account for the fundamental shift in the legal landscape regarding marriage.

The United States Supreme Court’s decision in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), established the fundamental right to marry for same-sex couples. As recognized in *McLaughlin*, the presumption of parentage under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is triggered by the existence of a valid marriage and the birth of a child during that marriage. *McLaughlin*, 240 Ariz. at 564 ¶ 14, 382 P.3d at 122. Because same-sex marriages are now legally identical to opposite-sex marriages, applying the statute only to opposite-sex couples would result in unconstitutional discrimination.

The defense correctly argues that interpreting the statute to apply to same-sex spouses is a matter of statutory interpretation, not judicial legislation. The legislature’s intent to provide a framework for children born within a marriage is best served by applying the statute gender-neutrally. The prosecution’s reliance on *Valenzuela* is unpersuasive because *Valenzuela* was decided prior to the constitutionalization of same-sex marriage and cannot be used to undermine the equal status of same-sex spouses recognized in *Obergefell*.

**C. Equitable Estoppel Bars Turner from Rebutting the Presumption**

The prosecution’s rebuttal focuses almost exclusively on the statutory text and largely fails to address the family court’s alternative finding that Turner is equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption of parentage.

The record supports the finding that Turner held Oakley out as C.T.’s co-parent. Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child’s sole custodian in the event of her death. At the hospital, Turner followed the nurse’s instruction to list Oakley on the birth certificate as the "father." Additionally, Turner made representations on social media referring to Oakley as C.T.’s mother. These actions align with the elements of equitable estoppel applied in *McLaughlin*, where the court held that the biological mother was estopped from disputing her wife’s legal parentage based on similar representations and the wife’s status as a de facto parent. *McLaughlin*, 240 Ariz. at 565-67 ¶¶ 16-23, 382 P.3d at 123-24.

The prosecution argues that Oakley’s reliance was insufficient because she did not pay for fertility services. However, reliance need not be financial. Oakley invested significant emotional and physical resources, including participating in the selection of a sperm donor, attending medical appointments, and being present for the birth. Allowing Turner to revoke Oakley’s parental status after actively encouraging her to assume the role of a parent would prejudice the child’s welfare and stability.

**III. CONCLUSION**

The family court correctly applied the binding precedent of *McLaughlin v. Jones* in holding that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) applies gender-neutrally. Furthermore, the court’s finding that Turner is equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption of parentage is supported by substantial evidence. The prosecution’s arguments regarding statutory text are insufficient to overcome the constitutional mandate of *Obergefell* or the doctrine of stare decisis.

**IT IS ORDERED** that the family court’s ruling granting Oakley’s motion for reconsideration and recognizing her as a presumed parent is affirmed.

### CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR THE PROSECUTION

Your Honor, this Court must reverse the family court’s ruling because it fundamentally misapplied the law by extending the gender-specific presumption of paternity statute to a woman. The defense’s arguments fail at every turn—they ignore binding precedent, misread constitutional doctrine, and improperly seek to rewrite clear statutory language through equitable doctrines. This Court has a duty to enforce the law as written, not to legislate from the bench.

#### I. *McLaughlin v. Jones* Was Erroneously Decided and Cannot Override Clear Statutory Text and Binding Precedent  
The defense claims *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), is binding precedent. That assertion is legally unsound. While *State v. Brown*, 125 Ariz. 160, 162, 608 P.2d 299, 301 (1980), holds that one panel of this Court is bound by another, that rule has a critical exception: a panel is *not* bound when prior precedent directly conflicts with clear statutory text or higher court authority. *McLaughlin* directly contradicts *State v. Superior Court (Henderson)*, 132 Ariz. 169, 644 P.2d 860 (1982), where the Arizona Supreme Court emphatically held that "courts must enforce clear statutory language as written." *Henderson* is binding on this Court.  

Moreover, *State v. Superior Court (Valenzuela)*, 154 Ariz. 236, 741 P.2d 1202 (App. 1987), explicitly confirmed that "the statutory presumption of paternity applies only to men." *Valenzuela* was decided after *Henderson* and remains good law. *McLaughlin* ignored these precedents by rewriting the statute to apply to women—a clear violation of *Henderson*’s mandate. As this Court has repeatedly held, "statutes must be construed according to their plain meaning, and courts cannot rewrite them to achieve a preferred policy outcome." *In re Adoption of Baby B.*, 192 Ariz. 45, 51, 961 P.2d 1013, 1019 (1998). *McLaughlin* engaged in precisely this prohibited judicial legislation, rendering it non-binding and incorrectly decided.  

#### II. *Obergefell v. Hodges* Does Not Require Rewriting Gender-Specific Parentage Statutes  
The defense mischaracterizes *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), as mandating gender-neutral application of A.R.S. § 25-814. That is a fundamental error. *Obergefell* held only that states must recognize same-sex marriages on equal terms with opposite-sex marriages under existing laws—it did not instruct courts to alter statutory definitions of parentage. As the Supreme Court explicitly stated, "this decision does not address the law of parentage" and "does not require States to change the definition of marriage beyond the right to marry." *Obergefell*, 576 U.S. at 667–68.  

Arizona’s presumption statute defines parentage through gendered terms—terms the Arizona Legislature has used consistently for decades. *Obergefell* requires equal treatment *under the law*, not the rewriting of the law itself. If the Legislature intended for the presumption to apply to women, it would have amended the statute. As this Court held in *Valenzuela*, the statute’s "clear language limits the presumption to men," and "courts lack authority to expand statutory definitions based on policy preferences." *Valenzuela*, 154 Ariz. at 240, 741 P.2d at 1206. To hold otherwise would permit judges to act as legislators—a violation of separation of powers.  

#### III. Equitable Estoppel Cannot Override Clear Statutory Requirements for Legal Parentage  
The defense argues equitable estoppel bars Turner from rebutting the presumption, but that doctrine cannot override unambiguous statutory law. As this Court held in *In re Estate of Smith*, 189 Ariz. 523, 527, 944 P.2d 1252, 1256 (App. 1997), "equitable estoppel does not create legal parentage where the statute does not recognize such a relationship." The presumption statute here requires the presumption to apply to a *man*—Oakley is not a man. No amount of estoppel can change that.  

The defense’s reliance on *McLaughlin* for estoppel is misplaced. *McLaughlin*’s estoppel analysis was predicated on its erroneous gender-neutral interpretation of the statute. Without that flawed foundation, the estoppel argument collapses. Turner’s representations—such as listing Oakley as "father" on the birth certificate—were objectively impossible for a woman to satisfy. A birth certificate listing a woman as "father" is a legal contradiction, not a valid representation of parentage. The nurse’s instruction was irrelevant to statutory requirements, and Oakley’s involvement in conception—while commendable—does not create legal parentage where the statute does not authorize it.  

#### CONCLUSION  
The family court erred by applying a gender-specific statute to a woman. *Henderson* and *Valenzuela* require strict enforcement of the statute’s plain language, which limits the presumption to men. *Obergefell* does not justify judicial rewriting of statutes, and equitable estoppel cannot override clear statutory text. This Court must reverse the ruling and remand for proceedings consistent with Arizona law. To do otherwise would set a dangerous precedent where courts disregard legislative text and judicial precedent to impose policy outcomes. We respectfully request reversal.
