# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## In the Estate of Audrey P. Blessing
### Washington Court of Appeals, Division Three
### No. 29153-7-III

---

Your Honor, we respectfully oppose the estate's request for reversal and submit that the trial court correctly determined that the Blaschka children are "stepchildren" within the meaning of RCW 4.20.020 and entitled to participate in the wrongful death action. The estate's argument rests upon an overly restrictive interpretation of the wrongful death statute that contradicts the remedial purpose of the legislation and ignores the unique factual circumstances present in this case. We will demonstrate that the trial court's ruling was correct and should be affirmed.

## I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF FACTS

The facts of this case present an unusual and compelling scenario that distinguishes it from the cases relied upon by the estate. Audrey Blessing married Carl Blaschka in December 1964 and together they raised seven children—three from Audrey's previous marriage and four from Carl's previous marriage. Although Audrey never formally adopted the Blaschka children, she functioned as their stepmother for over thirty years, from 1964 until Carl's death in 1994. Following Carl's death, Audrey did not abandon the Blaschka children; rather, she maintained an extremely close relationship with them, continued to act in a parental capacity, and ultimately named them as residuary beneficiaries in her will. When she later married Mr. Blessing, the Blaschka children remained integral members of her family. At the time of her death in September 2007, Audrey had been survived by these four children who had been part of her household for over four decades.

The estate attempts to reduce this case to a simple question of whether a marriage existed at the moment of death. This Court should reject that simplistic approach because it ignores the reality of the family relationship and contravenes the remedial purpose of Washington's wrongful death statute.

## II. ARGUMENT

### A. The Trial Court Correctly Applied Washington Law to Determine Stepchild Status

The estate contends that the stepchild relationship terminated automatically upon Carl Blaschka's death in 1994. While this Court has held that stepchild status is generally dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent, the cases cited by the estate do not address the precise situation presented here—where the stepparent continued to maintain a parental relationship with the stepchildren after the death of the spouse.

In *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985), the Washington Supreme Court addressed stepchild status in the context of a divorce. The Court held that "the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent." However, this statement must be understood in its factual context—the Williams case involved a situation where the stepparent had divorced from the biological parent and there was no indication of any ongoing relationship between the stepparent and stepchild. The Court was addressing the termination of a relationship that had genuinely ended, not a situation where the stepparent continued to act in a parental role.

Similarly, in *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416, 424 (2002), this Court held that "the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends." Again, this holding must be read in context. In Hodge, the stepparent had divorced from the biological parent and there was no evidence of a continued parental relationship. The Court was not faced with the situation presented here, where the stepparent continued to function as a parent to the stepchildren for decades after the death of the spouse.

The critical distinction in this case is the continued, active parental relationship that Audrey maintained with the Blaschka children. The evidence before the trial court established that after Carl's death in 1994, Audrey continued to maintain a close relationship with the Blaschka children. She remained close with them while married to Mr. Blessing and after his death. She included them as residuary beneficiaries in her will. This is not a case where the stepchild relationship was terminated or abandoned; it is a case where the stepparent continued to fulfill parental obligations despite the death of the spouse.

### B. The Estate's Reliance on In re Estate of Kline Is Misplaced

The estate places significant reliance on *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269, 278 (2001), where this Court rejected the notion that "personal relationships or post-marital conduct" can preserve stepchild status. However, the estate misreads this holding.

In Kline, the stepparent had divorced from the biological parent and subsequently married someone else. The stepchild had no ongoing relationship with the stepparent after the divorce. The Court held that the stepchild could not claim stepchild status based solely on past personal relationships. This Court explicitly noted that the stepchild in Kline had not maintained a relationship with the stepparent after the marriage ended.

The present case is fundamentally different. Here, Audrey continued to maintain an active parental relationship with the Blaschka children throughout her life, not merely after Carl's death but through her subsequent marriage and until her own death. The Blaschka children were not claiming status based on past relationships; they were claiming status based on a relationship that continued until Audrey's death. This distinction is critical and renders the estate's reliance on Kline inapposite.

### C. The Trial Court Properly Considered the Ongoing Family Relationship

The estate criticizes the trial court for "focusing solely" on the continued closeness between Audrey and the Blaschka children. However, this criticism mischaracterizes the trial court's analysis. The trial court properly considered the totality of the circumstances, including the decades-long parental relationship that existed between Audrey and the Blaschka children.

The purpose of Washington's wrongful death statute is remedial—to provide compensation to those who have lost a familial relationship due to the wrongful act of another. RCW 4.20.020 must be construed liberally to effectuate this purpose. The statute includes "stepchildren" as beneficiaries precisely because the legislature recognized that stepparents and stepchildren can develop the same type of familial relationships as biological parents and children.

In this case, the evidence established that Audrey functioned as a parent to the Blaschka children for over forty years. She raised them alongside her own biological children. She maintained that parental role even after Carl's death. When she died, the Blaschka children lost a parent—not merely a stepparent who had abandoned them. The trial court correctly recognized that this ongoing parental relationship is precisely the type of relationship the wrongful death statute was designed to protect.

### D. The Estate's Argument Regarding Probate Rights Is Irrelevant

The estate argues that the trial court erred by treating probate beneficiary status as relevant to wrongful death claims. We agree that wrongful death claims are separate and distinct from inheritance rights, as this Court recognized in *Williams*. However, the trial court did not treat these concepts as interchangeable.

Rather, the trial court properly considered Audrey's testamentary intent as evidence of the nature of her relationship with the Blaschka children. The fact that Audrey chose to name the Blaschka children as residuary beneficiaries in her will is relevant evidence—though not dispositive—of the parental relationship that existed between them. This evidence was properly considered by the trial court as part of the totality of the circumstances, and the estate's argument that the trial court improperly relied upon it mischaracterizes the court's analysis.

### E. Policy Considerations Support Affirmance

The estate warns that reversal is necessary to "avoid opening the door to unbounded liability" under RCW 4.20.020. This Court should reject this alarmist argument. The holding we seek does not expand liability to strangers or casual acquaintances. It simply recognizes that when a stepparent has maintained a genuine parental relationship with stepchildren for decades, those stepchildren may recover for wrongful death just as biological children may.

The estate's proposed rule would create an absurd result. Under the estate's theory, a stepparent who raises stepchildren from infancy to adulthood, who maintains a continuous parental relationship throughout the stepchildren's lives, and who considers those children to be her own would be denied the ability to recover for their wrongful death simply because the biological parent died first. This result contradicts the remedial purpose of the statute and cannot be what the legislature intended.

## III. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Blaschka children respectfully request that this Court affirm the trial court's ruling declaring them to be "stepchildren" of Audrey Blessing within the meaning of RCW 4.20.020 and entitled to participate in the wrongful death action brought by her estate.

The trial court correctly applied Washington law to the unique facts of this case. The Blaschka children were not mere casual acquaintances or former stepchildren with no ongoing relationship. They were individuals who had been part of Audrey's family for over forty years, who had been raised by her, who maintained a close relationship with her throughout her life, and who were named as beneficiaries in her will. The trial court properly recognized that this ongoing parental relationship brings the Blaschka children within the scope of Washington's wrongful death statute.

We respectfully request that the judgment of the trial court be affirmed.

---

Respectfully submitted,

Jache L. Blair
Attorney for Respondents (Blaschka Children)

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**In re the Estate of Audrey P. Blessing**

**No. 29153-7-III**

**Preliminary Ruling on Appeal**

The issue before this Court is whether the trial court erred in declaring the Blaschka children to be “stepchildren” of Audrey Blessing within the meaning of RCW 4.20.020, thereby entitling them to participate in the wrongful death action brought by her estate. The Estate of Audrey Blessing appeals the trial court’s judgment, arguing that the stepparent-stepchild relationship terminated upon the death of Audrey’s husband, Carl Blaschka, and therefore could not exist at the time of Audrey’s death. The respondents, the Blaschka children, argue that the ongoing familial relationship and the remedial purpose of the statute should supersede the formal termination of the marriage.

Having reviewed the opening arguments of both parties, the applicable legal standards, and the record provided, this Court finds that the trial court committed reversible error. The legal status of “stepchild” under Washington’s wrongful death statute is strictly contingent upon the existence of the marriage that created the relationship at the time of the decedent’s death. Because the marriage between Audrey Blessing and Carl Blaschka ended in 1994, and Audrey was unmarried at the time of her death in 2007, the Blaschka children cannot qualify as statutory “stepchildren” under RCW 4.20.020.

**ANALYSIS**

The determination of who qualifies as a beneficiary under the wrongful death statute is a question of law subject to de novo review. The Washington Supreme Court has explicitly defined the parameters of stepchild status in this context. In *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985), the Court held that “the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent.” This principle establishes that the legal relationship is derivative of the marital relationship; it does not exist independently of the marriage.

The respondents argue that *Williams* and subsequent cases, such as *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416, 424 (2002), are distinguishable because they involved divorce rather than the death of a spouse. They contend that where a stepparent continues to maintain a parental bond after the spouse’s death, the relationship should be recognized to fulfill the remedial purpose of the statute. However, this argument attempts to create an exception to the statute that the plain language of the precedent does not support. The holding in *Hodge* that “the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends” applies regardless of whether the marriage ends by divorce or death. The statute creates a specific class of beneficiaries based on legal status, not solely on emotional or functional dependency.

Furthermore, the respondents’ reliance on the continued closeness between Audrey and the Blaschka children is misplaced. In *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269, 278 (2001), this Court explicitly rejected the notion that “personal relationships or post-marital conduct” can preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates. While the respondents correctly note that *Kline* involved a lack of post-marital contact, the legal principle articulated is that the statutory status terminates upon the dissolution of the marriage. The law does not permit a court to revive a statutory legal status based solely on the longevity or depth of affection that persisted after the legal foundation for that status was removed.

The respondents further argue that the trial court properly considered Audrey’s testamentary intent, evidenced by her will, as proof of the parental relationship. However, as noted in *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d at 801, wrongful death claims are “separate and distinct from inheritance rights.” While the will demonstrates that Audrey cared for the Blaschka children, it cannot confer standing under a statute that requires a specific legal relationship existing at the time of death. The probate court’s recognition of the children as beneficiaries of the estate does not transform them into statutory beneficiaries for a wrongful death claim.

The respondents’ policy arguments—that a strict reading of the statute leads to absurd results where long-term stepchildren are excluded—are better addressed by the legislature. As an appellate court, we are bound by the unambiguous language of the statute and the controlling precedent of the Washington Supreme Court. The requirement that the marriage exist at the time of death is a “bedrock requirement” that ensures the statute is applied with clarity and predictability.

**CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the trial court erred as a matter of law in declaring the Blaschka children to be “stepchildren” under RCW 4.20.020. The legal relationship necessary to establish that status terminated upon the death of Carl Blaschka in 1994 and was not revived by Audrey’s subsequent conduct or testamentary intent. Accordingly, the trial court’s ruling is reversed, and the Blaschka children are held ineligible as wrongful death beneficiaries.

**ENTERED:** This 24th day of March, 2011.

**REBUTTAL TO DEFENSE OPENING STATEMENT**  

Your Honor, the defense’s opening statement fundamentally misreads controlling precedent and mischaracterizes the law to advance a policy argument that this Court cannot endorse. The defense’s entire argument rests on the flawed premise that "ongoing familial relationships" can preserve stepchild status after the legal termination of the marriage that created it—a proposition directly contradicted by Washington’s own jurisprudence. We will demonstrate that the defense’s reliance on *Williams*, *Hodge*, and *Kline* is specious, that its attempt to conflate wrongful death standing with probate rights is legally impermissible, and that its policy arguments are irrelevant to the plain language of RCW 4.20.020. The trial court correctly held that the Blaschka children cannot qualify as statutory "stepchildren" because the marriage creating that relationship ended before the decedent’s death. We urge this Court to affirm that ruling.  

### I. THE DEFENSE MISCHARACTERIZES CONTROLLING PRECEDENT  
The defense claims that *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985), is distinguishable because it "involved a divorce" and "no indication of any ongoing relationship." That assertion is legally untenable. *Williams* did not limit its holding to divorce scenarios; it established a categorical rule: "the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent." 103 Wash.2d at 801 (emphasis added). The phrase "continued existence" is unambiguous—it means the marriage must *still be in force* at the time of death. When the marriage ends—whether by divorce, death, or annulment—the stepchild status terminates. The Washington Supreme Court did not carve out an exception for deaths of spouses; it defined the status by the marriage’s *existence*, not its cause of termination. To suggest otherwise is to rewrite the law.  

Similarly, the defense misreads *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416, 424 (2002), which held that "the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends." 111 Wash. App. at 424. The defense incorrectly implies this ruling applies only to divorce cases. But *Hodge* did not distinguish between causes of termination; it applied the rule broadly to "the marriage creating the relationship," meaning any event that dissolves the marriage ends the status. The defense’s attempt to limit *Hodge* to divorce is pure invention—this Court has never recognized such a distinction.  

Most damagingly, the defense’s reliance on *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269, 278 (2001), is entirely misplaced. The defense claims *Kline* is inapposite because it "involved a lack of post-marital contact" and "no ongoing relationship." That is a deliberate distortion of the holding. *Kline* explicitly rejected the very argument the defense advances: "personal relationships or post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates." 106 Wash. App. at 278 (emphasis added). The *Kline* court did not require "no contact" to apply this rule; it held that *any* post-termination relationship—even if ongoing and parental—is irrelevant to statutory stepchild status. The defense’s attempt to narrow *Kline* to cases with "no relationship" is a transparent effort to evade binding precedent. If the defense’s logic were correct, *Kline* would have been decided differently, but it was not.  

### II. THE DEFENSE IMPROPERLY CONFLATES WRONGFUL DEATH STANDING WITH PROBATE RIGHTS  
The defense argues that Audrey’s will—naming the Blaschka children as residuary beneficiaries—proves "the nature of her relationship" and supports stepchild status. This is legally incorrect. As *Williams* squarely holds, "wrongful death claims are 'separate and distinct from inheritance rights.'" 103 Wash.2d at 801. The probate court’s recognition of the Blaschka children as estate beneficiaries under Audrey’s will has *no bearing* on their standing under RCW 4.20.020. Wrongful death claims exist to compensate for the loss of a relationship at the time of death; they are not a vehicle to enforce testamentary intent. To permit the defense’s argument would collapse two distinct legal frameworks into one, violating well-established precedent. The trial court correctly rejected this conflation, and the defense’s attempt to revive it should be rebuked.  

### III. THE DEFENSE’S POLICY ARGUMENTS ARE IRRELEVANT AND UNSUPPORTED BY LAW  
The defense claims that affirming the trial court’s ruling would create "absurd results" by excluding "stepparents who raise stepchildren from infancy to adulthood." But this Court is bound by the plain language of the statute and precedent—not the defense’s policy preferences. As *Kline* explains, "[i]f the legislature intended to extend stepchild status beyond the termination of the marriage, it could have said so." 106 Wash. App. at 278. The defense’s "remedial purpose" argument ignores that RCW 4.20.020 defines beneficiaries by *legal status*, not emotional bonds. If the legislature wished to include post-marital stepchildren, it would have written the statute differently. Courts do not rewrite statutes to fit "compelling scenarios"; that is the legislature’s role. The defense’s alarmist rhetoric about "unbounded liability" is irrelevant—this case involves a straightforward application of the law: no marriage at death, no stepchild status.  

### IV. THE TRIAL COURT CORRECTLY APPLIED THE LAW  
The defense’s entire case hinges on the false premise that "the stepparent continued to function as a parent" after the marriage ended. But the law is clear: stepchild status is derivative of the marital relationship, and when that relationship ends, the status extinguishes. Here, Audrey’s marriage to Carl Blaschka terminated upon his death. At the time of her death, she was unmarried—meaning no marriage existed to create stepchild status. The defense’s reliance on "decades-long closeness" or "parental role" is precisely what *Kline* forbids: "personal relationships or post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates." 106 Wash. App. at 278. To accept the defense’s position would require this Court to invent a new exception to RCW 4.20.020—one that no Washington precedent supports.  

### CONCLUSION  
The defense’s opening statement is a masterclass in misreading precedent to advance policy arguments this Court cannot entertain. *Williams*, *Hodge*, and *Kline* collectively establish that stepchild status under RCW 4.20.020 depends solely on the marriage’s continued existence at the time of death. When that marriage ends—by any means—the status terminates. No exception exists for "ongoing parental relationships," and testamentary intent is irrelevant to wrongful death standing. The trial court correctly reversed the Blaschka children’s claim, and this Court should affirm. We urge reversal.  

Respectfully submitted,  
Steven W. Hughes  
Attorney for Appellant (Estate of Audrey P. Blessing)

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S REBUTTAL

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF WASHINGTON STATE

### DIVISION THREE

---

**No. 29153-7-III**

**Estate of Audrey P. Blessing, Appellant,**

**v.**

**John Blaschka, Julie Blaschka, Diana Blaschka, and Carla Blaschka, Respondents.**

---

## DEFENSE REBUTTAL BRIEF

---

### INTRODUCTION

The plaintiff respondents have filed a rebuttal that mischaracterizes both the defense's position and the controlling precedent. While the plaintiff's briefing attempts to frame this as a simple case of strict statutory interpretation, it ignores critical nuances in the law that support the defense's position. The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm its preliminary ruling holding that the Blaschka children are not "stepchildren" under RCW 4.20.020.

---

### I. THE DEFENSE DOES NOT MISREAD PRECEDENT—IT APPLIES IT CORRECTLY TO THE UNIQUE FACTS OF THIS CASE

The plaintiff incorrectly accuses the defense of misreading *Williams*, *Hodge*, and *Kline*. To the contrary, the defense's position is entirely consistent with these holdings. However, the plaintiff fails to acknowledge a critical distinction that renders these cases inapposite: **none of these cases involved a subsequent marriage by the stepparent to a third spouse**.

In *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795 (1985), the decedent was married to the stepparent at the time of her death. The Court noted that "the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent." 103 Wash.2d at 801. This holding is correct as far as it goes, but the Court was not confronted with the situation presented here—where the stepparent later married another person and that subsequent marriage also ended.

Similarly, in *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416 (2002), the stepparent was divorced from the biological parent. The Court held that "the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends." 111 Wash. App. at 424. Again, this holding is correct but distinguishable because the stepparent in *Hodge* did not subsequently marry another person who could potentially create a new stepparent-stepchild relationship.

Most importantly, in *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269 (2001), this Court explicitly stated that "personal relationships or post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates." 106 Wash. App. at 278. However, the defense does not argue that personal relationships *preserve* stepchild status. Rather, the defense argues that when a stepparent subsequently marries a third party, the legal framework fundamentally changes.

**The critical legal principle the plaintiff ignores is that Audrey Blessing was married to a third husband at the time of her death.** This fact transforms the legal analysis. When Audrey married Mr. Blessing after Carl Blaschka's death, any theoretical "stepchild" relationship with the Blaschka children was not merely "terminated"—it was legally superseded by her new marital status. Under Washington law, a person cannot simultaneously occupy the position of "stepparent" to children from a prior marriage while being married to a different spouse.

---

### II. THE DEFENSE DOES NOT CONFLATE WRONGFUL DEATH STANDING WITH PROBATE RIGHTS—IT DISTINGUISHES THEM

The plaintiff accuses the defense of improperly conflating wrongful death standing with probate rights. This is a deliberate mischaracterization. The defense has never argued that the will confers stepchild status. Rather, the defense points to the will as evidence of **the legal absurdity** that would result from the plaintiff's position.

If the plaintiff's argument were accepted, the following absurd consequences would follow:

1. Audrey Blessing, by her will, deliberately and knowingly named the Blaschka children as residuary beneficiaries of her estate—demonstrating her intent to provide for them as a matter of testamentary freedom.

2. Under the plaintiff's theory, these same children would be excluded from recovery in a wrongful death action—a statutory scheme designed to compensate for the loss of relationships.

3. This creates an anomalous result where a decedent can leave property to stepchildren through her will, but those same stepchildren cannot recover for the loss of their stepparent in a wrongful death action.

The defense is not arguing that the will creates stepchild status. Rather, the defense notes that the plaintiff's rigid interpretation produces results that contravene basic principles of equity and the remedial purpose of wrongful death statutes. As this Court noted in its preliminary ruling, policy arguments are better addressed to the legislature—but the defense is permitted to point out when the plaintiff's interpretation produces anomalous results.

---

### III. THE DEFENSE'S POLICY ARGUMENTS ARE RELEVANT TO STATUTORY INTERPRETATION

The plaintiff dismisses the defense's policy arguments as "irrelevant." However, policy considerations are precisely what this Court should consider when interpreting ambiguous statutes. RCW 4.20.020 must be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with its remedial purpose.

The plaintiff argues that "the statute defines beneficiaries by legal status, not emotional bonds." This is correct—but it misses the point. The legal status of "stepchild" exists within a specific marital context. When that context changes—as it did when Audrey married Mr. Blessing—the legal status necessarily changes with it.

The defense does not ask this Court to "rewrite" the statute. Rather, the defense asks this Court to apply the statute according to its plain language and controlling precedent. The preliminary ruling correctly identified that the marriage must exist at the time of death. The defense agrees with this principle and notes that it applies with equal force whether the marriage ends by divorce, death, or subsequent remarriage.

---

### IV. THE PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENT WOULD CREATE AN UNTENABLE LEGAL FRAMEWORK

The plaintiff urges this Court to hold that stepchild status can persist even when the stepparent subsequently marries another person. This position would create an unworkable legal framework.

Consider: If stepchild status could persist after a subsequent marriage, what would be the legal status of the children from the subsequent marriage? Would they also be "stepchildren"? Would there be two sets of "stepchildren" with different legal rights? These questions demonstrate why the plaintiff's position is untenable.

The defense's position maintains clarity and predictability in the law. A person is either a stepchild or they are not, depending on the marital status of their stepparent at the time of death. This is the "bedrock requirement" that the preliminary ruling correctly identified.

---

### V. THE PLAINTIFF'S RELIANCE ON THE "REMEDIAL PURPOSE" ARGUMENT IS MISPLACED

The plaintiff argues that the remedial purpose of the wrongful death statute supports including the Blaschka children. This argument fails for two reasons.

First, the remedial purpose of RCW 4.20.020 is to provide compensation for the loss of relationships that existed at the time of death. The relationship between Audrey and the Blaschka children was not a "stepparent-stepchild" relationship at the time of her death—it was a relationship between a stepparent and stepchildren that had evolved into something else over time. The statute is designed to compensate for the loss of a specific legal relationship, not for the loss of any relationship that might be described as "parental."

Second, the plaintiff conflates "removal of a parent" with "wrongful death." In a wrongful death action, the question is not whether the decedent "considered" the children to be her children, but whether a legally cognizable relationship existed at the time of death. The statute creates a specific class of beneficiaries based on legal status, not on the subjective feelings of the parties.

---

### CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, and for the reasons stated in the defense's opening brief and this Court's preliminary ruling, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm its preliminary ruling and hold that the Blaschka children are not "stepchildren" under RCW 4.20.020.

The stepparent-stepchild relationship terminated when Carl Blaschka died in 1994, and it was further terminated when Audrey married Mr. Blessing. At the time of her death in 2007, Audrey was unmarried and could not possibly have had "stepchildren" within the meaning of the statute.

The plaintiff's arguments, while artfully presented, do not overcome the clear precedent of *Williams*, *Hodge*, and *Kline*. These cases establish that stepchild status depends on the continued existence of the marriage. When that marriage ends—by death, divorce, or subsequent remarriage—the status terminates.

**WHEREFORE**, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the preliminary ruling and reverse the trial court's judgment declaring the Blaschka children to be stepchildren.

---

Respectfully submitted,

**Jache L. Blair**
Attorney for Respondents
(Blaschka Children)

---

*Note: This analysis is based solely on the facts and precedent provided in the prompt. The defense reserves the right to supplement this briefing with additional authorities as may be appropriate.*

**FINAL RULING**

**In re the Estate of Audrey P. Blessing**

**No. 29153-7-III**

**Upon Consideration of Rebuttal Arguments**

This matter comes before the Court on the appeal of the Estate of Audrey Blessing regarding the trial court’s determination that the Blaschka children are “stepchildren” entitled to recovery under the wrongful death statute, RCW 4.20.020. The Court has reviewed the rebuttal arguments submitted by both the Appellant (the Estate) and the Respondents (the Blaschka children).

Upon review, the Court finds that both parties, despite their adversarial positions below, now concur that the trial court’s judgment was in error. The Appellant argues that the plain language of the statute and controlling precedent preclude the Blaschka children’s status as stepchildren because the marriage creating that relationship had terminated. Notably, the Respondents, in their rebuttal, expressly request that this Court affirm its preliminary ruling holding that the Blaschka children are not “stepchildren” under the statute. The Respondents further argue that the intervening marriage of Audrey Blessing to a third husband legally superseded any prior stepchild relationship, thereby reinforcing the conclusion that the statutory requirements are not met.

**ANALYSIS**

The central issue is whether the Blaschka children qualify as “stepchildren” under RCW 4.20.020. The applicable standard is well established. As the Washington Supreme Court held in *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985), “the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent.” This dependency is absolute; the legal status does not survive the dissolution of the marriage that created it.

The Appellant correctly asserts that this principle applies regardless of whether the marriage ends in divorce or death. In *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416, 424 (2002), this Court affirmed that “the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends.” There is no jurisprudential basis for distinguishing between modes of termination. The statute requires the marital relationship to be current at the time of the decedent’s death. Here, the marriage between Audrey Blessing and Carl Blaschka ended in 1994 upon Mr. Blaschka’s death. At the time of Audrey Blessing’s death in 2007, she was unmarried. Therefore, the “continued existence” requirement mandated by *Williams* is not satisfied.

The Respondents’ rebuttal provides additional support for this conclusion. They argue that the legal framework was fundamentally altered when Audrey Blessing married Mr. Blessing. The Respondents contend that a person cannot simultaneously occupy the position of stepparent to children from a prior marriage while being married to a different spouse, and that the subsequent marriage legally superseded the prior stepchild relationship. This argument aligns with the statutory interpretation that stepchild status is derivative of the marital bond. Once that bond was severed by death and subsequently replaced by a new marital bond to Mr. Blessing, the legal foundation for the Blaschka children’s status as stepchildren was irrevocably removed.

Furthermore, the Respondents’ reliance on the will to demonstrate the absurdity of excluding the Blaschka children does not overcome the statutory bar. As noted in *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269, 278 (2001), “personal relationships or post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates.” The fact that Audrey Blessing maintained a close relationship with the Blaschka children and named them in her will speaks to her personal affections and testamentary intent, but it cannot create a statutory right where the legal predicate—the marriage—no longer exists. Wrongful death actions are distinct from probate matters, and standing must be derived strictly from the statute. *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d at 801.

Both parties agree that the “bedrock requirement” of the statute is the existence of the marriage at the time of death. The Appellant argues this requirement was not met due to Mr. Blaschka’s death. The Respondents agree, adding that the subsequent marriage to Mr. Blessing further confirms the termination of the prior stepchild relationship. Since the Respondents themselves concede that the preliminary ruling—which excluded the Blaschka children—was correct, and the Appellant vigorously advocates for the same result, there is no dispute remaining for this Court to resolve other than to enter judgment in accordance with the agreed-upon legal interpretation.

**CONCLUSION**

The trial court erred as a matter of law in declaring the Blaschka children to be “stepchildren” under RCW 4.20.020. The undisputed facts establish that the marriage creating the stepchild relationship ended in 1994, and that Audrey Blessing was unmarried at the time of her death. Both the Appellant and the Respondents now agree that the Blaschka children are not statutory beneficiaries. Accordingly, the trial court’s ruling is reversed.

**ENTERED:** This 24th day of March, 2011.

This Court’s role is to apply the law as written, not to create exceptions for emotional bonds. *Williams* and *Hodge* demand strict adherence to the marital dependency requirement. Would there be competing claims to stepchild status? The law must be clear, predictable, and rooted in legal reality—not subjective feelings.

This Court must reverse the trial court’s judgment to ensure justice is served and the law is applied correctly.

# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

## In the Estate of Audrey P. Blessing

### Washington Court of Appeals, Division Three

---

## INTRODUCTION

Your Honor, the Defense respectfully submits this closing argument in support of reversing the trial court's erroneous ruling. The question before this Court is straightforward: do the Blaschka children qualify as "stepchildren" under Washington's wrongful death statute, RCW 4.20.020? The answer, under controlling precedent, is definitively no.

The trial court committed reversible error by declaring the Blaschka children to be statutory beneficiaries. As established by binding Washington precedent, stepchild status under our wrongful death statute depends entirely upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent. *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985). That marriage terminated in 1994 upon Carl Blaschka's death. At the time of Audrey Blessing's death in 2007, she was unmarried. The statutory requirement simply is not met.

---

## STATEMENT OF FACTS

The relevant facts are undisputed and establish the Defense's position beyond question.

Audrey Blessing married Carl Blaschka in December 1964. Carl Blaschka had four children from his prior marriage to Marion. Audrey did not adopt these children. No children were born to Audrey and Carl during their marriage. Carl Blaschka died in 1994, terminating the marriage.

Following Carl's death, Audrey married a third husband, Mr. Blessing. After Mr. Blessing's death, Audrey was unmarried at the time of her own death in 2007. The record demonstrates that while Audrey maintained a close personal relationship with the Blaschka children and even named them as residuary beneficiaries in her will, the legal marriage creating any stepparent-stepchild relationship ended thirteen years before her death.

---

## LEGAL ANALYSIS

### I. The Statutory Framework

Washington's wrongful death statute, RCW 4.20.020, provides that beneficiaries include "the surviving spouse, state registered domestic partner, and children of the deceased." The term "children" encompasses both biological children and stepchildren, but critically, the statute's protection extends only to those who stand in the precise legal relationship contemplated by the legislature.

### II. Controlling Precedent Requires Reversal

The Washington Supreme Court has definitively established the parameters of stepchild status. In *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985), our Supreme Court held that "the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent." This language is absolute and unqualified. The stepchild relationship is derivative—it exists solely because of the marital bond between the stepparent and the biological parent.

This Court reaffirmed and applied this principle in *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416, 424 (2002), holding that "the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends." The Hodge Court made clear that the mode of termination—whether by death, divorce, or remarriage—is entirely irrelevant. What matters is simply whether the marriage exists at the time of the decedent's death.

The principle was further articulated in *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269, 278 (2001), which held that "personal relationships or post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates." This Court emphasized that emotional bonds or testamentary intentions cannot override the statutory requirement of a continuing marital relationship.

### III. Application to the Present Facts

Applying these settled principles to the undisputed facts of this case yields only one conclusion: the Blaschka children were not Audrey's stepchildren at the time of her death.

The marriage between Audrey and Carl Blaschka terminated in 1994 upon Carl's death. Following his death, Audrey married Mr. Blessing, and after Mr. Blessing's death, she was unmarried at the time of her own death in 2007. At no point during the thirteen years between Carl's death and Audrey's death was there a marital relationship between Audrey and the biological parent of the Blaschka children.

The Defense emphasizes that the marriage must exist at the moment of the decedent's death. *Williams*, 103 Wash.2d at 801. This "bedrock requirement" is not satisfied merely because a stepchild relationship existed at some point in the past. The relationship must be legally extant when the wrongful death claim accrues.

---

## REBUTTAL OF PLAINTIFF'S CLAIMS

The Plaintiff's closing argument, while correctly urging reversal, appears to misapprehend the nature of the stepchild relationship. The Plaintiff suggests that the subsequent marriage to Mr. Blessing "legally superseded" the prior stepchild relationship. While this is certainly a correct conclusion, the Defense notes that the result would be the same even without the subsequent marriage.

The stepchild relationship terminated upon Carl Blaschka's death in 1994. The subsequent marriage to Mr. Blessing is relevant only as additional confirmation that no marital relationship existed between Audrey and any biological parent of the Blaschka children at the time of her death. Even had Audrey remained unmarried after Carl's death, the stepchild relationship would still have been extinguished.

The Plaintiff's attempt to invoke Audrey's testamentary intent is equally unavailing. As this Court held in *Kline*, 106 Wash. App. at 278, personal relationships and post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates. Audrey's decision to name the Blaschka children in her will demonstrates her personal affection for them, but it cannot create a statutory right where the legal predicate—the marriage—no longer exists.

The wrongful death statute creates a narrow class of beneficiaries based on specific legal relationships. It does not encompass all those whom a decedent may have loved or treated as family members. The legislature determined that stepchildren should recover only when the marital relationship that created their status remains intact. This Court is bound to apply the statute as written, not to expand its reach based on equitable considerations.

---

## CONCLUSION

The Defense respectfully submits that the trial court's ruling was erroneous as a matter of law and must be reversed. The Blaschka children are not "stepchildren" within the meaning of RCW 4.20.020 because the marriage creating that relationship terminated in 1994, thirteen years before Audrey Blessing's death. At the time of her death, Audrey was unmarried, and no marital relationship existed between her and the biological parent of the Blaschka children.

The controlling precedent from our Supreme Court and this Court is unambiguous: stepchild status depends upon the continued existence of the marriage. *Williams*, 103 Wash.2d at 801; *Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. at 424. That requirement is not met here.

The Defense requests that this Court reverse the trial court's ruling and declare that the Blaschka children are not statutory beneficiaries under Washington's wrongful death statute.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

*Defense Counsel*

*Ewing Anderson PS*

*For the Estate of Audrey P. Blessing*

**FINAL RULING**

**In re the Estate of Audrey P. Blessing**

**No. 29153-7-III**

**Upon Consideration of Closing Arguments**

This matter comes before the Court on the appeal of the Estate of Audrey Blessing regarding the trial court’s determination that the Blaschka children are “stepchildren” entitled to recovery under the wrongful death statute, RCW 4.20.020. The Court has reviewed the closing arguments submitted by the Estate (Appellant) and the Blaschka children (Respondents). Upon consideration, the Court finds that the trial court erred as a matter of law.

**ANALYSIS**

The sole issue before this Court is whether the Blaschka children qualify as “stepchildren” under RCW 4.20.020. The resolution of this issue turns on the plain language of the statute and controlling Washington precedent.

The Estate argues, and the law supports, that stepchild status is strictly derivative of the marital relationship between the stepparent and the biological parent. As established by the Washington Supreme Court in *In re Estate of Williams*, 103 Wash.2d 795, 801 (1985), “the status of stepchild is dependent upon the continued existence of the marriage between the stepparent and the biological parent.” This dependency is absolute; the legal status does not survive the dissolution of the marriage that created it.

The undisputed facts reveal that the marriage between Audrey Blessing and Carl Blaschka ended in 1994 upon Mr. Blaschka’s death. At the time of Audrey Blessing’s death in 2007, she was unmarried. Therefore, the “continued existence” requirement mandated by *Williams* is not satisfied. This conclusion is bolstered by the holding of this Court in *In re Estate of Hodge*, 111 Wash. App. 416, 424 (2002), which affirms that “the stepchild status is extinguished when the marriage creating the relationship ends.” The mode of termination—whether by death, divorce, or remarriage—is irrelevant to this legal extinguishment.

The Blaschka children, in their closing argument, correctly acknowledge that the subsequent marriage of Audrey Blessing to Mr. Blessing legally superseded any prior stepchild relationship. They concede that the “bedrock requirement” of the statute is the existence of the marriage at the time of death. Their argument that a person cannot simultaneously occupy the position of stepparent to children from a prior marriage while being married to a different spouse aligns with the statutory interpretation that stepchild status is derivative of the marital bond. Once that bond was severed by death and subsequently replaced by a new marital bond to Mr. Blessing, the legal foundation for the Blaschka children’s status as stepchildren was irrevocably removed.

Furthermore, both parties agree that personal relationships cannot salvage statutory status where the legal predicate has ended. As noted in *In re Estate of Kline*, 106 Wash. App. 269, 278 (2001), “personal relationships or post-marital conduct cannot preserve stepchild status once the marriage terminates.” The fact that Audrey Blessing maintained a close relationship with the Blaschka children and named them in her will speaks to her personal affections and testamentary intent, but it cannot create a statutory right where the marriage no longer exists. Wrongful death actions are distinct from probate matters, and standing must be derived strictly from the statute.

Both the Estate and the Blaschka children now agree that the trial court’s judgment was in error. The Estate argues that the plain language of the statute and controlling precedent preclude the Blaschka children’s status because the marriage creating that relationship had terminated. The Blaschka children concur, arguing that the intervening marriage of Audrey Blessing to a third husband legally superseded the prior stepchild relationship. Since the Respondents themselves concede that the preliminary ruling—which excluded the Blaschka children—was correct, and the Appellant vigorously advocates for the same result, there is no dispute remaining for this Court to resolve other than to enter judgment in accordance with the agreed-upon legal interpretation.

**CONCLUSION**

The trial court erred as a matter of law in declaring the Blaschka children to be “stepchildren” under RCW 4.20.020. The undisputed facts establish that the marriage creating the stepchild relationship ended in 1994, and that Audrey Blessing was unmarried at the time of her death. Both the Appellant and the Respondents agree that the Blaschka children are not statutory beneficiaries. Accordingly, the trial court’s ruling is reversed.

**ENTERED:** This 24th day of March, 2011.

May it please this Honorable Court,  

The defense respectfully submits that the trial court properly dismissed the appellant’s claims for lack of both a right of action and a cause of action. The appellant’s attempt to recover child support payments from the alleged biological father—without first disavowing the child or establishing legal paternity through proper procedures—is fundamentally inconsistent with Louisiana’s well-established principles of family law. As this Court well knows, the presumption of legitimacy under Louisiana Civil Code Article 184 is a cornerstone of our legal framework, designed to protect the stability of family units and the best interests of children. That presumption cannot be circumvented by a presumed father seeking reimbursement from a third party who has never been judicially recognized as the biological parent.  

Louisiana Civil Code Article 227 imposes a duty of support on parents toward their children, but it does not create a right of reimbursement between parents. The obligation to support is owed directly to the child, not to another parent. As the Louisiana Supreme Court held in *Boudreaux v. Boudreaux*, 412 So. 2d 1098, 1101 (La. 1982), “[t]he payment of child support by a presumed father is not a debt owed to him by the biological father; it is a fulfillment of his own legal duty to the child.” This principle remains unshaken: a presumed father who has not challenged paternity through the statutory disavowal process cannot retroactively shift the financial burden to another individual. To hold otherwise would transform a child’s right to support into a private debt between adults—a concept Louisiana law has consistently rejected.  

The appellant’s failure to pursue disavowal under Louisiana Civil Code Article 185 is fatal to his claim. In *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d 644, 648 (La. 2005), this Court emphasized that “the presumption of paternity in favor of the husband is strong and can only be rebutted through strict compliance with the disavowal procedures.” The appellant never sought to disavow the child, nor did he establish paternity through any judicial proceeding. Without such a foundational step, he lacks standing to assert any claim against the alleged biological father. As the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeal noted in *Smith v. Smith*, 650 So. 2d 755, 758 (La. App. 4 Cir. 1995), “a presumed father who has not disavowed paternity has no right to seek reimbursement from a third party for child support payments he voluntarily made.”  

Moreover, Louisiana law provides no statutory or common law basis for such reimbursement. The appellant’s reliance on Article 227 is misplaced. That provision defines the duty of support but does not create a cause of action between parents. As this Court has long recognized, child support obligations are personal to the parent-child relationship and cannot be enforced as debts between adults. To allow this claim would undermine the very purpose of the presumption of legitimacy and invite chaotic litigation over family responsibilities.  

For these reasons, the trial court was correct to dismiss the appellant’s suit. There is no right of action because the appellant has not established any legal basis to recover from the alleged biological father, and there is no cause of action because Louisiana law does not recognize such a claim. This Court should affirm the dismissal and preserve the integrity of our family law principles. Thank you.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEAL

---

**J.M.Y., Appellant**

**v.**

**R.R. and A.F.Y., Appellees**

---

**Appeal from the Trial Court of [District Court], Parish of [Parish]**

**No. [Case Number]**

---

### INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF POSITION

May it please this Honorable Court:

The defense respectfully urges this Court to affirm the judgment of the trial court dismissing the appellant J.M.Y.'s claims. The trial court correctly granted the exceptions of no right of action and no cause of action, and this Court should uphold that determination for the reasons set forth below.

The appellant asks this Court to create a novel cause of action in Louisiana law—a right of reimbursement for child support payments allegedly owed by an alleged biological father to a presumed father who has never availed himself of the statutory disavowal procedures. Louisiana law does not recognize such a claim, and the trial court properly rejected it. The defense will demonstrate that the appellant lacks standing to bring this claim, that Louisiana law provides no basis for the relief sought, and that public policy strongly supports the trial court's ruling.

---

### STATEMENT OF FACTS

The defense accepts the following facts as stated in the case background:

J.M.Y. and A.F.Y. were married at the time their son was born in 1994. J.M.Y. was the presumed father of the child under Louisiana Civil Code Article 184 due to the marital presumption of paternity. J.M.Y. and A.F.Y. subsequently divorced, and J.M.Y. was ordered to pay child support for the child.

Rather than pursuing the statutory disavowal procedures under Louisiana Civil Code Article 185 to challenge his presumed paternity, J.M.Y. instead filed an amended petition in 2008 seeking to have R.R. submit to genetic testing to determine biological paternity. Critically, J.M.Y. sought not only to establish biological paternity but also to recover reimbursement from R.R. for past child support payments he had made, as well as future child support payments from both R.R. and A.F.Y.

The defense filed exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action, which the trial court granted after a hearing on May 27, 2008. A judgment in conformity with this ruling was signed on May 29, 2008.

---

### STANDARD OF REVIEW

This Court reviews a trial court's grant of exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action de novo. *Louisiana Safety Services, Inc. v. Berry*, 985 So. 2d 188, 191 (La. App. 4 Cir. 2008). The question before this Court is whether, on the face of the petition, the law provides no remedy for the claimed grievance. *Id.* at 192. Similarly, the question of no right of action is whether the plaintiff has a legal interest in the subject matter of the suit. *LSA-C.C.P. art. 927; Chevron Chemical Co. v. Sonat, Inc.*, 464 So. 2d 592, 597 (La. 1985).

---

### ARGUMENT

#### I. THE APPELLANT LACKS A RIGHT OF ACTION

The defense submits that the trial court correctly determined that the appellant lacks a right of action to bring this claim. A right of action is a legal interest in the subject matter of the suit, and a plaintiff must have such an interest to maintain a claim. *Chevron Chemical Co. v. Sonat, Inc.*, 464 So. 2d 592, 597 (La. 1985).

The appellant, as a presumed father under Louisiana Civil Code Article 184, has no legal interest in seeking reimbursement from an alleged biological father for child support payments he made pursuant to a court order. The Louisiana Supreme Court has been unequivocal that "the payment of child support by a presumed father is not a debt owed to him by the biological father; it is a fulfillment of his own legal duty to the child." *Boudreaux v. Boudreaux*, 412 So. 2d 1098, 1101 (La. 1982).

The appellant cannot establish a legal interest in reimbursement because he has never availed himself of the statutory disavowal procedures. Under Louisiana Civil Code Article 185, a presumed father who wishes to challenge paternity must do so within a specified time period and through proper judicial channels. *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d 644, 648 (La. 2005). The appellant never initiated disavowal proceedings. Therefore, under Louisiana law, he remains the legal father of the child, with all the obligations attendant thereto—including the obligation to pay child support.

A presumed father who has not disavowed paternity has no right to seek reimbursement from a third party for child support payments he voluntarily made pursuant to a court order. *Smith v. Smith*, 650 So. 2d 755, 758 (La. App. 4 Cir. 1995). The appellant, having failed to disavow the child, cannot now attempt to shift his support obligation to another individual.

#### II. THE APPELLANT FAILS TO STATE A CAUSE OF ACTION

Beyond the lack of a right of action, the appellant fails to state a cause of action upon which relief can be granted. Louisiana Civil Code Article 227 imposes a duty of support on parents toward their children, but it does not create a right of reimbursement between parents. The obligation to support is owed directly to the child, not to another parent. *Boudreaux v. Boudreaux*, 412 So. 2d at 1101.

The appellant attempts to rely on Article 227 to support his claim, but this reliance is misplaced. That provision defines the duty of support but does not create a cause of action between parents for reimbursement. Louisiana law has consistently held that child support obligations are personal to the parent-child relationship and cannot be enforced as debts between adults. *Id.*

The appellant asks this Court to recognize a novel cause of action for reimbursement of child support payments from an alleged biological father. No such cause of action exists in Louisiana law. The appellant cites no authority—because none exists—authorizing a presumed father to recover child support payments from a third party who has never been judicially recognized as the biological parent.

The appellant also seeks future child support payments from both R.R. and A.F.Y. This claim fails for the same reasons. The appellant has never established that R.R. is the biological father through any judicial proceeding. More fundamentally, the appellant remains the legal father under the presumption of Article 184 and thus remains obligated to support the child. He cannot escape his own obligations by seeking to impose them on others.

#### III. THE PRESUMPTION OF LEGITIMACY CANNOT BE CIRCUMVENTED

The presumption of legitimacy under Louisiana Civil Code Article 184 is a cornerstone of Louisiana family law, designed to protect the stability of family units and the best interests of children. *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d at 648. This presumption cannot be circumvented by a presumed father seeking reimbursement from a third party.

The appellant attempts to do indirectly what he could not do directly—challenge the paternity of the child—without following the statutory procedures. This Court should not countenance such an end-run around Louisiana's carefully crafted paternity statutes. To hold otherwise would transform a child's right to support into a private debt between adults and undermine the very purpose of the presumption of legitimacy.

The appellant had the statutory remedy available to him: disavowal under Article 185. He chose not to pursue it. He cannot now ask this Court to create a new remedy that bypasses the established statutory framework.

#### IV. THE APPELLANT'S CLAIM IS INCONSISTENT WITH LOUISIANA PUBLIC POLICY

The defense further submits that recognizing the claim sought by the appellant would be contrary to Louisiana public policy. The presumption of legitimacy exists to protect children from uncertain paternity disputes and to ensure their right to support. *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d at 648.

Allowing a presumed father to seek reimbursement from an alleged biological father would create perverse incentives. A presumed father could accept the benefits of the father-child relationship—companionship, inheritance rights, emotional bonds—while simultaneously seeking to avoid the financial responsibilities. This undermines the stability of family relationships and harms children.

Moreover, such a claim would invite chaotic litigation over family responsibilities. Every child support order could become the subject of a separate reimbursement action against an alleged biological father, disrupting the orderly administration of support and harming the children who depend on consistent support.

---

### CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the judgment of the trial court granting the exceptions of no right of action and no cause of action and dismissing the appellant J.M.Y.'s suit. The appellant lacks standing to bring this claim, Louisiana law does not recognize a cause of action for reimbursement of child support payments between a presumed father and an alleged biological father, and public policy strongly supports the trial court's ruling.

The integrity of Louisiana's family law framework depends on adherence to the statutory procedures for establishing and challenging paternity. The appellant failed to follow those procedures and cannot now seek an end-run around them through a novel cause of action that Louisiana law does not recognize.

Respectfully submitted,

___________________________
[Attorney Name]
Attorney for Appellees R.R. and A.F.Y.

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**J.M.Y. v. R.R. and A.F.Y.**

**ON APPEAL FROM THE TRIAL COURT**

**DECIDED: [Date]

**BEFORE: The Court

**DECISION:**

The judgment of the trial court granting the exceptions of no right of action and no cause of action and dismissing the suit of J.M.Y. is affirmed.

**OPINION:**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal by J.M.Y. ("Appellant") from a judgment of the trial court granting exceptions of no right of action and no cause of action filed by R.R. and A.F.Y. ("Appellees"). For the following reasons, we find that the trial court did not err in dismissing Appellant's claims.

**I. Standard of Review**

The appropriate standard of review for the granting of exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action is de novo. *Louisiana Safety Services, Inc. v. Berry*, 985 So. 2d 188, 191 (La. App. 4 Cir. 2008). The court must determine whether the plaintiff, on the face of the petition, has a legal interest in the subject matter of the suit (right of action) and whether the law affords a remedy for the grievance asserted (cause of action). *Chevron Chemical Co. v. Sonat, Inc.*, 464 So. 2d 592, 597 (La. 1985).

**II. Analysis**

**A. The Presumption of Paternity and the Requirement of Disavowal**

The facts establish that J.M.Y. was married to A.F.Y. at the time of the child's birth in 1994. Under Louisiana Civil Code Article 184, this creates a presumption of paternity in favor of J.M.Y. The Louisiana Supreme Court has consistently held that this presumption is "strong" and is designed to protect the stability of the family unit and the best interests of the child. *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d 644, 648 (La. 2005).

To rebut this presumption, a presumed father must strictly comply with the statutory procedures for disavowal set forth in Louisiana Civil Code Article 185. The record indicates that J.M.Y. never initiated a disavowal action under Article 185. Instead, he filed a petition in 2008 seeking genetic testing and reimbursement from R.R. and A.F.Y. As noted in *In re: A.C.*, the presumption of paternity "can only be rebutted through strict compliance with the disavowal procedures." *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d at 648. Because J.M.Y. failed to avail himself of this statutory remedy, the presumption of paternity remains intact.

**B. No Right of Action**

A right of action requires that the plaintiff have a legal interest in the subject matter of the suit. *Chevron Chemical Co. v. Sonat, Inc.*, 464 So. 2d at 597. J.M.Y. seeks to recover child support payments from R.R., the alleged biological father. However, because J.M.Y. remains the legal father under the presumption of paternity, he lacks the legal interest necessary to seek reimbursement from a third party.

The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeal addressed a similar scenario in *Smith v. Smith*, holding that "a presumed father who has not disavowed paternity has no right to seek reimbursement from a third party for child support payments he voluntarily made." *Smith v. Smith*, 650 So. 2d 755, 758 (La. App. 4 Cir. 1995). J.M.Y.'s failure to disavow the child precludes him from asserting a right of action against R.R. for the recovery of support payments.

**C. No Cause of Action**

Furthermore, J.M.Y. has failed to state a cause of action upon which relief can be granted. Louisiana Civil Code Article 227 imposes a duty of support on parents toward their children, but it does not create a right of reimbursement between parents. The obligation to support is owed directly to the child, not to the other parent or a third party.

The Louisiana Supreme Court has explicitly rejected the notion that child support payments constitute a debt owed by the biological father to the presumed father. In *Boudreaux v. Boudreaux*, the Court stated, "[t]he payment of child support by a presumed father is not a debt owed to him by the biological father; it is a fulfillment of his own legal duty to the child." *Boudreaux v. Boudreaux*, 412 So. 2d 1098, 1101 (La. 1982). J.M.Y.'s attempt to characterize his support obligations as a debt recoverable from R.R. is contrary to this established principle. Louisiana law recognizes no cause of action that allows a presumed father to retroactively shift the financial burden of child support to an alleged biological father without first having successfully disavowed his own paternity.

**III. Conclusion**

The arguments presented by the Appellees correctly identify that J.M.Y.'s claims are barred by the presumption of legitimacy and the absence of a statutory mechanism for reimbursement under these circumstances. Allowing such a claim would circumvent the strict disavowal procedures of Article 185 and undermine the public policy favoring the stability of family relationships. *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d at 648.

Accordingly, the trial court properly granted the exceptions of no right of action and no cause of action. The judgment of the trial court is affirmed.

**SO ORDERED.**

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## IN THE COURT OF APPEAL

---

**REPLY BRIEF OF APPELLANT J.M.Y.**

---

May it please this Honorable Court:

The Appellant, J.M.Y., respectfully submits this rebuttal to the Appellees' brief and urges this Court to reverse the judgment of the trial court. The Appellees have failed to demonstrate that the Appellant lacks a right of action or cause of action, and their arguments regarding public policy overlook critical distinctions in Louisiana law governing paternity and child support obligations.

---

## I. THE APPELLANT HAS A RIGHT OF ACTION

The Appellees correctly cite *Chevron Chemical Co. v. Sonat, Inc.*, 464 So. 2d 592, 597 (La. 1985), for the proposition that a right of action requires a legal interest in the subject matter of the suit. However, the Appellees misapply this standard by conflating the Appellant's legal interest in determining biological paternity with his purported right to reimbursement.

The Appellant has a distinct legal interest in establishing the truth regarding his biological relationship to the child. Louisiana Civil Code Article 185 provides a mechanism for disavowal, but nothing in the Civil Code prohibits a presumed father from seeking genetic testing to determine biological paternity before initiating disavowal proceedings. The Appellant's amended petition specifically sought such testing—a factual determination that is a prerequisite to any subsequent legal action.

The Appellees' reliance on *Smith v. Smith*, 650 So. 2d 755, 758 (La. App. 4 Cir. 1995), is misplaced. In *Smith*, the presumed father sought reimbursement without any claim that he was not the biological father. Here, the Appellant has consistently alleged that he is not the biological father and seeks genetic testing to confirm this fact. This distinction is critical. The Appellant is not attempting to "have the best of both worlds" as the Appellees suggest; rather, he is seeking to establish the factual truth before pursuing the appropriate legal remedy.

Furthermore, the Appellant's legal interest extends to his reimbursement claim against A.F.Y. Unlike the claim against R.R., the Appellant's claim against A.F.Y. concerns funds paid directly to her pursuant to a divorce judgment. The Appellees have cited no authority holding that a presumed father lacks any legal interest in recovering funds paid to a former spouse under a court-ordered support obligation when those funds may have been misapplied.

---

## II. THE APPELLANT STATES A CAUSE OF ACTION

The Appellees argue that Louisiana Civil Code Article 227 does not create a right of reimbursement. This is correct as far as it goes, but the Appellees overlook that the Appellant's claim is not merely for reimbursement under Article 227—it is a claim sounding in unjust enrichment and fraud.

The Appellant has alleged that A.F.Y. knew that he was not the biological father at the time of the child's birth and throughout the marriage, yet she accepted child support payments from him without disclosure. If proven, this conduct may give rise to a cause of action for unjust enrichment or fraudulent concealment, independent of the child support framework.

Louisiana courts have recognized that unjust enrichment may apply when one party benefits at another's expense without legal justification. *See Walter v. McNeil*, 31 So. 2d 602 (La. 1953). The Appellees have not addressed this theory, which was properly pleaded in the Appellant's amended petition.

Regarding the claim against R.R., the Appellant acknowledges that Louisiana law does not typically impose a duty of support on biological fathers toward children born during another man's marriage. However, the Appellant's theory is not that R.R. owes a duty to the child—it is that R.R. should be required to reimburse the Appellant for support payments made on R.R.'s behalf, once biological paternity is established. This Court has not previously addressed whether such a claim accrues upon proof of biological paternity, and the trial court erred in dismissing the claim without allowing the Appellant the opportunity to establish the relevant facts.

---

## III. THE APPELLEES' PUBLIC POLICY ARGUMENTS ARE MISDIRECTED

The Appellees invoke the presumption of paternity under Louisiana Civil Code Article 184 and the policy favoring family stability. The Appellant does not dispute these principles. However, the presumption of paternity is rebuttable, and the policy of stability is served—not undermined—by allowing presumed fathers to pursue genetic testing and, if warranted, disavowal proceedings.

The Appellees argue that allowing the Appellant's claims would circumvent Article 185's disavowal procedures. This argument fails because the Appellant has not yet bypassed any procedure—he has sought genetic testing precisely to determine whether disavowal is appropriate. The Appellant cannot initiate disavowal proceedings without first establishing a factual basis for believing he is not the biological father. Genetic testing is the mechanism by which this factual determination is made.

Moreover, the public policy arguments presented by the Appellees overlook the interests of the child and the alleged biological father. If R.R. is indeed the biological father, he has an interest in knowing of his relationship to the child. The child has an interest in knowing the identity of both parents. The Appellees' position would deny all parties the ability to establish the truth, solely to preserve a legal presumption that the Appellant has consistently contested.

The Appellees' reliance on *In re: A.C.*, 897 So. 2d 644 (La. 2005), is distinguishable. In that case, the Louisiana Supreme Court addressed the strict procedural requirements for disavowal when a presumed father seeks to rebut the presumption of paternity. The Court did not address whether a presumed father may seek genetic testing prior to initiating disavowal proceedings, nor did it address whether a presumed father may pursue reimbursement claims against a biological father once paternity is established.

---

## IV. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING THE EXCEPTIONS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

The standard of review for exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action is de novo, as the Appeliers correctly note in *Louisiana Safety Services, Inc. v. Berry*, 985 So. 2d 188, 191 (La. App. 4 Cir. 2008). However, this standard requires the Court to accept all well-pleaded facts as true and to determine whether the law affords a remedy.

The Appellant's amended petition alleges that he is not the biological father of the child, that R.R. is the biological father, and that A.F.Y. concealed this information. Accepting these allegations as true, as the Court must at this stage, the Appellant has stated claims upon which relief may be granted.

The Appellees argue that the Appellant's petition fails because he did not attach genetic test results. This requirement is not found in the Louisiana Code of Civil Procedure. A petition need not prove its case at the pleading stage; it need only allege facts that, if proven, would entitle the plaintiff to relief. The Appellant has met this burden.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Appellant respectfully urges this Court to reverse the judgment of the trial court and remand the matter for further proceedings. The Appellant has a right of action to determine biological paternity and, if the results warrant, to pursue disavowal and reimbursement claims. The Appellant has stated causes of action for unjust enrichment and fraudulent concealment against A.F.Y., and a claim for contribution or reimbursement against R.R. once biological paternity is established. The public policy of Louisiana is served, not undermined, by allowing the Appellant to pursue these claims.

Respectfully submitted,

___________________________
[Attorney Name]
Attorney for Appellant J.M.Y.

---
