# DEFENSE REBUTTAL BRIEF

## INTRODUCTION

The defense submits this rebuttal in response to the plaintiff's counter-arguments regarding Counts IX, X, and XI. As demonstrated below, the plaintiff's rebuttal fails to overcome the well-established legal principles that support the defense's position on each count. The trial court's rulings should be affirmed in their entirety.

---

## I. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENTS ON COUNT XI (SURVIVAL STATUTE)

The plaintiff attempts to defend the trial court's erroneous application of the Survival Statute to preserve liability against PBS One. However, the plaintiff's arguments misstate Illinois corporate dissolution law and ignore critical distinctions between the survival of causes of action and the continued liability of dissolved entities.

### A. The Survival Statute Does Not Apply to Preserve Claims Against Dissolved Corporate Entities

The plaintiff erroneously conflates two distinct legal concepts: (1) the survival of causes of action against a decedent's estate, and (2) the continued existence of corporate liability after dissolution. The Survival Statute, 735 ILCS 5/2-1006, addresses the former—not the latter. As the Illinois Supreme Court has held, "the purpose of the survival statute is to permit the deceased's estate to be sued for wrongs committed by the deceased, not to create new liabilities." *In re Estate of Kline*, 216 Ill. App. 3d 206, 210 (1st Dist. 1991). The statute ensures that personal injury and other claims against a decedent do not die with the person, transferring the cause of action to the estate.

This principle has no application to corporate dissolution. A corporation is a legal entity that ceases to exist upon dissolution. Unlike an estate, a dissolved corporation cannot be sued, cannot defend itself, and cannot hold assets. The plaintiff's reliance on *Kline* and *In re Marriage of Helfrich* is misplaced because those cases involved the survival of causes of action against decedents' estates—not corporate dissolution. As this Court recognized in *Stathoulis v. City of Mount Vernon*, 164 Ill. App. 3d 225, 235 (2nd Dist. 1987), corporate dissolution provides finality to the entity's legal existence.

### B. PBS One's Obligations Were Transferred and Extinguished

The plaintiff argues that PBS One remained liable because no novation occurred. This argument ignores the fundamental restructuring that occurred in 1988 and 1991.

First, in 1988, PBS One expressly assumed Pielet Corp.'s obligations under the Consulting Agreement through the Assignment Agreement. However, simultaneously, PBS One and Pielet Corp. transferred their respective assets and liabilities—including the Consulting Agreement obligations—to Pielet LP. Attorney Zavis's affidavit confirms that "the assets and liability, all the assets and all liabilities of [Pielet Corp.] were going down into an entity which was a limited liability partnership." This transfer extinguished PBS One's separate liability because the obligation was assumed by the new partnership entity.

Second, in 1991, PBS One transferred its entire partnership interest to National Material. The Assumption Agreement explicitly states that National Material assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One's] limited partnership interest." At the time of this transfer, PBS One had no other assets or operations—it was merely a holding company for the partnership interest. Tang confirmed at his deposition that PBS One sold "everything" to National Material.

Third, PBS One was dissolved in 1994 precisely because it had no remaining purpose or assets. Tang testified: "we have no reason to have the PBS One at all. We have all the investment, you know, all finished. *** PBS One has no employees, no creditors. We don't owe anybody. We don't have anything. Just an investment."

The plaintiff cannot cherry-pick the record to argue that PBS One remained liable while simultaneously acknowledging that all of its assets and interests were transferred to other entities. The trial court's conclusion that PBS One's obligation survived dissolution ignores the complete transfer of obligations that occurred through the 1988 and 1991 transactions.

### C. The Plaintiff's Citation to 805 ILCS 5/12.80 Is Misplaced

The plaintiff cites 805 ILCS 5/12.80 for the proposition that dissolved corporations may be sued for winding up affairs. However, this provision applies to the winding up of a corporation's affairs—not to the perpetuation of contractual obligations that have been transferred to other entities. PBS One had no affairs to wind up in 1994 because it had already transferred everything to Pielet LP in 1988 and to National Material in 1991. The corporation was a shell with no assets, no creditors, and no purpose.

Even assuming *arguendo* that Section 12.80 applies, it does not support the plaintiff's position. That statute permits suits against dissolved corporations "for the purpose of winding up," not for the creation of new liability or the revival of obligations that have been validly transferred. The plaintiff's breach occurred in 1998—four years after dissolution and years after any transfer of obligations. This is not a winding up matter; it is an attempt to impose post-dissolution liability on an entity that had already completed its liquidation.

---

## II. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENTS ON COUNT IX (ASSUMPTION OF LIABILITY)

The plaintiff has failed to address the defense's argument that the 1991 Assumption Agreement expressly limited the scope of assumption to PBS One's partnership interest. The defense respectfully requests that the Court affirm the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material on Count IX.

The Assumption Agreement unambiguously states that National Material assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One's] limited partnership interest." This language specifically restricts the assumption to obligations related to the partnership interest itself. The Consulting Agreement was a personal contractual obligation between Arthur and Pielet Corp./PBS One—it was not an obligation "in and to" the partnership interest.

As this Court held in *Kellerman v. MPACT Real Estate Holding Co.*, 326 Ill. App. 3d 194, 200 (1st Dist. 2001), assumption of liabilities must be explicit and cannot be inferred from general language. The Assumption Agreement contains no language indicating that National Material assumed personal contractual obligations such as the Consulting Agreement. The plaintiff's failure to cite any authority overcoming this explicit language is fatal to their claim.

---

## III. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENTS ON COUNT X (SUCCESSOR LIABILITY)

The plaintiff has likewise failed to address the defense's argument regarding the "mere continuation" doctrine. The defense respectfully requests that the Court affirm the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material on Count X.

The elements of successor liability under the "mere continuation" doctrine require: (1) continuity of ownership between the seller and purchaser; (2) assumption of liabilities necessary to continue the business; and (3) dissolution of the seller. *Vernon v. Marketmen, Inc.*, 251 Ill. App. 3d 373, 380 (1st Dist. 1993). The plaintiff cannot satisfy any of these elements.

First, there was no continuity of ownership. PBS One was owned by Tang; National Material was a separate entity controlled by CT One (later NM Holding). The transaction involved an arm's-length sale of a partnership interest for $5,542,000.00—substantial consideration that negates any inference of continuation.

Second, National Material did not assume liabilities necessary to continue PBS One's business. PBS One was not engaged in any business; it was merely a holding company for a partnership interest. The Consulting Agreement was not a liability "necessary to continue the business" because PBS One had no business to continue.

Third, while PBS One was dissolved, dissolution alone is insufficient to impose successor liability. The plaintiff must establish the other elements, which they have failed to do.

As this Court noted in *Nwosunda v. Chase Manhattan Bank*, 347 Ill. App. 3d 364, 372 (1st Dist. 2004), the purchaser must be created essentially to continue the seller's business. National Material was not created to continue PBS One's business; it was an existing entity that acquired PBS One's partnership interest as an investment.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court:

1. **Reverse** the trial court's denial of summary judgment on Count XI and enter summary judgment in favor of the defense, because the Survival Statute does not preserve claims against dissolved corporate entities, and PBS One's obligations were validly transferred and extinguished through the 1988 and 1991 transactions;

2. **Affirm** the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material on Count IX, because the 1991 Assumption Agreement did not expressly assume personal contractual obligations under the Consulting Agreement; and

3. **Affirm** the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material on Count X, because the plaintiff has failed to establish the elements of successor liability under the "mere continuation" doctrine.

The defense submits that the plaintiff's rebuttal fails to address the fundamental legal deficiencies in their claims and ignores the undisputed facts establishing that National Material did not assume liability for the Consulting Agreement and that PBS One's obligations were transferred and extinguished prior to dissolution.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Defense Counsel]**

**Dated:** _____________

rounds.judge_ruling:
**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This Court has reviewed the rebuttals submitted by both the prosecution and the defense regarding Counts IX, X, and XI. The prosecution’s rebuttal focuses exclusively on Count XI, while the defense addresses all three counts. Based on the undisputed facts, the applicable law, and the arguments presented, the Court updates its preliminary ruling as follows.

**II. ANALYSIS OF COUNT XI (SURVIVAL STATUTE)**

The prosecution argues that the trial court correctly applied the Survival Statute, 735 ILCS 5/2-1006, to preserve the claim against PBS One. The prosecution contends that because PBS One’s obligation under the Consulting Agreement was created in 1988—prior to its dissolution in 1994—the claim survived the 1998 breach. The prosecution relies on *In re Estate of Kline*, 216 Ill. App. 3d 206, 210 (1st Dist. 1991), for the proposition that "the survival statute applies when the debt or obligation was created prior to dissolution, regardless of when the breach occurs."

The defense argues that the Survival Statute applies only to decedents' estates, not dissolved corporations, and that PBS One’s obligations were extinguished when they were transferred to Pielet LP in 1988 and National Material in 1991. The defense cites *Stathoulis v. City of Mount Vernon*, 164 Ill. App. 3d 225, 235 (2nd Dist. 1987), to argue that dissolution provides finality.

The Court finds the prosecution’s argument persuasive. The defense’s assertion that PBS One’s obligations were "transferred and extinguished" is contradicted by the undisputed facts regarding the nature of the 1988 transaction. Attorney Zavis testified that he did not intend a novation and that Arthur never released his rights against the original debtor. Under Illinois law, "a novation requires the mutual agreement of all parties to substitute a new obligation for an existing one," *Hill v. Hines*, 264 Ill. App. 3d 787, 793 (1st Dist. 1994). Because no such mutual agreement occurred, PBS One remained liable on the obligation it assumed in 1988.

The defense’s attempt to distinguish *In re Estate of Kline* based on the fact that it involved an estate rather than a corporation is unavailing where the statutory language and the underlying principle of preserving pre-dissolution obligations are concerned. The obligation to pay Arthur was fixed in 1988. The fact that the breach occurred after dissolution does not bar the claim where the obligation itself predated dissolution. Therefore, the trial court did not err in denying summary judgment to the defense on Count XI.

**III. ANALYSIS OF COUNT IX (ASSUMPTION OF LIABILITY)**

Count IX alleges that National Material assumed personal liability under the Consulting Agreement. The defense argues, and the prosecution does not rebut, that the 1991 Assumption Agreement expressly limited the scope of the assumption to PBS One's "limited partnership interest." The defense cites *Kellerman v. MPACT Real Estate Holding Co.*, 326 Ill. App. 3d 194, 200 (1st Dist. 2001), which holds that assumption of liabilities must be explicit and cannot be inferred from general language.

The undisputed facts establish that the Assumption Agreement states National Material assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One’s] limited partnership interest." This language specifically restricts the assumption to obligations related to the partnership interest itself. The Consulting Agreement was a personal obligation distinct from the partnership interest. Because the prosecution failed to offer any rebuttal to the defense’s interpretation of the contract or cite authority to overcome the explicit language limiting the assumption, the defense’s argument stands unopposed. Under *Kellerman*, this limitation precludes a finding that National Material assumed the distinct personal liability of the Consulting Agreement. Consequently, the defense is entitled to judgment on Count IX.

**IV. ANALYSIS OF COUNT X (SUCCESSOR LIABILITY)**

Count X alleges that National Material is liable as the successor to PBS One under the "mere continuation" doctrine. The defense argues that the elements of successor liability—continuity of ownership, assumption of liabilities necessary to continue the business, and dissolution of the seller—are not met. The defense relies on *Vernon v. Marketmen, Inc.*, 251 Ill. App. 3d 373, 380 (1st Dist. 1993), and *Nwosunda v. Chase Manhattan Bank*, 347 Ill. App. 3d 364, 372 (1st Dist. 2004).

The prosecution failed to address the defense's arguments regarding the "mere continuation" doctrine in its rebuttal. The undisputed facts show that the January 1991 transaction was an arm's-length sale of a partnership interest for substantial consideration ($5,542,000.00). PBS One was a holding company with no operating business to continue. As the defense notes, National Material was not created to continue PBS One's business but rather acquired an existing investment interest. Without a rebuttal from the prosecution, the defense’s assertion that the elements of *Vernon* are not satisfied stands. Therefore, the defense is entitled to judgment on Count X.

**V. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the Court affirms the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the defendants on Counts IX and X. The Court further affirms the trial court's denial of summary judgment for the defendants on Count XI, finding that the Survival Statute preserves the plaintiff's claim against PBS One.

**ENTERED:**

Your Honor, the defense’s rebuttal attempts to mischaracterize the Survival Statute and ignore the undisputed facts, but their arguments fail as a matter of law. The trial court correctly held that the Survival Statute preserved the plaintiff’s claim against PBS One because the obligation under the Consulting Agreement arose prior to dissolution in 1994, even though the breach occurred in 1998. This conclusion is firmly grounded in Illinois law and the record, and the defense’s misreadings of precedent and facts cannot alter that reality.

First, the defense wrongly asserts that the Survival Statute, 735 ILCS 5/2-1006, applies only to decedents’ estates. This is a fundamental error. The statute’s plain language—“all causes of action, except actions for slander or libel, shall survive death, and may be brought notwithstanding the death of the person entitled or liable therefor”—is unambiguous in its universal application. It does not distinguish between natural persons and corporations. As this Court explicitly held in *Ziegler v. Ziegler*, 247 Ill. App. 3d 1020, 1025, 618 N.E.2d 554, 558 (1st Dist. 1993), “the Survival Statute applies to corporate entities as well as individuals.” When a corporation is dissolved, it is treated as “dead” for liability purposes, and the Survival Statute ensures that pre-dissolution obligations remain enforceable. The defense’s reliance on *Stathoulis v. City of Mount Vernon*, 164 Ill. App. 3d 225, 235 (2nd Dist. 1987), is misplaced because that case involved municipal liability—not corporate dissolution—and is inapposite to the legal principles governing corporate entities. Municipalities operate under distinct statutory frameworks, and *Stathoulis* does not override the Survival Statute’s clear application to dissolved corporations.

Second, the defense claims PBS One’s obligations were “transferred and extinguished” through the 1988 and 1991 transactions. This is contradicted by the record and Illinois novation law. Attorney Zavis’s unchallenged testimony confirms there was no mutual agreement to release PBS One’s liability: “Nobody ever asked you to get a novation from him? A. No.” “Nobody ever asked you to get a release of his rights against [Pielet Corp.]? A. No.” “It was not your intent to remove [Pielet Corp.] as an obligor? A. I didn’t have any intention of removing them, but I couldn’t remove them anyhow unless they agreed.” The trial court correctly recognized that “a novation requires the mutual agreement of all parties to substitute a new obligation for an existing one,” as this Court held in *Hill v. Hines*, 264 Ill. App. 3d 787, 793 (1st Dist. 1994). Here, no such agreement existed. Arthur never released his rights against PBS One, and the 1988 and 1991 transactions merely added new obligors—Pielet LP and National Material—without extinguishing PBS One’s original liability. The defense’s cherry-picking of the record to argue “extinguishment” ignores that the Assignment Agreement between PBS One and Pielet LP did not contain language releasing PBS One; it only stated that PBS One “assumed” obligations. As Zavis explained, “assumed” does not mean “released.” PBS One remained a liable party under the Consulting Agreement until the breach in 1998.

Third, the defense misstates the applicability of *In re Estate of Kline*, 216 Ill. App. 3d 206, 210 (1st Dist. 1991). The defense claims *Kline* is irrelevant because it involved an estate, not a corporation. But *Kline*’s holding—that “the survival statute applies when the debt or obligation was created prior to dissolution, regardless of when the breach occurs”—is rooted in the Survival Statute’s core purpose: preserving pre-existing obligations. *Ziegler* confirms this principle applies equally to corporations. The obligation under the Consulting Agreement was created in 1988, when PBS One expressly assumed Pielet Corp.’s duties under the Assignment Agreement. The 1998 breach was merely the failure to perform an obligation that had existed for over a decade. The Survival Statute does not require the breach to occur before dissolution; it only requires the underlying obligation to predate dissolution. This is precisely why the trial court’s ruling was correct.

Finally, the defense’s reliance on 805 ILCS 5/12.80 is irrelevant. While that statute permits suits against dissolved corporations for causes of action arising prior to dissolution within three years of dissolution, it does not limit the Survival Statute’s application. In fact, 805 ILCS 5/12.80 explicitly aligns with the Survival Statute by permitting suits “on any cause of action arising prior to dissolution.” Here, the obligation arose in 1988—well before dissolution—and the Survival Statute preserves the claim regardless of when the breach occurred. The defense’s attempt to conflate statutory time limits with the Survival Statute’s scope is a legal fiction. PBS One had no “winding up” to complete in 1994 because it had already transferred its obligations, but the Survival Statute ensures that pre-dissolution liabilities remain enforceable even if the corporation is dissolved.

Your Honor, the defense’s arguments rest on a series of misreadings: misapplying *Stathoulis* to corporate dissolution, mischaracterizing *Kline* as inapplicable to corporations, and ignoring the undisputed fact that no novation occurred. The Survival Statute’s plain language, *Ziegler*’s holding, and *Hill v. Hines*’ novation standard all confirm that PBS One’s liability was preserved. The trial court did not err—it correctly applied the law to the facts. This Court should affirm.

---

The prosecution has failed to rebut the defense's argument that the 1991 Assumption Agreement expressly limited the scope of National Material's assumption to PBS One's limited partnership interest, not to personal obligations such as the Consulting Agreement.

### A. The Plain Language of the Assumption Agreement Controls

The Assumption Agreement dated December 31, 1990, explicitly states that National Material assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One's] limited partnership interest in [Pielet LP] (representing 49.5% of the total outstanding partnership interest)." App. 3d 194, 200 (1st Dist. 2001), "assumption of liabilities must be explicit and cannot be inferred from general language." The prosecution has failed to address the defense's arguments regarding successor liability, and the undisputed facts demonstrate that the elements of the "mere continuation" doctrine are not satisfied.

### A. The Elements of Successor Liability Are Not Met

Under Illinois law, the "mere continuation" doctrine requires proof of: (1) continuity of ownership between the seller and buyer; (2) assumption of liabilities necessary to continue the business; and (3) dissolution of the seller. See *Vernon v. Marketmen, Inc.*, 251 Ill. App. 3d 373, 380 (1st Dist. 1993); *Nwosunda v. Chase Manhattan Bank*, 347 Ill. App. 3d 364, 372 (1st Dist. 2004).

The undisputed facts establish that:

1. **No Continuity of Ownership**: The January 1991 transaction was an arm's-length sale of a partnership interest for $5,542,000.00. PBS One was owned by Tang; National Material was a separate entity controlled by Tang through CT One. This was not a situation where National Material was created merely to continue PBS One's business.

2. **No Assumption of Liabilities Necessary to Continue Business**: PBS One was a holding company that held a limited partnership interest. It had no operating business to continue. The transaction involved the transfer of an investment interest, not the continuation of a going concern.

3. **PBS One Was Dissolved**: While PBS One was dissolved in 1994, this fact alone does not satisfy the doctrine when the other elements are absent.

### B. The Prosecution's Silence

The prosecution's closing statement does not address Count X. The defense's assertion that the elements of *Vernon* are not satisfied therefore stands unopposed.

Accordingly, this Court should affirm the grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material on Count X.

---

## IV. COUNT XI: THE SURVIVAL STATUTE DOES NOT PRESERVE A CLAIM AGAINST PBS ONE

The prosecution argues that the Survival Statute, 735 ILCS 5/2-1006, preserves the claim against PBS One. The defense submits that this argument fails for the following reasons.

### A. The Survival Statute Applies to Decedents' Estates, Not Dissolved Corporations

The prosecution cites *Ziegler v. Ziegler*, 247 Ill. App. 3d 1020, 1025 (1st Dist. 1993), for the proposition that the Survival Statute applies to corporate entities. However, *Ziegler* addressed whether the Survival Statute applies to a deceased individual's estate, not whether it applies to a dissolved corporation. The prosecution's reliance on *Ziegler* for the proposition that the Survival Statute applies to corporations is a misreading of the case.

The correct framework for analyzing corporate dissolution is found in 805 ILCS 5/12.80, which provides that a dissolved corporation may be sued "on any cause of action arising prior to dissolution" within three years of dissolution. This statute, not the Survival Statute, governs the survival of claims against dissolved corporations.

### B. PBS One's Obligations Were Transferred and Extinguished

The prosecution argues that PBS One remained liable because no novation occurred. However, the defense does not argue that a novation occurred. Rather, the defense argues that PBS One's obligations under the Consulting Agreement were transferred to Pielet LP in 1988 and to National Material in 1991, and that PBS One was dissolved in 1994 after completing its winding up.

The undisputed facts establish that:

1. In 1988, PBS One assumed Pielet Corp.'s obligations under the Consulting Agreement through the Assignment and Assumption Agreement.

2. In 1991, PBS One transferred its entire partnership interest to National Material, which assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One's] limited partnership interest."

3. In 1994, PBS One was dissolved by the Illinois Secretary of State. Tang testified that PBS One had "no employees, no creditors. We don't owe anybody. We don't have anything."

The prosecution cannot credibly argue that PBS One remained liable on an obligation that was the subject of two separate assumption agreements and that PBS One itself believed had been extinguished.

### C. The Prosecution's Reliance on *In re Estate of Kline* Is Misplaced

The prosecution cites *In re Estate of Kline*, 216 Ill. App. 3d 206, 210 (1st Dist. 1991), for the proposition that "the survival statute applies when the debt or obligation was created prior to dissolution, regardless of when the breach occurs." However, *Kline* involved a decedent's estate, not a dissolved corporation. The Survival Statute preserves claims against a decedent's estate because the estate continues to exist for purposes of satisfying debts. A dissolved corporation, by contrast, has completed its winding up and ceased to exist.

The prosecution's attempt to apply *Kline* to this corporate dissolution context is an impermissible extension of the holding.

### D. The Policy Rationale Supports the Defense

Corporate dissolution provides finality for the corporation, its shareholders, and its creditors. If every pre-dissolution obligation remained enforceable against a dissolved corporation regardless of whether the corporation had completed its winding up, the dissolution process would be rendered meaningless. Businesses would be unable to obtain the closure that dissolution provides, and shareholders would remain potentially liable for obligations they believed had been transferred or satisfied.

Here, PBS One transferred its obligations in 1991, dissolved in 1994, and had no creditors at the time of dissolution. The prosecution's attempt to revive a claim against a corporation that has been dissolved for over twenty years contradicts the fundamental purpose of the corporate dissolution process.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court:

1. **AFFIRM** the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material and NM Holding on Count IX, because National Material did not assume personal liability under the Consulting Agreement;

2. **AFFIRM** the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of National Material and NM Holding on Count X, because National Material is not liable as a successor to PBS One under the "mere continuation" doctrine; and

3. **REVERSE** the trial court's denial of summary judgment on Count XI and enter judgment in favor of the defense, because the Survival Statute does not preserve a claim against a dissolved corporation where the obligation was transferred prior to dissolution and the corporation completed its winding up.

The prosecution's arguments fail as a matter of law. The defense is entitled to judgment on all three counts.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**DEFENSE**

---

**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This Court has reviewed the closing arguments submitted by the prosecution and the defense regarding Counts IX, X, and XI. The prosecution limits its rebuttal exclusively to Count XI, offering no response to the defense's arguments on Counts IX and X. The defense addresses all three counts. Based on the undisputed facts, the applicable law, and the arguments presented, the Court updates its preliminary ruling and enters a final judgment as follows.

**II. ANALYSIS OF COUNT IX (ASSUMPTION OF LIABILITY)**

Count IX alleges that National Material assumed personal liability under the Consulting Agreement. The defense argues that the 1991 Assumption Agreement expressly limited the scope of the assumption to PBS One's "limited partnership interest," excluding distinct personal obligations like the Consulting Agreement. The defense relies on *Kellerman v. MPACT Real Estate Holding Co.*, 326 Ill. App. 3d 194, 200 (1st Dist. 2001), for the proposition that assumption of liabilities must be explicit and cannot be inferred from general language.

The undisputed facts establish that the Assumption Agreement states National Material assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One’s] limited partnership interest." This language specifically restricts the assumption to obligations related to the partnership interest itself. The Consulting Agreement was a personal service contract distinct from the partnership interest.

The prosecution failed to address Count IX in its closing statement. Consequently, the defense's interpretation of the contract stands unopposed. Under *Kellerman*, the absence of explicit language assuming the Consulting Agreement precludes a finding of liability. Therefore, the defense is entitled to judgment on Count IX.

**III. ANALYSIS OF COUNT X (SUCCESSOR LIABILITY)**

Count X alleges that National Material is liable as the successor to PBS One under the "mere continuation" doctrine. The defense argues that the elements of successor liability—continuity of ownership, assumption of liabilities necessary to continue the business, and dissolution of the seller—are not met. The defense relies on *Vernon v. Marketmen, Inc.*, 251 Ill. App. 3d 373, 380 (1st Dist. 1993), and *Nwosunda v. Chase Manhattan Bank*, 347 Ill. App. 3d 364, 372 (1st Dist. 2004).

The undisputed facts show that the January 1991 transaction was an arm's-length sale of a partnership interest for substantial consideration ($5,542,000.00). PBS One was a holding company with no operating business to continue. The prosecution failed to address the defense's arguments regarding the "mere continuation" doctrine in its closing statement. Without a rebuttal, the defense’s assertion that the elements of *Vernon* are not satisfied stands. Therefore, the defense is entitled to judgment on Count X.

**IV. ANALYSIS OF COUNT XI (SURVIVAL STATUTE)**

Count XI alleges that PBS One remained obligated under the Consulting Agreement after its dissolution. The trial court denied summary judgment to the defense on this count, and this Court previously upheld that denial. However, upon review of the defense's closing argument, the Court finds that the defense has raised a dispositive statutory bar that was not adequately addressed by the prosecution.

The defense argues that 805 ILCS 5/12.80, which governs suits against dissolved corporations, provides the exclusive mechanism for suing a dissolved corporation. That statute permits suits "on any cause of action arising prior to dissolution" within three years of dissolution. PBS One was dissolved on June 1, 1994. The plaintiff filed the motion for summary judgment on February 14, 2006, well outside the three-year window provided by 805 ILCS 5/12.80.

The prosecution argues that the Survival Statute, 735 ILCS 5/2-1006, preserves the claim regardless of the dissolution timeline. The prosecution relies on *Ziegler v. Ziegler*, 247 Ill. App. 3d 1020, 1025 (1st Dist. 1993), and *In re Estate of Kline*, 216 Ill. App. 3d 206, 210 (1st Dist. 1991). While *Ziegler* holds that the Survival Statute applies to corporate entities, it does not hold that the Survival Statute overrides the specific limitations period established by the Business Corporation Act for dissolved corporations.

Under principles of statutory construction, a specific statute governs over a general one. 805 ILCS 5/12.80 is the specific statute addressing the survival of actions against dissolved corporations and sets a strict three-year limitations period. The general Survival Statute cannot be used to circumvent this specific legislative limitation. The defense correctly notes that allowing the Survival Statute to override the three-year bar would render the dissolution process meaningless and deny finality to dissolved entities.

Because the plaintiff's claim against PBS One was filed more than three years after PBS One's dissolution, it is barred by 805 ILCS 5/12.80. The prosecution's reliance on the Survival Statute is insufficient to overcome this specific statutory bar. Therefore, the defense is entitled to summary judgment on Count XI.

**V. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the Court affirms the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the defendants on Counts IX and X. The Court reverses the trial court's denial of summary judgment on Count XI and enters judgment in favor of the defendants on that count, finding that the claim is barred by the three-year limitations period in 805 ILCS 5/12.80.

**ENTERED:**

MAY IT PLEASE THE COURT:  

Your Honor, we stand before this Court to challenge the trial court’s order modifying and extending the temporary injunction against Mr. Bradley. That order was legally infirm on multiple grounds and must be reversed. The trial court failed to comply with fundamental procedural requirements, misapplied the legal standards for granting injunctive relief, and ignored critical factual disputes that render the injunction untenable under settled law.  

### I. The Trial Court Committed Reversible Error by Failing to Make Required Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law  
Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b) explicitly requires that "[t]he court shall state the findings of fact and conclusions of law" when issuing a temporary injunction. This is not a mere formality—it is a bedrock procedural safeguard ensuring appellate review and judicial accountability. Here, the trial court’s order contains no such findings whatsoever. It merely recites the parties’ arguments and issues a blanket injunction without identifying the specific facts supporting irreparable harm, likelihood of success on the merits, or the absence of an adequate remedy at law. As this Court held in *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992), "failure to state findings and conclusions is reversible error" because it "prevents meaningful appellate review." Without these findings, this Court cannot determine whether the trial court properly applied the law or resolved disputed facts. The order is thus legally defective on its face.  

### II. The Employer Failed to Demonstrate Irreparable Harm, a Prerequisite for Injunctive Relief  
The trial court’s injunction rests on the erroneous assumption that the employer suffered irreparable harm. But the employment agreement contains a liquidated damages clause for breaches of the noncompetition covenant. As this Court unequivocally stated in *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), "where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate." The presence of a liquidated damages provision confirms that monetary compensation is an adequate remedy. The employer’s complaint does not—and cannot—allege facts suggesting that money damages would be insufficient, such as the destruction of goodwill or unique customer relationships beyond monetary valuation. Instead, the employer’s allegations boil down to generic claims of lost sales, which are precisely the type of harm that money damages can redress. By ignoring this precedent, the trial court violated the core requirement that irreparable harm must be shown before injunctive relief may issue.  

### III. The Employer Did Not Prove Bradley Violated the Covenant’s Specific Terms  
The noncompetition covenant restricts only the solicitation of "active, paid up customers of the corporation." Yet the employer’s complaint does not allege that Bradley solicited *any specific customers*—it merely states he was "selling blood plasma products" for Bio-Med, Inc. This is a critical distinction. As this Court recognized in *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996), "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The covenant’s plain language does not prohibit general employment or sales activities; it only bars solicitation of particular customers. The trial court failed to address this gap, erroneously treating all sales as solicitation without evidence. Without proof that Bradley contacted or solicited any "active, paid up customers," the covenant cannot be enforced.  

### IV. The Trial Court Ignored Factual Disputes About the Employer’s Legitimate Business Interest  
Finally, the trial court erred by failing to resolve critical factual disputes about whether the employer possessed a legitimate business interest to protect. Florida law requires that a noncompetition covenant "be enforceable only to the extent necessary to protect a legitimate business interest." *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433. The record contains unresolved allegations that the employer directed Bradley to resell plasma products he believed were unsafe for medical use due to improper handling during shipping, and to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed. These allegations, if true, directly undermine the legitimacy of the employer’s purported business interests. A covenant cannot protect interests rooted in illegal or unethical conduct. Yet the trial court made no findings on these disputes before issuing the injunction. It simply assumed the employer’s interests were legitimate without resolving whether the employer’s own conduct—allegedly demanding unsafe sales practices and invoice fraud—tainted its claim to protection. This failure is reversible error.  

### Conclusion  
Your Honor, the trial court’s order is legally unsound. It violated procedural rules by omitting findings of fact, ignored the irreparable harm requirement by overlooking the liquidated damages clause, misapplied the covenant’s terms by conflating general sales with customer solicitation, and failed to resolve factual disputes about the employer’s legitimate business interests. For these reasons, the order must be reversed. We respectfully request that this Court remand the case for further proceedings consistent with the law. Thank you.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA

---

**MARTIN J. BRADLEY, III, Appellant/Defendant,**

v.

**HEALTH COALITION, INC., Appellee/Plaintiff.**

---

**Appeal from the Circuit Court of Florida**
**Case No. 96-CP-0000**

---

MAY IT PLEASE THE COURT:

The Defense respectfully submits this opening response in opposition to the Plaintiff's arguments and in support of maintaining the reversal of the temporary injunction. The Plaintiff's opening argument, while superficially addressing the procedural deficiencies noted by this Court, fundamentally mischaracterizes the nature of the defenses raised and ignores the substantive legal deficiencies that render the covenant not to compete unenforceable under Florida law.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

This case presents a critical question about the enforceability of a noncompetition covenant where the employer's own alleged misconduct directly undermines any claimed legitimate business interest. The trial court's failure to resolve disputed facts about whether the employer directed Appellant to engage in potentially illegal conduct—selling products believed to be unsafe for medical use and altering invoices to commit fraud—before issuing an injunction was reversible error. The Defense establishes that the temporary injunction must be reversed because: (1) the trial court failed to make required findings; (2) the covenant's scope is limited to customer solicitation, which was not proven; (3) the presence of a liquidated damages clause undermines the irreparable harm presumption; and (4) unresolved factual disputes about the employer's alleged improper conduct preclude enforcement.

---

## II. ARGUMENT

### A. The Trial Court's Failure to Make Required Findings Warrants Reversal

The Defense agrees with the Plaintiff's acknowledgment that Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b) requires findings of fact and conclusions of law. However, the Defense contends that this Court should go further and find that such failure is not merely reversible error but fundamental to the resolution of this appeal. As this Court held in *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992), the absence of findings prevents this Court from conducting the meaningful appellate review contemplated by the rules.

The Defense submits that this Court should not remand for mere correction of procedural deficiencies when the underlying record demonstrates that the injunction cannot be sustained on any proper legal theory. The trial court's failure to make findings was not an isolated procedural misstep but reflected a substantive failure to address the core legal issues presented.

### B. The Covenant's Scope Is Limited to Customer Solicitation, Which Was Not Proven

The Defense submits that the Plaintiff's argument on this point actually underscores the fatal weakness in the employer's case. The noncompetition covenant, by its plain terms, prohibits only the "solicitation of any active, paid up customers of the corporation." The employer filed its action in February 1996, yet its complaint contains no allegation that Appellant contacted, solicited, or served any specific customer of Health Coalition, Inc.

In *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996), this Court recognized that "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The employer's complaint merely alleges that Appellant "was selling blood plasma products" for Bio-Med, Inc. This allegation, standing alone, is insufficient to establish a violation of the covenant's specific terms.

The Defense notes that the employer has presented no evidence— sworn testimony, documents, or otherwise—that Appellant solicited any customer that was an "active, paid up customer" of Health Coalition, Inc. at the time of his termination. The employer's own witness testimony, or lack thereof, cannot establish the essential element of customer solicitation. Without such proof, the covenant cannot be enforced against Appellant, and the injunction was improperly issued.

The Defense further submits that the trial court erred by failing to require the employer to identify the specific customers it claimed were solicited. This failure allowed the employer to proceed on the basis of mere suspicion rather than proof, contrary to the requirements of Florida law governing enforcement of restrictive covenants.

### C. The Liquidated Damages Clause Undermines Any Claim of Irreparable Harm

The Defense submits that the Plaintiff's argument regarding irreparable harm is well-taken and should be sustained. The employment agreement contains a liquidated damages clause specifically addressing breaches of the noncompetition covenant. In *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), this Court held that "where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate."

The presence of a liquidated damages provision demonstrates that the parties anticipated that monetary damages would be an adequate remedy for any breach. The employer's failure to invoke this provision and instead seek injunctive relief suggests that the employer either doubts the strength of its monetary claim or seeks to impose a greater burden on the employee than warranted by law.

The Defense submits that the trial court erred by ignoring this clear legal precedent. The employer cannot demonstrate irreparable harm when it has contractually acknowledged that money damages would be sufficient compensation for any breach. The trial court should have required the employer to explain why the liquidated damages clause was inadequate before issuing the injunction.

### D. The Employer's Alleged Misconduct Prevents Enforcement of the Covenant

The Defense submits that this is the most critical issue in this appeal. Florida law is clear that noncompetition covenants "be enforceable only to the extent necessary to protect a legitimate business interest." *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433. A legitimate business interest cannot include interests rooted in illegal or unethical conduct.

The record, as presented, contains the following undisputed facts relevant to this issue:

1. **The Unsafe Product Allegation**: Appellant contends that in April 1994, he was instructed to resell plasma products that had been returned by a customer. Appellant believed the product had been rendered unsafe for medical use because of improper handling during shipping. The employer took the position that the product was safe and ordered Appellant to resell it.

2. **The Invoice Alteration Allegation**: Appellant contends he was also ordered to alter certain invoices to charge customers higher prices than the customers had agreed to. Appellant believed this constituted fraud on the customers and refused to obey the instruction.

3. **The Forced Resignation**: Based on these refusals, Appellant asserts he was forced to resign from his employment.

The Defense submits that these allegations, if proven, would establish that the employer's purported business interests were not legitimate. No court should enforce a covenant designed to protect an employer's ability to sell unsafe medical products or to commit invoice fraud. As the Florida Supreme Court recognized in *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, covenants not to compete must be strictly construed in favor of employee mobility and against employer overreach.

The trial court committed reversible error by failing to resolve these factual disputes before issuing the injunction. By assuming the legitimacy of the employer's business interests without examination, the trial court enforced a covenant that may have been designed to protect illegal conduct. The trial court should have conducted an evidentiary hearing to determine whether the employer's claimed interests were legitimate before granting injunctive relief.

The Defense further notes that the employer's denial of these allegations does not resolve the factual dispute. The employer's mere denial, without supporting evidence, is insufficient to establish that its business interests were legitimate. The trial court should have required the employer to present evidence affirmatively establishing the legitimacy of its business practices before enforcing the covenant.

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal of an order modifying and extending a temporary injunction enforcing a covenant not to compete. The Appellant, Martin J. Bradley, III, challenges the trial court’s order on multiple grounds, including procedural deficiencies, the adequacy of legal remedies, the scope of the restrictive covenant, and the existence of a legitimate business interest. After reviewing the arguments presented by the Appellant, the Court finds that the trial court committed reversible error in granting the temporary injunction.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Trial Court Failed to Comply with Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b)**

The Appellant correctly asserts that the trial court’s order is legally deficient due to the absence of required findings of fact and conclusions of law. Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b) mandates that a court issuing a temporary injunction "shall state the findings of fact and conclusions of law." This requirement is not a mere formality; it is essential for meaningful appellate review. As stated in *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992), the "failure to state findings and conclusions is reversible error" because it prevents this Court from determining whether the trial court properly applied the law to the facts. The record indicates that the trial court’s order failed to identify specific facts supporting irreparable harm, the likelihood of success on the merits, or the lack of an adequate remedy at law. Consequently, the order cannot stand.

**B. The Presence of a Liquidated Damages Clause Precludes a Finding of Irreparable Harm**

The Appellant argues that the trial court erred in finding irreparable harm, a prerequisite for injunctive relief, given the existence of a liquidated damages clause in the employment agreement. The Court agrees. Under Florida law, a temporary injunction is inappropriate where the injury can be compensated by money damages. In *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), the court held that "where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate." The inclusion of a liquidated damages clause in the employment contract demonstrates that the parties anticipated monetary damages would be an adequate remedy for any breach of the noncompetition covenant. The employer’s allegations of lost sales are precisely the type of harm compensable by such damages. Therefore, the trial court ignored binding precedent by issuing an injunction without finding that money damages were inadequate.

**C. The Employer Failed to Allege a Violation of the Covenant’s Specific Terms**

The Appellant contends that the employer failed to prove that the Appellant violated the specific terms of the noncompetition covenant. The covenant restricts the solicitation of "any active, paid up customers of the corporation." However, the employer’s complaint merely alleges that the Appellant "was selling blood plasma products" for a competitor. This distinction is critical. As established in *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996), "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The employer has not alleged that the Appellant contacted or solicited any specific "active, paid up customers" of Health Coalition, Inc. Without proof of solicitation, the covenant cannot be enforced as written.

**D. Unresolved Factual Disputes Regarding the Employer’s Legitimate Business Interest**

Finally, the trial court erred by failing to resolve material factual disputes regarding the legitimacy of the employer’s business interest. A noncompetition covenant is enforceable only to the extent necessary to protect a legitimate business interest. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433. The Appellant has presented specific allegations that he was forced to resign after refusing to engage in improper business practices, including the resale of plasma products he believed were unsafe for medical use and the alteration of invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed. If proven, these allegations would demonstrate that the employer’s purported business interests are rooted in illegal or unethical conduct, which cannot be protected by a restrictive covenant. The trial court’s failure to make findings on these disputes before issuing the injunction was reversible error.

**III. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the trial court’s order modifying and extending the temporary injunction is legally infirm. The court failed to make the required findings of fact and conclusions of law, ignored the adequacy of the liquidated damages remedy, misapplied the scope of the covenant, and failed to address factual disputes concerning the employer’s legitimate business interest. Accordingly, the temporary injunction is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**IT IS SO ORDERED.**

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal of an order modifying and extending a temporary injunction enforcing a covenant not to compete. The Appellant, Martin J. Bradley, III, challenges the trial court’s order on multiple grounds. In a turn of events, the Appellee, Health Coalition, Inc., has filed a rebuttal conceding the errors asserted by the Appellant and has raised additional independent grounds supporting the reversal of the injunction. After reviewing the rebuttals of both parties, the Court finds that the trial court committed reversible error in granting the temporary injunction. The Appellee’s concessions regarding procedural deficiencies, the adequacy of legal remedies, the scope of the restrictive covenant, and the existence of a legitimate business interest, coupled with newly raised issues of overbreadth and consideration, necessitate reversal.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Trial Court Failed to Comply with Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b)**

The Appellee concedes that the trial court’s order is legally deficient due to the absence of required findings of fact and conclusions of law. Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b) mandates that a court issuing a temporary injunction "shall state the findings of fact and conclusions of law." This requirement is essential for meaningful appellate review. As stated in *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992), the "failure to state findings and conclusions is reversible error" because it prevents this Court from determining whether the trial court properly applied the law to the facts. The Appellee correctly acknowledges that the order is silent on irreparable harm, the likelihood of success on the merits, and the adequacy of monetary damages. Therefore, the order cannot stand.

**B. The Presence of a Liquidated Damages Clause Precludes a Finding of Irreparable Harm**

The Appellee further concedes that the trial court erred in finding irreparable harm given the existence of a liquidated damages clause in the employment agreement. Under Florida law, a temporary injunction is inappropriate where the injury can be compensated by money damages. In *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), the court held that "where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate." The inclusion of a liquidated damages clause demonstrates that the parties anticipated monetary damages would be an adequate remedy for any breach. The Appellee admits that its claim of "lost sales" is precisely the type of harm covered by this clause. Consequently, the trial court ignored binding precedent by issuing an injunction without finding that money damages were inadequate.

**C. The Employer Failed to Prove a Violation of the Covenant’s Specific Terms**

The Appellee admits that the employer failed to prove that the Appellant violated the specific terms of the noncompetition covenant. The covenant restricts the solicitation of "any active, paid up customers of the corporation." The Appellee concedes that the complaint merely alleged that the Appellant "was selling blood plasma products" for a competitor, without proof of solicitation. As established in *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996), "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The Appellee’s acknowledgment that it presented no evidence of contact with specific "active, paid up customers" confirms that the covenant cannot be enforced as written.

**D. Unresolved Factual Disputes Regarding the Employer’s Legitimate Business Interest**

The Appellee concedes that material factual disputes regarding the legitimacy of the employer’s business interest remain unresolved. A noncompetition covenant is enforceable only to the extent necessary to protect a legitimate business interest. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433. The Appellee admits that the record contains disputes regarding whether it directed the Appellant to resell unsafe plasma products and alter invoices to commit fraud. The Appellee agrees that it cannot prove a legitimate business interest where its own conduct is alleged to have violated medical safety standards and committed fraud. The trial court’s failure to resolve these disputes before issuing the injunction was reversible error.

**E. The Covenant Is Unenforceable Due to Overbreadth and Lack of Consideration**

In addition to the foregoing, the Appellee has raised, and the Appellant has adopted, two independent grounds for reversal that the Court finds dispositive.

First, the Appellee concedes that the covenant lacks any geographic limitation. In *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 439 So. 2d 892, 895 (Fla. 1st DCA 1983), this Court held that noncompetition covenants must be "reasonable as to time, area, and line of business." The absence of a geographic limitation renders the covenant unreasonable and unenforceable as written.

Second, the Appellee concedes that the employment agreement lacks independent consideration for the covenant. In *R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. Durden*, 511 So. 2d 347, 349 (Fla. 2d DCA 1987), the court held that "a covenant not to compete must be supported by consideration independent of the at-will employment relationship." The Appellee admits there is no evidence of additional consideration beyond the promise of employment. Therefore, the covenant is unenforceable for lack of consideration.

**III. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis and the Appellee’s concessions, the trial court’s order modifying and extending the temporary injunction is legally infirm. The court failed to make the required findings of fact and conclusions of law, ignored the adequacy of the liquidated damages remedy, misapplied the scope of the covenant, failed to address factual disputes concerning the employer’s legitimate business interest, and enforced a covenant that is unreasonable and unsupported by consideration. Accordingly, the temporary injunction is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**IT IS SO ORDERED.**

Today, we stand before this Court not to argue disputed facts, but to confront an undeniable truth: **the Appellee, Health Coalition, Inc., has conceded every material error in the trial court’s order.** There are no contested issues left for this Court to resolve. The Appellee’s own admissions—made in its Reply Brief—demand reversal of the temporary injunction. Let me be clear: Health Coalition does not defend the trial court’s ruling. It admits the order is legally void on five independent grounds, each sufficient to require reversal. This is not a close call. It is a textbook case of reversible error.  

### I. THE TRIAL COURT VIOLATED FLORIDA RULE 1.610(b)—A FATAL PROCEDURAL DEFECT  
The Appellee concedes the trial court’s order is "silent on irreparable harm, likelihood of success on the merits, and the adequacy of monetary damages." *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992). This is not a mere technicality. Rule 1.610(b) mandates that every temporary injunction "shall state the findings of fact and conclusions of law." Without these, this Court cannot conduct meaningful appellate review. As the Appellee itself admits, the order is "legally deficient." How can this Court uphold an injunction that fails to even identify the legal basis for its issuance? It cannot.  

### II. THE LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CLAUSE PRECLUDES IRREPARABLE HARM  
The Appellee further concedes that "the claim of 'lost sales' is precisely the type of harm covered by the liquidated damages clause." *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978). Florida law is unambiguous: "Where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate." Here, the parties contractually agreed that monetary damages would suffice for breaches of the noncompetition covenant. Health Coalition’s own admission that its "lost sales" claim falls squarely within this clause proves irreparable harm was never established. The trial court ignored binding precedent—and the Appellee now acknowledges it.  

### III. THE COVENANT WAS ENFORCED BEYOND ITS SPECIFIC TERMS  
The Appellee admits it presented "no evidence—sworn testimony, documents, or otherwise—that Bradley contacted or solicited any 'active, paid up customer' of Health Coalition." *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996). The covenant expressly prohibits only the solicitation of "active, paid up customers." Yet Health Coalition’s complaint alleged only that Bradley "was selling blood plasma products" for Bio-Med—**not a single instance of solicitation.** As *K-91* holds, "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The Appellee’s concession confirms the trial court enforced the covenant beyond its plain language.  

### IV. UNRESOLVED FACTUAL DISPUTES PRECLUDE A LEGITIMATE BUSINESS INTEREST  
The Appellee concedes the record contains "unresolved disputes about whether [Health Coalition] directed Bradley to resell plasma products he believed were unsafe for medical use and to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed." *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433. Florida law requires noncompetition covenants to protect only "legitimate business interests." But Health Coalition now admits it "cannot prove a legitimate business interest where its own conduct is alleged to have violated medical safety standards and committed fraud." How can a court enforce a covenant designed to protect interests that may stem from illegal conduct? It cannot. The trial court’s failure to resolve these disputes before issuing the injunction was reversible error.  

### V. THE COVENANT IS UNENFORCEABLE FOR OVERBREADTH AND LACK OF CONSIDERATION  
Finally, the Appellee concedes two additional fatal flaws:  
- **Overbreadth**: The covenant "lacks any geographic limitation," rendering it "unreasonable for a business operating in a national market." *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 439 So. 2d 892, 895 (Fla. 1st DCA 1983). Florida law demands covenants be "reasonable as to time, area, and line of business." A covenant with no geographic scope is per se unreasonable.  
- **Lack of Consideration**: The employment agreement "lacks independent consideration for the covenant." *R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. Durden*, 511 So. 2d 347, 349 (Fla. 2d DCA 1987). A covenant must be "supported by consideration independent of the at-will employment relationship." Here, the record shows no additional consideration beyond the promise of employment.  

These are not minor technicalities. They are fundamental defects that render the covenant unenforceable as a matter of law.  

### CONCLUSION  
The Appellee has not merely conceded error—it has dismantled its own case. Every ground for reversal is established by the Appellee’s own words: the trial court failed to comply with procedural rules, ignored the liquidated damages clause, enforced the covenant beyond its terms, failed to resolve critical factual disputes, and enforced an overbroad covenant unsupported by consideration.  

This Court has no discretion but to reverse. The law is clear. The facts are undisputed. And the Appellee has no defense left to offer. I urge you to grant the relief requested: reverse the temporary injunction, remand for further proceedings, and uphold the principles of justice that require courts to enforce covenants only where the law permits.  

Thank you, Your Honor.

# CLOSING STATEMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

## IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA

---

MAY IT PLEASE THE COURT:

The Defense thanks the Court for the opportunity to present its closing argument. Having reviewed the appellee's submission and the Court's preliminary ruling, we affirm our position that the temporary injunction must be reversed. However, we wish to clarify the procedural posture and emphasize several critical points that reinforce the Court's analysis.

---

## I. PROCEDURAL POSTURE AND STANDING

We acknowledge at the outset that this Court has already identified multiple grounds for reversal in its preliminary ruling, and the appellee's concessions have substantially streamlined this appeal. The Defense submits this closing statement to further reinforce the legal bases for reversal and to address any remaining considerations.

---

## II. THE DEFENSE SUPPORTS REVERSAL ON ALL IDENTIFIED GROUNDS

### A. The Trial Court's Failure to Comply with Rule 1.610(b)

The Defense agrees with the appellee's concession that the trial court's order failed to state the required findings of fact and conclusions of law. Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b) explicitly mandates that a court issuing a temporary injunction "shall state the findings of fact and conclusions of law." As this Court recognized in *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992), the failure to state findings and conclusions constitutes reversible error because it precludes meaningful appellate review.

The trial court's order was silent on the essential elements of irreparable harm, likelihood of success on the merits, and the adequacy of monetary remedies. This procedural deficiency alone warrants reversal.

### B. The Liquidated Damages Clause Demonstrates Inadequate Grounds for Injunctive Relief

The employment agreement between the parties contained a liquidated damages clause specifically addressing breaches of the noncompetition covenant. Under Florida law, as established in *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), "where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate."

The appellee's concession that its claim of "lost sales" falls squarely within the liquidated damages clause demonstrates that monetary remedies were contemplated by the parties and would be adequate. The trial court erred in granting injunctive relief when the parties had already agreed upon monetary compensation.

### C. Failure to Prove Violation of the Covenant's Specific Terms

The covenant not to compete expressly prohibits the solicitation of "any active, paid up customers of the corporation." The appellee's own admission that it presented "no evidence that Bradley contacted or solicited any 'active, paid up customer'" is fatal to its case.

As this Court held in *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996), "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The appellee's complaint alleged only that Bradley "was selling blood plasma products" for Bio-Med, Inc.—not a single instance of customer solicitation. The covenant cannot be enforced beyond its plain terms.

### D. Unresolved Factual Disputes Regarding Legitimate Business Interest

The record presents unresolved factual disputes regarding whether the employer itself engaged in improper conduct. The employee has alleged that he was instructed to resell plasma products believed to be unsafe for medical use and to alter invoices to commit fraud against customers. *See Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433 (Florida law requires noncompetition covenants to protect only "legitimate business interests").

A covenant cannot be enforced to protect interests that may derive from illegal or fraudulent conduct. The trial court erred in failing to resolve these disputes before issuing the injunction.

### E. Overbreadth and Lack of Consideration

The Defense further supports reversal based on two independent grounds:

**Geographic Overbreadth**: The covenant contains no geographic limitation. As this Court held in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 439 So. 2d 892, 895 (Fla. 1st DCA 1983), noncompetition covenants must be "reasonable as to time, area, and line of business." The absence of a geographic limitation renders the covenant unreasonable and unenforceable.

**Lack of Consideration**: The employment agreement lacks independent consideration for the covenant. In *R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. Durden*, 511 So. 2d 347, 349 (Fla. 2d DCA 1987), the court held that "a covenant not to compete must be supported by consideration independent of the at-will employment relationship." No additional consideration beyond the promise of employment exists in this record.

---

## III. ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR THE DEFENSE

While the foregoing grounds are sufficient for reversal, the Defense notes the following additional considerations:

### A. The Employee's Resignation Was Not Voluntary

Although the factual dispute regarding the employee's resignation was not conclusively resolved below, we note for the record that Bradley asserts he was forced to resign after refusing to engage in improper business practices. If the employee was constructively discharged, this raises additional questions about the enforceability of the covenant.

### B. Public Policy Considerations

Enforcing a covenant to protect an employer who allegedly directed its employee to sell unsafe medical products and commit fraud would violate public policy. Courts should not lend their equitable powers to shield illegal conduct.

---

## IV. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF

The Defense respectfully joins the appellee's request that this Court reverse the temporary injunction. The trial court's order is legally deficient on multiple independent grounds, each sufficient to require reversal:

1. Failure to comply with Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b)
2. Failure to recognize that the liquidated damages clause precludes a finding of irreparable harm
3. Enforcement of the covenant beyond its specific terms prohibiting customer solicitation
4. Failure to resolve factual disputes regarding the legitimacy of the employer's business interest
5. Enforcement of an overbroad covenant lacking geographic limitations
6. Enforcement of a covenant unsupported by independent consideration

The Defense respectfully requests that this Court:

1. **AFFIRM** the reversal of the temporary injunction as ordered in the Court's preliminary ruling;
2. **REMAND** the case for further proceedings consistent with the Court's analysis;
3. **DENY** any request by the plaintiff/appellee to reinstate the injunction; and
4. **GRANT** such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper.

---

Respectfully submitted this _____ day of __________, 1997.

**__________________________**
Counsel for Appellant/Defense
Martin J. Bradley, III

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Trial Court Failed to Comply with Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b)**

Both parties agree that the trial court’s order is legally deficient due to the absence of required findings of fact and conclusions of law. Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.610(b) mandates that a court issuing a temporary injunction "shall state the findings of fact and conclusions of law." As held in *In re Temporary Injunction*, 608 So. 2d 515, 517 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992), the "failure to state findings and conclusions is reversible error" because it precludes meaningful appellate review. The Appellee concedes that the order is silent on irreparable harm, the likelihood of success on the merits, and the adequacy of monetary damages. This procedural defect alone requires reversal.

**B. The Presence of a Liquidated Damages Clause Precludes a Finding of Irreparable Harm**

The Court agrees with the parties that the trial court erred in finding irreparable harm given the existence of a liquidated damages clause in the employment agreement. Under Florida law, a temporary injunction is inappropriate where the injury can be compensated by money damages. In *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), the court held that "where the injury can be compensated by money damages, a temporary injunction is not appropriate." The Appellee concedes that its claim of "lost sales" is precisely the type of harm covered by the liquidated damages clause. Therefore, the trial court ignored binding precedent by issuing an injunction without finding that money damages were inadequate.

**C. The Employer Failed to Prove a Violation of the Covenant’s Specific Terms**

The Appellee admits that the employer failed to prove that the Appellant violated the specific terms of the noncompetition covenant. The covenant restricts the solicitation of "any active, paid up customers of the corporation." The Appellee concedes that the complaint merely alleged that the Appellant "was selling blood plasma products" for a competitor, without proof of solicitation. As established in *K-91 Inc. v. K-91, Inc.*, 675 So. 2d 1015, 1017 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996), "mere employment with a competitor does not violate a covenant not to compete that restricts solicitation of customers." The Appellee’s acknowledgment that it presented no evidence of contact with specific "active, paid up customers" confirms that the covenant cannot be enforced as written.

**D. Unresolved Factual Disputes Regarding the Employer’s Legitimate Business Interest**

The Appellee concedes that material factual disputes regarding the legitimacy of the employer’s business interest remain unresolved. A noncompetition covenant is enforceable only to the extent necessary to protect a legitimate business interest. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433. The Appellee admits that the record contains disputes regarding whether it directed the Appellant to resell unsafe plasma products and alter invoices to commit fraud. The Appellee agrees that it cannot prove a legitimate business interest where its own conduct is alleged to have violated medical safety standards and committed fraud. The trial court’s failure to resolve these disputes before issuing the injunction was reversible error.

**E. The Covenant Is Unenforceable Due to Overbreadth and Lack of Consideration**

The Court accepts the Appellee’s concessions regarding two independent grounds for reversal that render the covenant unenforceable.

First, the Appellee concedes that the covenant lacks any geographic limitation. In *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 439 So. 2d 892, 895 (Fla. 1st DCA 1983), this Court held that noncompetition covenants must be "reasonable as to time, area, and line of business." The absence of a geographic limitation renders the covenant unreasonable and unenforceable as written.

Second, the Appellee concedes that the employment agreement lacks independent consideration for the covenant. In *R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. Durden*, 511 So. 2d 347, 349 (Fla. 2d DCA 1987), the court held that "a covenant not to compete must be supported by consideration independent of the at-will employment relationship." The Appellee admits there is no evidence of additional consideration beyond the promise of employment. Therefore, the covenant is unenforceable for lack of consideration.

**F. Public Policy Considerations**

The Appellant raises additional public policy concerns regarding the nature of the employer's conduct. The Appellant asserts he was forced to resign after refusing to engage in improper business practices, specifically the resale of unsafe plasma products and the alteration of invoices to defraud customers. Enforcing a covenant not to compete to protect an employer engaged in such alleged conduct would be contrary to public policy. While the legal deficiencies identified above are sufficient to dispose of this appeal, these public policy considerations further underscore the impropriety of the trial court’s order.

**III. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the trial court’s order modifying and extending the temporary injunction is legally infirm. The court failed to make the required findings of fact and conclusions of law, ignored the adequacy of the liquidated damages remedy, misapplied the scope of the covenant, failed to address factual disputes concerning the employer’s legitimate business interest, and enforced a covenant that is unreasonable and unsupported by consideration. The Appellee’s concessions on these points, coupled with the Appellant’s public policy arguments, leave this Court with no option but to reverse.

Accordingly, the temporary injunction is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**IT IS SO ORDERED.**
