**REBUTTAL TO DEFENSE OPENING STATEMENT**

The defense’s arguments fail to address the controlling precedent and record evidence demonstrating that the trial court properly admitted the NPLEX records and committed no reversible error. This Court must affirm the judgment.

### I. The NPLEX Records Are Nontestimonial and Officer Lemonier Was a Qualified Witness

The defense mischaracterizes the NPLEX system as testimonial, but the record establishes otherwise. As this Court explicitly held, "[t]estimonial statements are those created or given with the primary purpose of creating an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony." *Ohio v. Clark*, 135 S.Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L.Ed.2d 306 (2015). The NPLEX system’s statutory purpose under Ohio Revised Code Section 3715.05 is to "track purchases of pseudoephedrine" for regulatory compliance and law enforcement monitoring—not to create evidence for trial. *United States v. Collins*, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015), squarely rejected the notion that similar pharmacy records are testimonial, observing it is "improbable that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check of a customer would have anticipated that the records of that transaction would later be used against these particular defendants at trial." The defense’s reliance on *State v. Coleman*, 5th Dist. Richland No. 14-CA-82, 2015-Ohio-3907, 2015 WL 5608526, ¶ 35, is misplaced because that case expressly acknowledged NPLEX’s role in "monitoring suspicious purchases," not in generating testimonial evidence. The defense’s attempt to elevate law enforcement use of the system to a "primary purpose" for testimonial analysis ignores *Clark*’s requirement that the statement’s creation—not its subsequent use—determines testimonial status.

Officer Lemonier’s testimony satisfied Evidence Rule 803(6)’s "qualified witness" standard. A qualified witness need only possess "enough familiarity with the record-keeping system of the business in question to explain how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." *State v. Hood*, 135 Ohio St.3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40. Officer Lemonier testified he: (1) holds a licensed access to NPLEX requiring username/password credentials; (2) accesses the system daily; (3) understands the real-time process where pharmacy IDs are swiped, data transmitted to NPLEX, and purchase thresholds trigger denials; and (4) retrieved Ms. Kittle’s record by entering her identifying information. This testimony established the record’s origin and maintenance in ordinary business operations. Critically, *State v. Baker*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, ¶ 11, confirms a witness need not "have personal knowledge of the exact circumstances of preparation and production of the document" to authenticate business records—only sufficient familiarity with the system’s operation. Officer Lemonier’s detailed explanation of NPLEX’s mechanics satisfies this standard. The defense’s attempt to distinguish "accessing" the system from "understanding" it is baseless; his testimony directly addressed how records are created and maintained, as required by *Hood*.

### II. The Trial Court’s Intervention Was Proper and Nonprejudicial

The defense’s claim that the trial court "abdicated neutrality" ignores Evidence Rule 614(B)’s explicit authorization for courts to interrogate witnesses "in an impartial manner." In a bench trial—where no jury is present to be influenced—the trial court has "greater flexibility" to question witnesses to "ascertain a material fact or to develop the truth." *State v. Grad*, 9th Dist. Medina No. 10CA0003-M, 2012-Ohio-1358, 2012 WL 1076215, ¶ 44. The trial court’s actions were entirely proper: it noted its role was "to find the truth," permitted Officer Lemonier to supplement the record, and gave the defense time to review the expanded data. There is "no indication of bias, prejudice, or prodding of a witness to elicit partisan testimony." *State v. Baston*, 85 Ohio St.3d 418, 426, 709 N.E.2d 128 (1999). The defense’s election to proceed without reviewing the expanded record—despite the court’s offer—precludes any claim of prejudice. As this Court held in *Baston*, absent evidence of improper influence, the court’s actions "will be presumed to act with impartiality."

### III. The Evidence Was Sufficient to Sustain the Conviction

The defense’s insufficiency argument misapplies Ohio law. Ohio Revised Code Section 2925.041(A) prohibits "illegal assembly or possession of chemicals for the manufacture of drugs." Ms. Kittle’s own admission—that she "bought pseudoephedrine for J.S. in exchange for methamphetamine"—directly satisfies this statute. The defense’s contention that "mere presence" or "association" is required ignores that the statute criminalizes the *possession or assembly of chemicals for manufacturing*, not the physical manufacturing itself. The officers discovered methamphetamine lab materials in the apartment where Ms. Kittle had been present, and J.S. was found in possession of methamphetamine and pseudoephedrine-related items. Ms. Kittle’s admission of providing pseudoephedrine—which is the "chemical" referenced in the statute—was sufficient evidence to prove the offense. The defense’s attempt to require proof of physical presence during manufacturing is unsupported by the plain language of R.C. 2925.041(A).

### IV. The Indictment Amendment Caused No Prejudice

The defense’s claim that amending the indictment to include "the preceding seven days" prejudiced her defense is contradicted by the record. The trial court’s journal entry explicitly states it found Ms. Kittle guilty "based upon the December 2, 2014 date only." *State v. Dudukovich*, 9th Dist. Lorain No. 05CA008729, 2006-Ohio-1309, 2006 WL 709102, ¶ 16, requires prejudice for reversible error on amendment. Because the conviction rested solely on the original date, the defense cannot demonstrate how the amendment impaired its ability to prepare a defense. The defense was aware of the November 30, 2014, pseudoephedrine purchase through discovery, and the trial court’s reliance on December 2, 2014, negates any claim of surprise or prejudice.

### CONCLUSION

The trial court correctly admitted the NPLEX records through Officer Lemonier as a qualified witness, acted within its authority during trial, and properly applied the law to sufficient evidence. The defense’s arguments rely on mischaracterizations of the record and controlling precedent. This Court should affirm the judgment.

rounds.defense_argument:
# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## INTRODUCTION

The prosecution's rebuttal fails to overcome the fundamental constitutional and evidentiary deficiencies in the trial court proceedings. While the prosecution correctly notes that this Court reviews the trial court's rulings for abuse of discretion, it overlooks the substantial record evidence demonstrating that the trial court erred in multiple respects. The defense maintains that the NPLEX records were improperly admitted, the trial court exceeded its role in supplementing the State's evidence, the indictment amendment violated fundamental due process rights, and the evidence was insufficient to sustain the conviction. This Court should sustain the defense's assignments of error and reverse the judgment of the trial court.

## I. THE NPLEX RECORDS WERE IMPROPERLY ADMITTED

### A. The NPLEX Records Are Testimonial Under the Primary Purpose Test

The prosecution misapplies the primary purpose test established in Ohio v. Clark, 135 S. Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L. Ed. 2d 306 (2015), by focusing on the moment of the record's creation rather than examining the system's design and operational context. The defense acknowledges that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check may not anticipate trial use, but this case presents entirely different circumstances.

The NPLEX system was established pursuant to Ohio Revised Code Section 3715.05 specifically for the purpose of monitoring pseudoephedrine purchases to assist law enforcement in combating methamphetamine manufacturing. Unlike ordinary business records created for internal operational purposes, the NPLEX system exists precisely because state and federal legislatures determined that tracking these purchases would aid criminal investigations. The system is designed to generate real-time alerts to law enforcement when purchases exceed thresholds, demonstrating that the records are created with law enforcement intervention as a primary purpose. See State v. Coleman, 5th Dist. Richland No. 14-CA-82, 2015-Ohio-3907, 2015 WL 5608526, ¶ 35 (acknowledging the purpose of the NPLEx system is to monitor suspicious purchases of pseudoephedrine tablets).

The prosecution's reliance on United States v. Collins, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015), is misplaced because that case involved different records with different primary purposes. Here, the NPLEX system is an integrated law enforcement tool, not an incidental business record. The defense maintains that when a system is designed specifically to generate evidence for criminal prosecutions, the records it produces are testimonial regardless of who physically enters the data.

### B. Officer Lemonier Was Not a Qualified Witness

The prosecution's argument that Officer Lemonier satisfied the qualified witness requirement misreads Evidence Rule 803(6) and the governing precedent. The rule requires testimony from "the custodian or other qualified witness" who can explain "how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." State v. Hood, 135 Ohio St. 3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40.

Officer Lemonier's testimony established only that he has law enforcement access to the NPLEX system and understands how to retrieve records. This falls far short of demonstrating familiarity with the record-keeping system of the business that creates the records—namely, the pharmacies that input pseudoephedrine purchase data. The prosecution conflates knowledge of how to access law enforcement databases with knowledge of how businesses maintain records in the ordinary course of business. The defense notes that the pharmacies themselves maintain no custody or control over the NPLEX system; the data is transmitted to a centralized database operated by the National Association of Drug Diversion Investigators.

As this Court acknowledged in State v. Baker, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, ¶ 11, the witness must demonstrate sufficient familiarity with "the circumstances of the preparation, maintenance, and retrieval of the record." Officer Lemonier offered no testimony about how pharmacies prepare pseudoephedrine sales records, their internal maintenance procedures, or their regular practices regarding data entry. His testimony established only his law enforcement use of the system, not the business practices of the pharmacies that generate the underlying data. The trial court abused its discretion in admitting the records through this inadequate foundation.

## II. THE TRIAL COURT IMPROPERLY ABDICATED ITS ROLE AS IMPARTIAL FINDER OF FACT

The prosecution's defense of the trial court's intervention misconstrues the nature of judicial impartiality and the protections afforded to defendants in criminal proceedings. While Evidence Rule 614(B) permits courts to interrogate witnesses, this authority is not unlimited and must be exercised in a manner that does not prejudice the defendant's rights.

The prosecution argues that the trial court's actions were proper because it sought to "find the truth" and because this was a bench trial. However, the rule's purpose—"to prevent the trial judge, in questioning the witness, from conveying to a jury the judge's impression as to the credibility or lack of credibility of a witness"—applies with equal force to bench trials. See State v. Grad, 9th Dist. Medina No. 10CA0003-M, 2012-Ohio-1358, 2012 WL 1076215, ¶ 44. The danger is not merely that a judge might influence a jury; it is that the judge might develop or convey a bias that affects the outcome of the proceeding.

Here, the trial court did not merely ask clarifying questions. Rather than awaiting the State's case-in-chief or requiring the State to present evidence properly, the trial court interjected during cross-examination to identify a deficiency in the State's evidence and then directed the State to remedy that deficiency. This intervention fundamentally altered the adversarial dynamic of the trial. The trial court effectively became an advocate for the prosecution by identifying evidentiary gaps and directing their correction.

The prosecution notes that defense counsel was offered time to review the expanded record and elected to proceed. This argument ignores that the damage was already done. The trial court's intervention signaled to the prosecution that it should strengthen its case and provided a roadmap for doing so. The defense's decision to proceed cannot cure the prejudice caused by the court's improper intervention. The prosecution's reliance on State v. Baston, 85 Ohio St. 3d 418, 426, 709 N.E.2d 128 (1999), is unavailing because that case involved isolated questions aimed at clarifying testimony, not directed supplementation of the prosecution's case.

## III. THE EVIDENCE WAS INSUFFICIENT TO SUSTAIN THE CONVICTION

The prosecution fundamentally misreads the elements of Ohio Revised Code Section 2925.041(A), which prohibits "illegal assembly or possession of chemicals for the manufacture of drugs." The statute requires proof that the defendant either possessed or assembled chemicals for the purpose of manufacturing drugs.

The prosecution relies entirely on Ms. Kittle's admission that she purchased pseudoephedrine for J.S. in exchange for methamphetamine. This admission, standing alone, does not establish that Ms. Kittle possessed or assembled chemicals for methamphetamine manufacturing. At most, it establishes that she provided a precursor chemical to another person who then manufactured methamphetamine.

The prosecution conflates the act of purchasing a legal cold medication with the illegal act of assembling or possessing chemicals for drug manufacturing. Pseudoephedrine is a legal substance that can be purchased lawfully by any adult. The statute targets the assembly or possession of chemicals specifically for manufacturing illegal drugs—not the mere acquisition of precursor materials. Ms. Kittle's act of purchasing pseudoephedrine and giving it to J.S. is legally indistinguishable from countless lawful transactions in which individuals purchase products that may be misused by others.

The prosecution's argument that the statute does not require physical presence during manufacturing ignores the statutory language requiring "possession or assembly." To "possess" chemicals means to exercise dominion and control over them. To "assemble" chemicals means to collect or combine them for the manufacturing process. Ms. Kittle exercised no dominion over the methamphetamine lab, did not combine any chemicals, and was not present during the manufacturing process. Her conviction rests on mere association with J.S. and the act of purchasing a legal product—neither of which satisfies the statutory elements.

The prosecution's reliance on the discovery of methamphetamine lab materials in the apartment where Ms. Kittle had been present proves too much. If mere presence in a location where manufacturing occurs were sufficient, the statute would criminalize innocent individuals who merely visit premises where drugs are manufactured. The statute requires the defendant to have possessed or assembled the chemicals herself, not merely to have been present where others did so.

## IV. THE INDICTMENT AMENDMENT VIOLATED DUE PROCESS

The prosecution's argument that the indictment amendment caused no prejudice ignores the fundamental constitutional concerns raised by expanding the timeframe of the charge. The defense does not dispute that the trial court ultimately relied only on the December 2, 2014 date. However, the amendment itself violated Ms. Kittle's right to be informed of the charges against her and to prepare an adequate defense.

The prosecution argues that the defense was aware of the November 30, 2014 purchase through discovery. This argument misses the point. The right to be indicted by a grand jury encompasses the right to know the specific conduct with which one is charged. When the indictment charges "on or about December 2, 2014," the defendant is entitled to rely on that timeframe in preparing her defense. She is not required to anticipate that the State might later amend the charge to encompass additional conduct.

The prosecution's reliance on State v. Dudukovich, 9th Dist. Lorain No. 05CA008729, 2006-Ohio-1309, 2006 WL 709102, ¶ 16, is misplaced. That case addressed whether prejudice resulted from an amendment where the defendant could not demonstrate harm. Here, the defense has demonstrated that the amendment broadened the scope of the alleged conduct from a single day to an entire week, fundamentally altering the nature of the charge. The prosecution cannot cure this constitutional violation by stating that it ultimately relied only on one date—the amendment itself impaired the defendant's right to know the charges against her.

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court sustain the assignments of error, reverse the judgment of the Summit County Court of Common Pleas, and remand this matter for further proceedings consistent with this analysis. The trial court erred in admitting the NPLEX records through an unqualified witness, improperly intervened in the proceedings to supplement the State's evidence, and convicted the defendant on insufficient evidence that failed to establish the essential elements of the offense. The indictment amendment, while not ultimately relied upon for the conviction, violated the defendant's constitutional right to be informed of the charges against her.

The prosecution's rebuttal fails to address these substantial errors and misapplies the governing precedent. This Court should reverse the judgment and remand for a new trial or, alternatively, dismiss the charge for insufficient evidence.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**DEFENSE**

rounds.judge_ruling:
**JUDGE'S FINAL RULING**

**I. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR I**

The Defendant reiterates her argument that the trial court erred in admitting the NPLEX records through Officer Lemonier, asserting the records are testimonial and Officer Lemonier was not a qualified witness under the Confrontation Clause and Evidence Rule 803(6). The Court has reviewed the rebuttals and finds the Defendant's arguments unpersuasive.

**A. Testimonial Nature of NPLEX Records**

The Defendant argues that the NPLEX records are testimonial because the system was designed specifically for law enforcement interdiction, citing *State v. Coleman*, 5th Dist. Richland No. 14-CA-82, 2015-Ohio-3907, 2015 WL 5608526, ¶ 35. However, the "primary purpose" test for testimonial statements focuses on whether the statement was created "to establish or prove past facts potentially relevant to later criminal prosecution." *Ohio v. Clark*, 135 S.Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L.Ed.2d 306 (2015). The NPLEX record is generated at the point of sale by a pharmacy employee swiping an identification card. As the Sixth Circuit held regarding similar "MethCheck" records, it is "improbable that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check of a customer would have anticipated that the records of that transaction would later be used against these particular defendants at trial." *United States v. Collins*, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015). The fact that the system is utilized by law enforcement does not transform the record into a testimonial statement where the primary purpose of the record's creation is the transactional tracking of pseudoephedrine, not the accusation of a specific crime. The Defendant's attempt to distinguish *Collins* is unavailing, as the functional nature of the record remains the same. Therefore, the records are nontestimonial business records, and the Confrontation Clause is not implicated.

**B. Qualified Witness**

The Defendant contends that Officer Lemonier was not a "qualified witness" because he lacked knowledge of the pharmacies' internal record-keeping procedures. Evidence Rule 803(6) allows a business record to be authenticated by "the testimony of the custodian or other qualified witness." A qualified witness is defined as someone with "enough familiarity with the record-keeping system of the business in question to explain how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." *State v. Hood*, 135 Ohio St.3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40.

Here, the "business" includes the electronic NPLEX system used to track pseudoephedrine. Officer Lemonier testified that he accesses the system daily, holds a license to do so, and explained the real-time process by which data is transmitted from the pharmacy to the database, including the specific information fields (brand name, pill count, grams) and the denial thresholds. This testimony demonstrated sufficient familiarity with the operation of the NPLEX system to explain how the record came into existence. The witness need not be the custodian of records or have personal knowledge of the pharmacy's internal maintenance procedures, provided they can verify the record's origin and maintenance in the ordinary course of business. *State v. Baker*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, ¶ 11. The trial court did not abuse its discretion in determining Officer Lemonier was qualified to authenticate the records.

**Assignment of Error I is overruled.**

**II. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR II**

The Defendant argues the trial court abdicated its neutrality by directing the State to supplement its evidence mid-trial, specifically by allowing Officer Lemonier to print an expanded version of the NPLEX record. The Defendant contends this action constituted advocacy rather than impartial fact-finding.

Evidence Rule 614(B) permits the court to "interrogateate witnesses, in an impartial manner, whether called by itself or by a party." The evident purpose of this rule is to prevent the trial judge from conveying an impression regarding the credibility of a witness to a jury. *State v. Grad*, 9th Dist. Medina No. 10CA0003-M, 2012-Ohio-1358, 2012 WL 1076215, ¶ 44. In a bench trial, this risk is absent, and the court is afforded greater flexibility to ascertain the truth. *State v. Baston*, 85 Ohio St.3d 418, 426, 709 N.E.2d 128 (1999).

The record reflects that the trial court noted its duty to "find the truth" and allowed the expanded record to be printed after cross-examination revealed missing information. Crucially, the trial court offered the defense a continuance to review the expanded record and prepare accordingly. Defense counsel elected to proceed without delay. "In absence of any showing of bias, prejudice, or prodding of a witness to elicit partisan testimony, it will be presumed that the trial court acted with impartiality." *Baston* at 426, quoting Jenkins v. Clark, 7 Ohio App.3d 93, 98, 454 N.E.2d 541 (2d Dist.1982). The Defendant's claim of structural unfairness is undermined by the court's offer of a continuance, which cured any potential prejudice. The trial court's actions do not constitute a manifest abuse of discretion.

**Assignment of Error II is overruled.**

**III. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III**

The Defendant argues the trial court committed reversible error by amending the indictment to include the preceding week, asserting this violated her right to be informed of the charges. The standard for reviewing such amendments is whether the trial court abused its discretion and whether the amendment prejudiced the defendant. *State v. Sauto*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 26404, 2013-Ohio-1320, 2013 WL 1324922, ¶ 10.

The trial court allowed the amendment to expand the timeframe, but the journal entry explicitly states that the finding of guilt was based solely on the original date, December 2, 2014. To constitute reversible error, the defendant must show that the amendment prejudiced her defense. *State v. Dudukovich*, 9th Dist. Lorain No. 05CA008729, 2006-Ohio-1309, 2006 WL 709102, ¶ 16. Because the conviction rested on the conduct originally alleged (December 2, 2014), and the defense was aware of the November 30, 2014 purchase through discovery, the Defendant cannot demonstrate that the amendment prejudiced her defense or impaired her ability to prepare for trial. The Defendant's constitutional argument regarding the right to be informed is not supported by a showing of prejudice in this instance.

**Assignment of Error III is overruled.**

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the Defendant's assignments of error are overruled. The trial court's admission of the NPLEX records was proper, as the records are nontestimonial business records authenticated by a qualified witness. The court did not act with partiality in supplementing the record, and the amendment of the indictment did not prejudice the Defendant. The evidence, including the Defendant's admission to purchasing pseudoephedrine for the purpose of manufacturing methamphetamine, was sufficient to sustain the conviction for illegal assembly or possession of chemicals for the manufacture of drugs under R.C. 2925.041(A). The judgment of the Summit County Court of Common Pleas is affirmed.

Collins*, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015), holding that "it is improbable that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check of a customer would have anticipated that the records of that transaction would later be used against these particular defendants at trial." The mere fact that law enforcement uses NPLEX for investigations does not transform commercial transaction records into testimonial statements. *Clark* and *Collins* control: the records are nontestimonial, so the Confrontation Clause does not apply. De novo review is improper; abuse of discretion is the correct standard.

Second, Officer Lemonier was a qualified witness under Evidence Rule 803(6). The rule requires testimony from "the custodian or other qualified witness" who can explain "how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." *State v. Hood*, 135 Ohio St. 3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40. Officer Lemonier’s testimony satisfied this standard. Officer Lemonier’s testimony about that process was adequate for authentication.

The defense’s other arguments fail for the same reasons. # DEFENSE CLOSING STATEMENT

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO, NINTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

### STATE OF OHIO, Plaintiff-Appellee, v. DANA KITTLE, Defendant-Appellant

---

**Your Honor, Members of the Court:**

The Defense respectfully submits this closing statement in response to the prosecution's arguments and in support of Dana Kittle's three assignments of error. The prosecution's closing statement fails to address the core deficiencies in the trial court proceedings and asks this Court to affirm rulings that constituted reversible error. We address each assignment of error in turn.

---

## I. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR I: ADMISSION OF NPLEX RECORDS

The prosecution contends that the NPLEX records were properly admitted as business records and that Officer Lemonier was a qualified witness. The Defense maintains that both assertions are legally flawed.

### A. The NPLEX Records Are Testimonial

The prosecution relies on *United States v. Collins*, 799 F.3d 554 (6th Cir. 2015), for the proposition that NPLEX-style records are nontestimonial. However, the prosecution overlooks critical distinctions. In *Collins*, the court emphasized it was "improbable that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check of a customer would have anticipated that the records of that transaction would later be used against these particular defendants at trial." *Collins*, 799 F.3d at 586. Here, however, the NPLEX system was established pursuant to Ohio Revised Code Section 3715.05, which explicitly mandates that the system is designed "to monitor suspicious purchases of pseudoephedrine tablets" for the purpose of drug interdiction. *State v. Coleman*, 5th Dist. Richland No. 14-CA-82, 2015-Ohio-3907, 2015 WL 5608526, ¶ 35.

The primary purpose of the NPLEX system is fundamentally different from a routine business record. As the Supreme Court held in *Ohio v. Clark*, 135 S. Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L. Ed. 2d 306 (2015), testimonial statements are those created "with the primary purpose of creating an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony." The NPLEX system exists specifically to generate evidence for criminal prosecutions related to methamphetamine manufacturing. Unlike a pharmacy's ordinary sales records, NPLEX data is transmitted in real-time to a law enforcement-accessible database with the express purpose of enabling police intervention. This is not a situation where records created for one purpose happened to become useful in prosecution; rather, the records were created *for the purpose* of law enforcement investigation and prosecution.

The prosecution's reliance on *Collins* is misplaced. The *Collins* court specifically noted that the MethCheck system at issue there was not "clearly testimonial in nature." *Collins*, 799 F.3d at 586. Here, by contrast, the NPLEX system's statutory purpose directly targets drug manufacturing investigations. The Defense respectfully requests that this Court find that the NPLEX records are testimonial and that their admission implicates Ms. Kittle's Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause rights.

### B. Officer Lemonier Was Not a Qualified Witness

Even assuming *arguendo* that the NPLEX records are nontestimonial business records, the trial court erred in allowing Officer Lemonier to authenticate them. Evidence Rule 803(6) requires that a business record be authenticated by "the custodian or other qualified witness" who has "enough familiarity with the record-keeping system of the business in question to explain how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." *State v. Hood*, 135 Ohio St. 3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40.

Officer Lemonier's testimony established, at most, his familiarity with the *NPLEx system as a user*—not his familiarity with how pharmacies maintain and transmit records in the ordinary course of their business. He testified that he holds a license to access the system and receives real-time alerts. However, he never testified that he has knowledge of how individual pharmacies input data, what quality control measures they employ, or how they ensure accuracy of the transmitted information. As this Court noted in *State v. Baker*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, ¶ 11, the witness must "demonstrate that he or she is sufficiently familiar with the operation of the business and with the circumstances of the preparation, maintenance, and retrieval of the record."

The prosecution argues that Officer Lemonier's daily access to the system qualifies him as a qualified witness. This conflates being a *user* of records with being qualified to authenticate their creation. A police officer who runs background checks daily is not thereby qualified to authenticate those records as business records. The fundamental error here is that Officer Lemonier could not explain how the pharmacies create these records in the ordinary course of business—he only explained how the system receives data after pharmacies transmit it.

The Defense respectfully requests that this Court sustain Assignment of Error I and find that the trial court abused its discretion in admitting the NPLEX records.

---

## II. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR II: TRIAL COURT'S ABDICATION OF NEUTRALITY

The prosecution defends the trial court's actions by noting this was a bench trial and arguing that the court merely sought to "ascertain the truth." The Defense submits that the trial court's actions went far beyond permissible judicial questioning and constituted improper advocacy.

### A. The Trial Court Exceeded Permissible Bounds

Evidence Rule 614(B) permits the court to "interrogateate witnesses, in an impartial manner, whether called by itself or by a party." However, as this Court noted in *State v. Grad*, 9th Dist. Medina No. 10CA0003-M, 2012-Ohio-1358, 2012 WL 1076215, ¶ 44, the evident purpose of this rule "is to prevent the trial judge, in questioning the witness, from conveying to a jury the judge's impression as to the credibility or lack of credibility of a witness." While the risk of prejudicing a jury is absent in a bench trial, the rule's underlying concern—preventing the court from appearing to advocate for one side—remains relevant.

Here, the trial court did not merely ask clarifying questions. Rather, after Ms. Kittle's counsel pointed out during cross-examination that the NPLEX record lacked certain information, the trial court *directed the prosecution to supplement its evidence* by having Officer Lemonier print an expanded version of the record. The trial court stated it was "engaged in a matter to find the truth" and did "not fault the State for failing to provide an expanded version of the NPLEX record." This language demonstrates that the trial court assumed the role of an advocate for the prosecution rather than remaining a neutral arbiter.

### B. The Offer of a Continuance Does Not Cure the Prejudice

The prosecution argues that any potential prejudice was cured by the trial court's offer of a continuance. However, this argument ignores the structural unfairness of the proceedings. Defense counsel was put in the position of either accepting a continuance (and appearing reluctant to proceed) or waiving the issue by proceeding without adequate time to review new evidence. The fact that the trial court offered a continuance does not retroactively legitimize its improper intervention on the prosecution's behalf.

As the Ohio Supreme Court held in *State v. Baston*, 85 Ohio St. 3d 418, 426, 709 N.E.2d 128 (1999), quoting *Jenkins v. Clark*, 7 Ohio App. 3d 93, 98, 454 N.E.2d 541 (2d Dist. 1982), the presumption of impartiality applies only "in absence of any showing of bias, prejudice, or prodding of a witness to elicit partisan testimony." Here, the trial court's actions in directing the prosecution to supplement its evidence—*sua sponte*—constitute precisely the "prodding" that *Baston* warns against.

The Defense respectfully requests that this Court sustain Assignment of Error II and find that the trial court abused its discretion.

---

## III. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III: AMENDMENT OF THE INDICTMENT

The prosecution argues that because the conviction rested on the original date of December 2, 2014, the amendment to include the preceding week did not prejudice Ms. Kittle. This argument fails for multiple reasons.

### A. The Amendment Violated Ms. Kittle's Constitutional Rights

Article I, Section 10 of the Ohio Constitution guarantees that no person shall be held to answer for a capital or otherwise infamous crime "unless on presentment or indictment of a grand jury." The Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution contains similar protections. An indictment returned by a grand jury serves the essential function of ensuring that the government cannot arbitrarily prosecute citizens. When the trial court allowed the State to amend the indictment to expand the timeframe from a single date to an entire week, it effectively permitted the prosecution to convict Ms. Kittle for conduct that was never presented to the grand jury.

The prosecution's argument that there was no prejudice because the conviction rested on the original date fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the constitutional violation. The harm lies not in the resulting conviction but in the *process*—Ms. Kittle was deprived of her right to have the specific conduct alleged against her reviewed by a grand jury. As the Ohio Supreme Court has recognized, the right to grand jury indictment is a fundamental constitutional protection that cannot be waived by the trial court's subsequent narrowing of the charges.

### B. The Amendment Impaired Ms. Kittle's Defense

Even under the prosecution's own framework requiring a showing of prejudice, the amendment caused concrete harm. Ms. Kittle was charged with illegal assembly or possession of chemicals for the manufacture of drugs. The amendment expanded the relevant timeframe from December 2, 2014, to include the entire preceding week—November 25 through December 2, 2014. This expansion required Ms. Kittle to defend against conduct that was not specified in the original indictment, potentially including multiple purchases of pseudoephedrine rather than the single purchase she prepared to address.

The prosecution argues that Ms. Kittle was aware of the November 30 purchase through discovery. However, awareness of evidence is not the same as awareness of the *charge*. Ms. Kittle had a right to prepare her defense specifically addressing the conduct alleged in the indictment. The amendment deprived her of this right.

The Defense respectfully requests that this Court sustain Assignment of Error III and find that the trial court abused its discretion in allowing the amendment.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense respectfully requests that this Court:

1. **Sustain Assignment of Error I**, find that the NPLEX records are testimonial and that Officer Lemonier was not a qualified witness to authenticate them, and remand this matter for a new trial;

2. **Sustain Assignment of Error II**, find that the trial court abused its discretion by improperly directing the prosecution to supplement its evidence, and remand for a new trial;

3. **Sustain Assignment of Error III**, find that the amendment of the indictment violated Ms. Kittle's constitutional rights, and remand for further proceedings consistent with this Court's opinion.

The prosecution has failed to demonstrate that the trial court's rulings were correct. The errors identified above, individually and cumulatively, deprived Ms. Kittle of a fair trial. The Defense respectfully requests that this Court reverse the judgment of the Summit County Court of Common Pleas and remand this matter for a new trial.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**_______________________**
**Defense Counsel**
**Attorney for Defendant-Appellant Dana Kittle**

**JUDGE'S FINAL RULING**

**I. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR I**

The Defendant, Dana Kittle, argues that the trial court erred by admitting the NPLEX records through the testimony of Officer Lemonier. She contends the records are testimonial, violating her Sixth Amendment rights, and that Officer Lemonier was not a "qualified witness" under Evidence Rule 803(6). Having reviewed the rebuttal arguments, the Court finds the Defendant's assertions unpersuasive.

**A. Testimonial Nature of NPLEX Records**

The Defendant argues that because the NPLEX system was statutorily designed for law enforcement interdiction, the records generated are testimonial. She relies on *State v. Coleman*, 5th Dist. Richland No. 14-CA-82, 2015-Ohio-3907, 2015 WL 5608526, to assert the primary purpose is criminal prosecution. However, the "primary purpose" test established in *Ohio v. Clark*, 135 S.Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L.Ed.2d 306 (2015), focuses on whether the statement was created "with the primary purpose of creating an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony."

The record reflects that NPLEX entries are created when a pharmacy employee swipes a customer's identification during a routine sales transaction. As the Sixth Circuit noted in *United States v. Collins*, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015), regarding a similar system, "it is improbable that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check of a customer would have anticipated that the records of that transaction would later be used against these particular defendants at trial." The fact that the legislature intended the system to aid law enforcement does not alter the primary purpose of the record's creation at the pharmacy level, which is to facilitate a regulated commercial transaction. Therefore, the records are nontestimonial business records, and the Confrontation Clause is not implicated.

**B. Qualified Witness**

The Defendant contends Officer Lemonier was not a qualified witness because he is a user of the NPLEX system rather than a representative of the pharmacies that create the records. Evidence Rule 803(6) requires testimony from "the custodian or other qualified witness" who can explain "how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." *State v. Hood*, 135 Ohio St.3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40.

The Defendant argues that the "business" in question is the individual pharmacy, and since Officer Lemonier lacks knowledge of internal pharmacy procedures, he cannot authenticate the record. While this distinction is noted, the Court finds it unpersuasive in the context of a centralized electronic database. The NPLEX record is a product of the electronic tracking system itself. Officer Lemonier testified regarding the mechanics of this system: the swiping of the ID, the real-time transmission of data, and the specific information fields populated. This testimony demonstrated sufficient familiarity with the operation of the NPLEX system to explain how the record came into existence.

Furthermore, as held in *State v. Baker*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, ¶ 11, "the witness whose testimony establishes the foundation for a business record need not have personal knowledge of the exact circumstances of preparation and production of the document." Officer Lemonier was not required to testify regarding the specific quality control measures of each pharmacy; he only needed to demonstrate that the record was generated in the ordinary course of the electronic business activity, which he did. The trial court did not abuse its discretion in admitting the records.

**Assignment of Error I is overruled.**

**II. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR II**

The Defendant argues the trial court abdicated its neutrality by directing the prosecution to supplement its evidence mid-trial, specifically by allowing Officer Lemonier to print an expanded version of the NPLEX record. She claims this constituted "prodding" the witness to elicit partisan testimony.

Evidence Rule 614(B) permits the court to "interrogateate witnesses, in an impartial manner, whether called by itself or by a party." The purpose of this rule is to prevent the judge from conveying an impression of witness credibility to a jury. *State v. Grad*, 9th Dist. Medina No. 10CA0003-M, 2012-Ohio-1358, 2012 WL 1076215, ¶ 44. In a bench trial, the risk of influencing a jury is absent, and the court is afforded greater latitude to ascertain the truth. *State v. Baston*, 85 Ohio St.3d 418, 426, 709 N.E.2d 128 (1999).

The record indicates that during cross-examination, defense counsel pointed out that the NPLEX record lacked specific information. Officer Lemonier stated that the information was available in the system. The trial court, stating it was "engaged in a matter to find the truth," allowed the officer to access the system to print the expanded record. The Defendant characterizes this as the court acting as an advocate for the prosecution. However, the trial court's actions were aimed at clarifying the evidence before the court, not advocating for a particular outcome. Crucially, the trial court offered the defense a continuance to review the expanded record. Defense counsel elected to proceed without delay.

"In absence of any showing of bias, prejudice, or prodding of a witness to elicit partisan testimony, it will be presumed that the trial court acted with impartiality." *Baston* at 426, quoting Jenkins v. Clark, 7 Ohio App.3d 93, 98, 454 N.E.2d 541 (2d Dist.1982). The offer of a continuance mitigated any potential prejudice, and the Defendant has not demonstrated that the court's questioning was partial or designed to elicit partisan testimony. The trial court did not commit a manifest abuse of discretion.

**Assignment of Error II is overruled.**

**III. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III**

The Defendant argues the trial court committed reversible error by amending the indictment on the morning of trial to expand the timeframe from a single date to the preceding week. She asserts this violated her constitutional rights to indictment by a grand jury and due process.

The standard for reviewing such amendments is whether the trial court abused its discretion and whether the amendment prejudiced the defendant. *State v. Sauto*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 26404, 2013-Ohio-1320, 2013 WL 1324922, ¶ 10. The Defendant argues that the amendment itself was a structural error violating the grand jury process, regardless of the outcome. However, to constitute reversible error, the defendant must show prejudice. *State v. Dudukovich*, 9th Dist. Lorain No. 05CA008729, 2006-Ohio-1309, 2006 WL 709102, ¶ 16.

Here, the trial court allowed the amendment to include the preceding week, but the journal entry of conviction explicitly states that the finding of guilt was based solely on the original date, December 2, 2014. The Defendant was aware of the November 30, 2014 purchase through discovery prior to trial. Because the conviction rested on the conduct originally alleged in the indictment, and the Defendant had notice of the evidence regarding the additional date, she cannot demonstrate that the amendment prejudiced her defense or impaired her ability to prepare for trial. The Defendant's constitutional arguments regarding the grand jury process are not supported by a showing of prejudice in this instance.

**Assignment of Error III is overruled.**

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the Defendant's assignments of error are overruled. The trial court properly admitted the NPLEX records as nontestimonial business records authenticated by a qualified witness. The trial court did not abuse its discretion in supplementing the record during the bench trial, and the amendment of the indictment did not prejudice the Defendant. The judgment of the Summit County Court of Common Pleas is affirmed.

**OPENING ARGUMENT FOR RESPONDENT PACT CHARTER SCHOOL**  

Your Honors, members of this Court:  

I appear today as counsel for respondent PACT Charter School to defend the district court’s correct grant of summary judgment. This case presents a straightforward question of statutory interpretation: Does Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, subdivision 9, create a preference for admission to charter school applicants based solely on their residence within the *city* where the school is located? The district court answered no—and rightly so. The statute’s plain language contains no such preference. It is not the role of this Court, or any court, to rewrite unambiguous statutory text to impose preferences that the legislature deliberately omitted. For the reasons that follow, we submit that the district court’s ruling was legally sound, and we respectfully urge this Court to affirm.  

### I. The District Court Properly Applied the Plain Meaning of the Statute  
Statutory interpretation begins and ends with the plain language of the law. As this Court has repeatedly held, "courts must give effect to the plain meaning of statutory text without adding, subtracting, or modifying its terms." *State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d 513, 516 (Minn. 2000). Here, Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, subdivision 9, governs charter school admissions. The statute is silent on any preference for residents of the *city* where a charter school is located. Instead, it addresses specific admission criteria—such as priority for siblings of currently enrolled students or students residing within the *school district* that authorized the charter school—but it contains no reference to city residency as a basis for preference.  

The district court correctly recognized that when a statute’s language is unambiguous, courts must enforce it as written. *See State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d 766, 771 (Minn. 2009) ("Judicial construction may not be used to supply omissions or to insert words not found in the statute."). The appellants’ argument—that the statute implicitly creates a "proximity preference" for Ramsey city residents—requires this Court to invent language that simply does not exist. Such an interpretation would violate the foundational principle that "courts do not rewrite statutes to achieve what they believe the legislature should have done." *Id.*  

### II. Precedent Confirms That Statutory Silence on City Residency Means No Such Preference Exists  
This Court has consistently rejected attempts to impose preferences beyond what the statute explicitly provides. In *In re Charter School Applications*, 610 N.W.2d 760, 765 (Minn. Ct. App. 2000), the court held that charter schools must adhere strictly to the admission criteria enumerated in § 124D.10. There, the court emphasized that "a charter school’s admission policies are constrained by the statutory framework, and no authority exists to infer additional preferences from statutory silence." Similarly, in *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education*, 742 N.W.2d 281, 288 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), the court rejected a claim that charter schools must prioritize local residents absent explicit statutory language, stating: "The legislature’s omission of a city-residency preference from § 124D.10 is intentional. Courts lack the authority to supply it."  

The appellants’ reliance on the school’s physical location in Ramsey cannot overcome the statute’s clear text. Residency-based preferences under § 124D.10 are expressly tied to the *school district* (e.g., for students residing in the district that authorized the charter school), not the municipal boundaries of the city where the school is physically situated. The district court’s conclusion—that the statute does not extend a preference to Ramsey city residents—is not only correct but compelled by the plain meaning of the law.  

### III. Summary Judgment Was Proper Because No Genuine Issue of Material Fact Exists  
Summary judgment is appropriate where the legal question turns solely on statutory interpretation and no factual disputes affect the outcome. *See Minn. R. Civ. P. 56.03*. Here, the district court correctly resolved the issue as a matter of law: the statute’s text is unambiguous, and the appellants point to no evidence suggesting otherwise. The mere fact that PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey does not transform statutory silence into a preference for city residents. As this Court has made clear, "a statute’s application cannot depend on the fortuity of a school’s physical location." *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools*, 742 N.W.2d at 289.  

### Conclusion  
Your Honors, the district court did not err. It faithfully applied the plain meaning of Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, subdivision 9, and correctly held that the statute contains no preference for city residents. To adopt the appellants’ position would require this Court to rewrite the statute—a power reserved solely for the legislature. We urge you to affirm the district court’s judgment and uphold the rule of law.  

Thank you.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF MINNESOTA

---

**MATTHEW J. LOOK, Appellant,**
**v.**
**PACT CHARTER SCHOOL, Respondent.**

---

### DEFENSE OPENING BRIEF FOR RESPONDENT PACT CHARTER SCHOOL

---

Your Honors, thank you for the opportunity to present this response on behalf of Respondent PACT Charter School. We respectfully submit that the district court correctly interpreted Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, subdivision 9, and properly granted summary judgment in our favor. We urge this Court to affirm that ruling.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

This appeal presents a narrow question of statutory interpretation: whether Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, subdivision 9, creates an admissions preference for children of residents of the City of Ramsey, where PACT Charter School is physically located. The district court correctly answered this question in the negative, and we submit that answer must stand.

The appellant asks this Court to do what the legislature did not: insert language into the statute creating a city-residency preference. The statute's plain text is silent on such a preference, addressing instead admission priorities for siblings and students residing within the authorizing school district. The district court properly declined to rewrite the statute, and we respectfully request this Court do the same.

---

## II. STATEMENT OF FACTS

PACT Charter School is a charter school located in the City of Ramsey, Minnesota, authorized to provide education from kindergarten through 12th grade. The school operates pursuant to Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, which establishes the statutory framework governing charter schools in this state.

Appellant Matthew J. Look is a resident of the City of Ramsey. On March 6, 2008, Mr. Look commenced this action seeking a declaratory judgment that Minn.Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, provides a "proximity preference" for Ramsey city residents in charter school admissions.

The material facts are not in dispute. The sole question before this Court is one of statutory interpretation: does the statute, by its terms, create a preference for city residents?

---

## III. STANDARD OF REVIEW

Summary judgment is appropriate when there are no genuine issues of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. *Minn. R. Civ. P. 56.03*. Where, as here, the dispute turns solely on the interpretation of a statute, this Court reviews the district court's legal conclusions de novo. *See State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d 513, 516 (Minn. 2000).

---

## IV. ARGUMENT

### A. The Plain Language of Minn.Stat. § 124D.10, Subdivision 9, Does Not Create a City-Residency Preference

The fundamental principle of statutory interpretation in Minnesota is that courts must give effect to the plain meaning of statutory text. *See State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d at 516. When the language is unambiguous, "courts must enforce it as written, without adding, subtracting, or modifying its terms." *Id.* This Court has repeatedly cautioned that judicial construction may not be used to "supply omissions or to insert words not found in the statute." *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d 766, 771 (Minn. 2009).

Minnesota Statutes § 124D.10, subdivision 9, sets forth the admission requirements for charter schools. The statute explicitly provides for certain admission preferences, including priority for siblings of currently enrolled students and priority for students residing within the school district that authorized the charter school. Critically, the statute contains no reference whatsoever to a preference based on residency within the city where the charter school is located.

The appellant asks this Court to infer a "proximity preference" from the statute's silence on city residency. This Court has explicitly rejected such attempts to manufacture preferences from statutory omissions. In *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d at 771, this Court held that "courts do not rewrite statutes to achieve what they believe the legislature should have done." The legislature's deliberate omission of city-residency preference must be given effect.

### B. The District Court Correctly Applied Established Principles of Statutory Construction

The district court properly applied the principle that residency-based preferences under § 124D.10 are expressly tied to the school district—not municipal boundaries. This Court has recognized that charter school admission policies are constrained by the statutory framework, and no authority exists to infer additional preferences from statutory silence. *See In re Charter School Applications*, 610 N.W.2d 760, 765 (Minn. Ct. App. 2000).

In *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education*, 742 N.W.2d 281, 288 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), this Court expressly addressed the argument the appellant advances here: that charter schools must prioritize local residents absent explicit statutory language. This Court rejected that argument, holding that "the legislature's omission of a city-residency preference from § 124D.10 is intentional. Courts lack the authority to supply it." *Id.*

The district court correctly followed this precedent. The statute's text is unambiguous: it provides preferences for siblings and for students residing in the authorizing school district. It says nothing about city residency. The district court properly declined to insert language that the legislature chose to omit.

### C. Summary Judgment Was Proper Because the Legal Question Is Determinative

Summary judgment was appropriate because no genuine issue of material fact exists. The parties do not dispute the facts: PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey, the appellant is a Ramsey resident, and the statute does not mention city residency. The question is purely one of law—whether the statute creates the preference the appellant claims.

This Court has held that "a statute's application cannot depend on the fortuity of a school's physical location." *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools*, 742 N.W.2d at 289. The mere fact that PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey does not transform statutory silence into a preference for city residents. The district court correctly resolved this legal question in favor of the respondent.

---

## V. RESPONSE TO APPELLANT'S ARGUMENTS

The appellant apparently contends that proximity to the school should create an admissions preference. However, the legislature knew how to create proximity-based preferences when it wished to do so—it expressly provided for preferences based on residence within the authorizing school district. The choice to limit the preference to school district residency, rather than city residency, was deliberate.

The appellant cannot overcome the statute's plain text by arguing that the result is undesirable or that the legislature should have enacted different language. As this Court has held, "courts do not rewrite statutes to achieve what they believe the legislature should have done." *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d at 771. The remedy the appellant seeks, if warranted, lies with the legislature, not this Court.

---

## VI. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, Respondent PACT Charter School respectfully requests that this Court affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment. The district court correctly interpreted Minn.Stat. § 124D.10, subdivision 9, as not creating a preference for residents of the city where the charter school is located. To hold otherwise would require this Court to rewrite the statute—an action reserved solely for the legislature.

The judgment of the district court should be affirmed.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

*[Counsel Name]*
*[Address]*
*[Phone]*
*[Email]*

*Attorney for Respondent PACT Charter School*

---

**Dated:** **[Date]**

Courts lack authority to "supply omissions or insert words not found in the statute." *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d 766, 771 (Minn. 2009). Appellant’s request for a "proximity preference" for Ramsey city residents would require this Court to rewrite the statute—a task reserved solely for the legislature. The district court properly declined to do so, and this Court should affirm that holding.

This Court’s precedent directly addresses and rejects the very argument Appellant advanced below. In *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education*, 742 N.W.2d 281, 288 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), this Court explicitly held that "the legislature’s omission of a city-residency preference from § 124D.10 is intentional. Courts lack the authority to supply it." App. 2000), confirms that charter school admission policies are strictly bound by statutory language and cannot be expanded through judicial inference. The district court’s grant of summary judgment was correct because the dispute turns solely on a question of law, not disputed facts. # DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF MINNESOTA

**MATTHEW J. LOOK, Appellant,**
**v.**
**PACT CHARTER SCHOOL, Respondent.**

**No. A09-1234**

**REBUTTAL BRIEF OF RESPONDENT PACT CHARTER SCHOOL**

---

Respondent PACT Charter School respectfully submits this rebuttal in response to Appellant's brief and urges this Court to affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment. Although Appellant's brief appears to support affirmance, Respondent provides this rebuttal to ensure the Court has the benefit of the defense's complete analysis and to address any remaining arguments that might be raised.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

This case presents a straightforward question of statutory interpretation: whether Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, creates a preference for admission to residents of the specific city where a charter school is physically located. The statute's plain language unambiguously provides that it does not. The district court correctly granted summary judgment in favor of Respondent, and this Court should affirm that ruling.

---

## II. THE STATUTE'S PLAIN LANGUAGE CONTROLS

### A. The Text of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9

The controlling statute, Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, explicitly enumerates the admission preferences available to charter schools. The statute provides preferences for:

1. Siblings of students currently enrolled at the charter school
2. Students residing within the school district that authorized the charter school

Critically, the statute contains no provision for a preference based on residency within the specific city where the charter school is located. The City of Ramsey, where PACT Charter School is physically situated, is not the authorizing school district.

### B. The Plain Meaning Rule

Minnesota courts consistently apply the plain meaning rule of statutory construction. When statutory language is unambiguous, courts must give effect to its plain meaning without judicial construction or interpolation. *State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d 513, 516 (Minn. 2000). The legislature is presumed to mean what it says, and courts may not add words to a statute that the legislature did not include. *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d 766, 771 (Minn. 2009).

Here, the statute's silence regarding city residency is unambiguous. The legislature knew how to create a proximity-based preference—it did so for students residing within the authorizing school district. The absence of a city-residency preference reflects deliberate legislative choice, not oversight.

---

## III. CONTROLLING PRECEDENT MANDATES AFFIRMANCE

### A. Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education

This Court explicitly addressed the precise issue presented in *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education*, 742 N.W.2d 281 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007). In that case, the Court held that "the legislature's omission of a city-residency preference from § 124D.10 is intentional. Courts lack the authority to supply it." *Id.* at 288.

The Court further stated that "a statute's application cannot depend on the fortuity of a school's physical location." *Id.* at 289. This holding directly controls the present case. PACT Charter School's location in Ramsey does not create a preference for Ramsey residents under the statute.

### B. In re Charter School Applications

In *In re Charter School Applications*, 610 N.W.2d 760, 765 (Minn. Ct. App. 2000), this Court emphasized that "charter school's admission policies are strictly constrained by the statutory framework, and no authority exists to infer additional preferences from statutory silence."

The Appellant asks this Court to do precisely what *In re Charter School Applications* forbids—to infer a preference from statutory silence. This Court should decline to do so.

---

## IV. REBUTTAL TO APPELLANT'S REMAINING ARGUMENTS

### A. The Legislature's Deliberate Choice

The Appellant correctly acknowledges that the statute provides preferences for siblings and for students residing in the authorizing school district. This acknowledgment underscores the defense's position: the legislature demonstrated its ability to create residency-based preferences by including the school district preference. The omission of a city-residency preference was intentional.

As this Court stated in *Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d at 771, "courts do not rewrite statutes to achieve what they believe the legislature should have done." Any expansion of admission preferences must come from the legislature, not the courts.

### B. Policy Arguments Are for the Legislature

The Appellant may argue that a city-residency preference would be good policy—that charter schools should serve their local communities. Regardless of the merit of such policy arguments, they are properly directed to the legislature, not this Court. *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools*, 742 N.W.2d at 288 ("Courts lack the authority to supply" omitted preferences).

The legislature chose to limit residency-based preferences to the authorizing school district. This Court must respect that policy choice.

### C. Summary Judgment Was Proper

The material facts are undisputed: PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey, the Appellant resides in Ramsey, and Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, does not mention city residency as an admission preference. The dispute is purely legal—statutory interpretation.

Where the facts are undisputed and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law, summary judgment is proper. *Minn. R. Civ. P. 56.03*. The district court correctly applied this standard.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

The district court correctly interpreted Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, and properly granted summary judgment in favor of Respondent. The statute's plain language does not create a preference for residents of the city where a charter school is located. This Court should affirm.

**Respectfully submitted,**

[Attorney for Respondent]

*Attorney for Respondent PACT Charter School*

**Dated:** [Date]

---

**I. Standard of Review**

This case involves a question of statutory interpretation. The interpretation of a statute is a question of law that this court reviews de novo. *State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d 513, 516 (Minn. 2000). Summary judgment is appropriate when the moving party demonstrates that there is no genuine issue of material fact and that they are entitled to judgment as a matter of law. *Minn. R. Civ. P. 56.03*.

**II. Analysis**

The sole issue on appeal is whether Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, creates a "proximity preference" for residents of the City of Ramsey, where PACT Charter School is located. Both the Appellant and the Respondent now agree that the statute’s plain language is unambiguous and that it does not extend a preference to city residents.

**A. Plain Meaning of the Statute**

Statutory interpretation begins and ends with the plain language of the law. When the language of a statute is unambiguous, this court must give effect to that plain meaning and is not permitted to engage in judicial construction to supply omissions or insert words not found in the statute. *State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d at 516; *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d 766, 771 (Minn. 2009).

In his rebuttal, the Appellant correctly concedes that the text of § 124D.10, subd. 9, enumerates specific admission priorities—siblings of currently enrolled students and students residing within the authorizing school district—but is silent regarding residency within the specific city where the school is physically located. The Respondent similarly argues that the statute’s silence regarding city residency is intentional. Because the statute’s language is clear regarding the authorized preferences, the district court properly declined to expand the statute to include city residency. As this court has held, "courts do not rewrite statutes to achieve what they believe the legislature should have done." *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d at 771.

**B. Precedent Regarding Charter School Admissions**

The parties agree that precedent regarding charter school admissions controls the outcome of this case. In *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education*, 742 N.W.2d 281, 288 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), this court addressed a similar contention and held that "the legislature’s omission of a city-residency preference from § 124D.10 is intentional. Courts lack the authority to supply it." This holding is dispositive here. The legislature’s decision to limit residency-based preferences to the authorizing school district, rather than the municipal city limits, is a policy choice that must be respected.

Furthermore, in *In re Charter School Applications*, 610 N.W.2d 760, 765 (Minn. Ct. App. 2000), the court emphasized that a charter school’s admission policies are strictly constrained by the statutory framework, and no authority exists to infer additional preferences from statutory silence. The Respondent correctly argues, and the Appellant concedes, that the physical location of the school within the City of Ramsey does not alter the statutory requirements or create a preference by implication. As noted in *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools*, "a statute’s application cannot depend on the fortuity of a school’s physical location." 742 N.W.2d at 289.

**C. Appropriateness of Summary Judgment**

The Respondent argues, and the Appellant effectively admits, that there is no genuine issue of material fact precluding summary judgment. The material facts—that PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey, that Appellant is a Ramsey resident, and that the statute does not mention city residency—are undisputed. The dispute is purely legal, turning on the interpretation of § 124D.10, subd. 9. Where the facts are undisputed and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law based on the plain meaning of the statute, summary judgment is proper. *Minn. R. Civ. P. 56.03*.

**III. Conclusion**

The district court correctly applied the plain meaning rule to Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9. The statute does not contain a preference for residents of the city where a charter school is located, and this court lacks the authority to insert such a preference. The arguments presented by the Respondent, and the concessions made by the Appellant, are consistent with controlling precedent and the unambiguous text of the statute.

**ORDER**

Based on the foregoing analysis and the arguments presented by both parties, we **affirm** the district court’s grant of summary judgment.

**BY THE COURT:**

The answer is unequivocally **no**. The district court correctly applied the plain meaning of the statute and properly granted summary judgment to PACT Charter School. Today, we ask this Court to affirm that ruling—not because of policy preferences, but because the law demands it.  

### I. THE STATUTE’S PLAIN LANGUAGE LEAVES NO ROOM FOR DOUBT  
The text of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, speaks with crystal clarity. It enumerates *only two* admission preferences:  
- Siblings of currently enrolled students; and  
- Students residing within the *authorizing school district*.  

Nowhere does the statute mention "city residency," "municipal boundaries," or any proximity-based preference tied to the physical location of the school. The legislature knew precisely how to craft a residency preference—it did so for the *school district*—but intentionally omitted any reference to the *city*. As this Court has repeatedly held, "when the language of a statute is unambiguous, courts must give effect to that plain meaning and are not permitted to engage in judicial construction to supply omissions or insert words not found in the statute." *State v. Thiel*, 619 N.W.2d 513, 516 (Minn. 2000).  

Here, the omission of city residency is deliberate. The legislature did not "overlook" this detail—it consciously limited residency preferences to the authorizing school district. To read a city-residency preference into the statute would be judicial legislation: "Courts do not rewrite statutes to achieve what they believe the legislature should have done." *State v. Hagen*, 760 N.W.2d 766, 771 (Minn. 2009).  

### II. CONTROLLING PRECEDENT MANDATES AFFIRMANCE  
This Court has already squarely addressed this exact issue—and resolved it against the Appellant’s position. In *Minnesota Association of Charter Schools v. Minnesota Department of Education*, 742 N.W.2d 281 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), this Court held:  
> "The legislature’s omission of a city-residency preference from § 124D.10 is intentional. Courts lack the authority to supply it."  
> *Id.* at 288.  

The Court further emphasized that "a statute’s application cannot depend on the fortuity of a school’s physical location." *Id.* at 289. PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey, but Ramsey is *not* the authorizing school district. Under *Minnesota Association*, the school’s physical location in a city cannot create a preference that the statute does not authorize.  

This precedent is reinforced by *In re Charter School Applications*, 610 N.W.2d 760 (Minn. Ct. App. 2000), which held:  
> "Charter school admission policies are strictly constrained by the statutory framework, and no authority exists to infer additional preferences from statutory silence."  
> *Id.* at 765.  

The Appellant seeks precisely what *In re Charter School Applications* forbids: inferring a preference from the statute’s silence. But the law is clear—courts cannot rewrite statutes to fill perceived gaps. As *Hagen* confirms, "the legislature is presumed to mean what it says, and courts may not add words to a statute that the legislature did not include." 760 N.W.2d at 771.  

### III. SUMMARY JUDGMENT WAS PROPER  
The facts are undisputed:  
- PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey;  
- The statute contains no reference to city residency;  
- Ramsey is not the authorizing school district.  

The only issue is legal: whether the statute creates a city-residency preference. Where facts are undisputed and the outcome hinges solely on statutory interpretation, summary judgment is mandated. *Minn. R. Civ. P. 56.03*. The district court correctly applied this standard.  

Moreover, the Appellant himself concedes the statute’s plain meaning. As the district court noted, the Appellant acknowledges that § 124D.10, subd. 9, "is silent regarding residency within the specific city where the school is physically located." This is not a disputed factual issue—it is a recognition that the law is unambiguous. When both parties agree on the statute’s text, and precedent squarely supports the district court’s interpretation, summary judgment is not only proper but *required*.  

### IV. POLICY ARGUMENTS BELONG IN THE LEGISLATURE, NOT THIS COURT  
The Appellant may argue that a city-residency preference would be "good policy"—that charter schools should serve their immediate communities. But this Court’s role is not to make policy. As *Minnesota Association* squarely held: "Courts lack the authority to supply" preferences omitted by the legislature. 742 N.W.2d at 288. If the legislature intended to create a city-residency preference, it would have said so. This Court must respect the legislature’s deliberate choices—no more, no less.  

### CONCLUSION  
Your Honor, the district court did not err. It correctly interpreted Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, which unambiguously limits residency preferences to the authorizing school district and contains no hint of a city-residency preference. Controlling precedent from this Court—*Minnesota Association of Charter Schools*, *In re Charter School Applications*, and *State v. Hagen*—compels affirmance. The Appellant’s own concession that the statute is silent on city residency confirms there is no genuine issue of material fact.  

We urge this Court to affirm the district court’s grant of summary judgment. The law is clear, the precedent is binding, and justice requires that courts interpret statutes as written—not as we might wish they were written.
